observations.text: In Isa.58.2, Ezra.6.21, and 1Chr.28.9 'seek/worship' sits squarely within the base cultic-consultation/devotion sense of H1875, with no further distinguishing nuance beyond ordinary devotional seeking of God.

disposition.reason: a lexical note: seek and worship in their cultic base sense, no shift

observations.text: M15 (know), M36 (serve), M34 (whole/forever), M47 (heart/mind), M64 (plan), M06 (thought), M30/M59 (forsake), M18 (willing) all co-occur with H1875 in 1Chr.28.9; H1875's own vantage is that the verse pairs two mirrored uses of darash -- human seeking of God and divine searching of the heart -- forming the verse's relational spine that the other M-codes (serving, willing heart, forsaking) orbit as conditions or consequences of that mutual seeking.

disposition.reason: a co-occurrence note: the M-codes beside seeking in 1Ch 28:9 listed, with no link drawn

observations.text: In Esth.6.2, Job.10.6, Ps.24.6, Ps.27.4, Ps.34.14, Ps.35.4, and Ps.37.36 baqash is used in its standard senses (hostile pursuit, investigative search, devotional seeking, seeking peace) with no notable divergence from the base gloss.

disposition.reason: a lexical note: baqash in its standard senses, no shift

observations.text: Other M-codes present in Ps.35.4: M07 (put to shame/dishonor/disappointed), M47 (life), M15/M64 (devise). Baqash (seek after my life) names the hostile pursuit that the psalmist prays will be met with shame (M07); it is the initiating act to which the shame-outcome responds, but does not modify the shame-terms themselves.

disposition.reason: a co-occurrence note: the M-codes in Psa 35:4 listed, with no link drawn

observations.text: In Ps.35.4, H1245 (seek) is an operation initiated by the psalmist's enemies, directed toward the psalmist's life ('my life') as the target — hostile pursuit.

disposition.reason: a co-occurrence note: who initiates the seeking in Psa 35:4, with no inner-being content

observations.text: 1Chr.28.9, Prov.11.27, and Job.39.8 all render darash as 'searches' but span three distinct registers: God searching all hearts (devotional-omniscient), a person searching for evil (moral-negative object), and a wild animal searching for pasture (literal/animal). This triad illustrates the verb's semantic elasticity across divine, moral, and mundane subjects within one surface form.

disposition.reason: a lexical note: darash rendered searches in three registers, with no inner-being content

observations.text: God's extension of the characteristic (his willingness to be sought/found) is shown as both conditional and responsive: conditional on genuine seeking ('If you seek him, he will be found by you, but if you forsake him, he will cast you off forever', 1Chr.28.9), yet also shown as gracious and unconditioned in Isa.65.1 ('I was ready to be sought by those who did not ask for me') -- God's self-disclosure as available to be inquired of exceeds strict conditionality, showing both a covenantal-conditional pattern and a gracious-responsive pattern.

Adjacent characteristics appearing alongside seeking include 'heart/mind' (M47, frequently paired as the seat/manner of seeking, e.g. 1Chr.22.19, 2Chr.15.12, Ps.119.2/10), 'trust' (M19, Ps.9.10, Isa.31.1), and 'forsake' (M30/M59, as antithetical pairing, Ps.9.10, 1Chr.28.9) -- these co-occur with notable frequency, showing seeking is characteristically bound to heart-language and its antithesis, forsaking.

Seeking consistently PRECEDES finding/being found and its resulting blessings: Jer.29.13 'You will seek me and find me'; Isa.55.6 'Seek the Lord while he may be found'; 1Chr.28.9 'If you seek him, he will be found by you' -- the sequence is invariably seek-then-find, never the reverse, establishing seeking as the necessary antecedent condition.

The seek-then-find sequence is causal-conditional rather than merely correlational or developmental: the finding is explicitly conditioned upon the seeking ('IF you seek him, he WILL be found'), establishing a covenantal cause-and-effect relationship rather than a coincidental temporal succession.
"Terror on every side": one phrase in many mouths.
observations.meaning: Meaning: the prophet's word is spoken as a name over a man ("a terror to yourself"). The same words are then whispered by his close friends against him. Implies: in both Jer 20 and Psa 31, the one who hears the whisper answers by turning to the Lord ("But the Lord is with me"; "But I trust in you"). The verses state both answers. In Lamentations it is God who summoned the terrors.

observations.text: Those who fear the Lord gather and speak: "Then those who feared the Lord spoke with one another. The Lord paid attention"; "I am a companion of all who fear you"; "Those who fear you shall see me and rejoice"
observations.meaning: Those who fear the Lord gather and speak: "Then those who feared the Lord spoke with one another. The Lord paid attention"; "I am a companion of all who fear you"; "Those who fear you shall see me and rejoice"

observations.text: Rage at the word
observations.meaning: Rage at the word that lowers the hearers' standing or exposes their guilt. It stops its ears

observations.text: Provoked to wrath: remember it.
observations.meaning: the provocation is kept as a memory to be spoken: to the children, to outsiders, and as the ground of a new promise.

observations.text: Without anger: in prayer, in the overseer, in love.
observations.meaning: anger is named by its absence: from hands lifted in prayer, from one who oversees, from love.

observations.text: When they heard: rage, the body, and killing.
observations.meaning: in all four the verse says when they heard. The rage goes at once into the body: rising up, grinding teeth, stopping ears, rushing, crying out. In three of the four it moves to killing (Luk 4:29; Act 5:33; Act 7:58). In Ephesus the speaker names the trade at risk (19:27). In the council a Pharisee's counsel stops it (5:34–35).

observations.text: Life kept in famine and danger.
observations.meaning: Life kept in famine and danger. "that he may deliver their soul from death and keep them alive in famine"; "the Lord protects him and keeps him alive"; "He does not keep the wicked alive, but gives the afflicted their right"; Joseph: "you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive". Kept alive is joined to fearing him: "to fear the Lord our God, for our good always, that he might preserve us alive"

observations.text: Death comes to all, and is not reversed by people.
observations.meaning: Death comes to all, and is not reversed by people. "We must all die; we are like water spilled on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again. But God will not take away life, and he devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast". "How the wise dies just like the fool!"; "he sees that even the wise die"; "a time to be born, and a time to die"; "it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment"

observations.text: Death spoken of as sleep.
observations.meaning: Death spoken of as sleep. "the girl is not dead but sleeping. And they laughed at him"; "Now Jesus had spoken of his death, but they thought that he meant taking rest in sleep"; "through Jesus, God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep"; "David, after he had served the purpose of God in his own generation, fell asleep and was laid with his fathers and saw corruption"

observations.text: Death named inside a living person.
observations.meaning: Death named inside a living person. "For to set the mind on the flesh is death, but to set the mind on the Spirit is life and peace"; "Whoever does not love abides in death"; "worldly grief produces death"; "Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?"; "For the end of those things is death"; to a church: "strengthen what remains and is about to die"; of false teachers: "fruitless trees in late autumn, twice dead, uprooted"

observations.text: Corruption.
observations.meaning: Corruption. "For you will not abandon my soul to Hades, or let your Holy One see corruption"; "For David, after he had served the purpose of God in his own generation, fell asleep and was laid with his fathers and saw corruption, but he whom God raised up did not see corruption"

observations.text: "The land of the living" and the records of the living.
observations.meaning: "The land of the living" and the records of the living. "I believe that I shall look upon the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living!"; "You are my refuge, my portion in the land of the living"; "I shall not see the Lord, the Lord in the land of the living"; "who considered that he was cut off out of the land of the living"; "he will uproot you from the land of the living"; the nations "who spread terror in the land of the living". Abigail: "the life of my lord shall be bound in the bundle of the living in the care of the Lord your God". "Let them be blotted out of the book of the living; let them not be enrolled among the righteous"; "everyone who has been recorded for life in Jerusalem"

observations.text: The spirit against death while living.
observations.meaning: Already woven (Ch 2 "Death in the living"; Ch 14). No new meaning beyond those places.

observations.meaning: The heart is where thoughts come from

observations.meaning: Thoughts arise unbidden, often at night, and can be tied to revelation

observations.meaning: The bed hosts both deliberate plotting and meditation on God. The same place carries opposite directions

observations.meaning: What rises is shaped from outside: God writes on minds; he gives skill to devise; instruction and counsel form thought; minds can be blinded

observations.meaning: yēṣer ("intention", "inclination") is the same word as the potter's thing formed, and as our frame. The inclination of the heart is itself something formed

observations.meaning: God knows the inclination before it acts ("what they are inclined to do even today")

observations.meaning: Thought as design: a neutral faculty whose direction makes it good or evil (maḥăšāvāh: artistry and plots; mᵊzimmāh: discretion and evil devices)

observations.meaning: Thought as reckoning, i.e. assigning worth. People misreckon; God reckons

observations.text: God also speaks in his heart.
observations.meaning: God also speaks in his heart. Faced with man's evil inclination, he says "I will never again curse the ground" (Gen 8:21). The same fact that grounded judgement in 6:5–7 grounds forbearance in 8:21

observations.meaning: The path: arising → lodging → reckoning → devising → expression (tongue, lips, eyes) → action (hand, feet)

observations.meaning: Responsibility sits from lodging onward. The commands address lodging, devising and saying, not arising; what arises shows the heart

observations.meaning: Thoughts are fully open to God and to Jesus. Jesus perceives inner questioning "in his spirit"

observations.meaning: The inclination can be kept, directed and stayed. David prays God to "keep … such purposes and thoughts … and direct their hearts"; "perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you"

observations.text: Design has three objects: God's house, the king's strength, and one's own ease.
observations.meaning: Design has three objects: God's house, the king's strength, and one's own ease. Skill is given, and what it serves changes its character

observations.meaning: Reckoning that serves release (jubilee, redemption), and trust that sets reckoning aside

observations.meaning: A cold calculation taken up into God's purpose

observations.text: Flow 5: what is devised comes back.
observations.meaning: Flow 5: what is devised comes back. The plan returns on the deviser's head (Est 9:25); the schemer is caught in his own scheme (Psa 10:2); disaster is "the fruit of their devices" (Jer 6:19). God answers "devise wickedness" with "I am devising disaster" (Mic 2:1, 3). It also comes back for good: "The plans of the diligent lead surely to abundance" (Pro 21:5); "Commit your work to the Lord, and your plans will be established" (16:3)

observations.text: People value and regard: "Are we not regarded by him as foreigners?" (Gen 31:15); "Let not my lord hold me guilty" (2Sa 19:19); "who have no regard for silver" (Isa 13:17); "there is no regard for man" (Isa 33:8); "they were considered reliable" (Neh 13:13); God's laws "would be regarded as a strange thing" (Hos 8:12); "The precious sons of Zion" "how they are regarded as earthen pots" (Lam 4:2); "will be counted as cursing" (Pro 27:14). And a person is regarded: "we are regarded as sheep to be slaughtered" (Psa 44:22); "I am counted among those who go down to the pit" (Psa 88:4); Israel "not counting itself among the nations" (Num 23:9).
observations.meaning: The word names an inner act of valuing a person or thing now, rightly or wrongly, and the experience of being so valued.

observations.text: The same word names design as skill: "to devise artistic designs, to work in gold, silver, and bronze" (Exo 31:4), given by God to Bezalel; Huram-abi, "trained" "to do all sorts of engraving and execute any design that may be assigned him" (2Ch 2:14).
observations.meaning: Devising is also craft: a skill God fills a person with, and a trained ability to carry out a design.

observations.text: The counting word is used for what is credited or imputed to a person before God: "neither shall it be credited to him" (Lev 7:18); "bloodguilt shall be imputed to that man" (Lev 17:4); "your contribution shall be counted to you" (Num 18:27, 30); Phinehas, "that was counted to him as righteousness from generation to generation forever" (Psa 106:31).
observations.meaning: These verses use the word's sense of reckoning to one's account, not of looking ahead.

observations.text: A thing can be devised from one's own heart: Jeroboam's feast "in the month that he had devised from his own heart" (1Ki 12:33); "you are inventing them out of your own mind" (Neh 6:8). The purposes are hidden until the Lord comes, "who will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness and will disclose the purposes of the heart" (1Co 4:5).
observations.meaning: What the heart devises on its own can be a rival worship or a false report, and its purposes are hidden until God discloses them.

observations.text: A purpose can be held ahead: "I have purposed that my mouth will not transgress" (Psa 17:3), after "You have tried my heart, you have visited me by night"; "to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast purpose" (Act 11:23); "my teaching, my conduct, my aim in life, my faith" (2Ti 3:10). The mind can be set: "the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God" (Rom 8:7).
observations.meaning: A person can set a course ahead for his own speech and faithfulness and hold it; the mind's setting decides its direction toward God.

observations.text: The plan to harm is named and checked: "Whoever plans to do evil will be called a schemer" (Pro 24:8); "if you have been devising evil, put your hand on your mouth" (Pro 30:32); of the false witness, "you shall do to him as he had meant to do to his brother" (Deu 19:19).
observations.meaning: The schemer is named by his plan, told to stop it at the mouth, and in the law receives what he meant for his brother.

observations.text: God also purposes and does not turn back: "I have spoken; I have purposed; I have not relented, nor will I turn back" (Jer 4:28); "so again have I purposed in these days to bring good to Jerusalem and to the house of Judah; fear not" (Zec 8:15); "the unchangeable character of his purpose, he guaranteed it with an oath" (Heb 6:17).
observations.meaning: Beside the purposes he relents of, God states fixed purposes, for judgement and for good; no verse here explains how the two stand together.

observations.text: God forms a plan and makes it known: "hear the plan that the Lord has made against Edom and the purposes that he has formed against the inhabitants of Teman" (Jer 49:20; 50:45); "the Lord has both planned and done what he spoke concerning the inhabitants of Babylon" (Jer 51:12); "the whole counsel of God" (Act 20:27). It is carried out and seen: "The Lord has done what he purposed; he has carried out his word" (Lam 2:17); "The Lord determined to lay in ruins the wall of the daughter of Zion" (Lam 2:8); and the fathers "repented and said, As the Lord of hosts purposed to deal with us for our ways and deeds, so has he dealt with us" (Zec 1:6).
observations.meaning: God's plan is announced, carried out, and recognised afterward by those it came upon, who repent.

observations.text: Plotting is also turned against God: "What do you plot against the Lord? He will make a complete end" (Nah 1:9); "From you came one who plotted evil against the Lord, a worthless counselor" (Nah 1:11); "Although I trained and strengthened their arms, yet they devise evil against me" (Hos 7:15).
observations.meaning: The same devising is aimed at God, by those he had strengthened.

observations.text: The looking-ahead words are used most often against another person. It is placed in the heart: "let none of you devise evil against another in your heart" (Zec 7:10), "do not devise evil in your hearts against one another" (Zec 8:17). It is done together: "Come, let us make plots against Jeremiah" (Jer 18:18); "In Heshbon they planned disaster against her" (Jer 48:2); "they made plans to put him to death" (Joh 11:53), and Lazarus as well (Joh 12:10); "The soldiers’ plan was to kill the prisoners" (Act 27:42). It is aimed at the righteous and the weak: "The wicked plots against the righteous and gnashes his teeth at him" (Psa 37:12); "who have planned to trip up my feet" (Psa 140:4). It hides behind a friendly word: "Come and let us meet together" "But they intended to do me harm" (Neh 6:2); Saul's bride-price, "Saul thought to make David fall by the hand of the Philistines" (1Sa 18:25). It is pinned on the other side: "you and the Jews intend to rebel" (Neh 6:6). Another pleads against it: Esther "pleaded with him to avert the evil plan of Haman" (Est 8:3; 9:24).
observations.meaning: Looking ahead in these verses is mostly turned against another: devised in the heart, done together, aimed at the righteous and the weak, covered by a friendly word, and met by the plea of another.

observations.text: The will resolves, intends and steers: Joseph, "unwilling to put her to shame, resolved to divorce her quietly" (Mat 1:19), until the angel spoke as he considered; Herod "intending after the Passover to bring him out to the people" (Act 12:4), and the intention was not carried out; "I wanted to come to you first" (2Co 1:15); "the centurion, wishing to save Paul, kept them from carrying out their plan" (Act 27:43); "guided by a very small rudder wherever the will of the pilot directs" (Jam 3:4).
observations.meaning: A resolve can still be weighed and redirected, an intention can be stopped, and one will can stand against a group's plan; the will sets the course of the whole.

observations.text: The will word is used of God, the Son and the Spirit: "anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him" (Mat 11:27; Luk 10:22); "Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done" (Luk 22:42); "For who can resist his will?" (Rom 9:19); the Spirit "who apportions to each one individually as he wills" (1Co 12:11); "Of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth" (Jam 1:18); "not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance" (2Pe 3:9).
observations.meaning: God's will is free and stands; the Son's will is given up to the Father's at Gethsemane.

observations.text: In the Greek the will is weighed against another's: "Pilate, wishing to satisfy the crowd, released for them Barabbas" (Mar 15:15), after "do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?" (Joh 18:39); "when Paul wished to go in among the crowd, the disciples would not let him" (Act 19:30); "when he wished to cross to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him" (Act 18:27); "they wished to set me at liberty" (Act 28:18), until the Jews objected; Diotrephes "stops those who want to and puts them out of the church" (3Jo 10); Paul "would have been glad to keep him with me" (Phm 13), and left the consent to Philemon.
observations.meaning: A person's will is bent to a crowd, held back or helped by friends, overruled by objection or by one in power, or left free by one who could have kept what he wanted.

observations.text: Looking ahead weighs before it acts: a king "will not sit down first and deliberate whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand" (Luk 14:31); "She considers a field and buys it" (Pro 31:16); "consider it, take counsel, and speak" (Judg 19:30). It plans without knowing: "on the chance that somehow they could reach Phoenix" (Act 27:12), "supposing that they had obtained their purpose" (Act 27:13), "they planned if possible to run the ship ashore" (Act 27:39). A plan carries a word: "Do I make my plans according to the flesh, ready to say Yes, yes and No, no at the same time?" (2Co 1:17). Plans part people: "Barnabas wanted to take with them John called Mark" (Act 15:37); Joseph of Arimathea "had not consented to their decision and action" (Luk 23:51). And a plan can be for another's good: "because an excellent spirit was in him. And the king planned to set him over the whole kingdom" (Dan 6:3).
observations.meaning: The capacity to look ahead weighs ability and cost first, plans under uncertainty, binds one's word, can part companions or set one apart from a council, and can plan another's good.

observations.text: God's plan takes in what people do against him without excusing them: "this Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men" (Act 2:23); "to do whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place" (Act 4:28).
observations.meaning: The plan and the guilt are stated in one sentence.

observations.text: The capacity is real, and it does not hold the outcome: "nothing that they propose to do will now be impossible for them" (Gen 11:6); "Take counsel together, but it will come to nothing; speak a word, but it will not stand, for God is with us" (Isa 8:10); "if this plan or this undertaking is of man, it will fail" (Act 5:38); "I have often intended to come to you (but thus far have been prevented)" (Rom 1:13).
observations.meaning: A human plan is real in its reach, and its outcome rests with God.

observations.text: The will word also carries wanting to know and stated wishes: "desiring to know the real reason" (Act 22:30; 23:28); "We wish to know therefore what these things mean" (Act 17:20); "I would like to hear the man myself" (Act 25:22); "I refuse to be a judge of these things" (Act 18:15). Paul's wishes in teaching each come with their reason: "I desire then that in every place the men should pray, lifting holy hands without anger or quarreling" (1Ti 2:8); "So I would have younger widows marry" (1Ti 5:14); "I want you to insist on these things, so that those who have believed in God may be careful to devote themselves to good works" (Tit 3:8); "I want you to know" (Phi 1:12); "so that our joy may be complete" (2Jo 12); "I want to remind you" (Jude 5).
observations.meaning: The Greek will word also names a desire to know, a refusal of a role, and a teacher's stated wish, each given its reason.

observations.text: "he who searches hearts knows what is the mind of the Spirit, because the Spirit intercedes for the saints according to the will of God" (Rom 8:27); "for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose" (Rom 8:28). And a person can refuse it: "the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected the purpose of God for themselves" (Luk 7:30).
observations.meaning: The Spirit's praying is matched to God's will, the purpose is turned toward those who love him, and it can be rejected for oneself.

observations.text: The will turned toward harm: "those who desire to be rich fall into temptation, into a snare, into many senseless and harmful desires" (1Ti 6:9); "whoever wishes to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God" (Jam 4:4). An intention is imputed: "you intend to bring this man's blood upon us" (Act 5:28).
observations.meaning: Wanting set on riches or the world leads into a snare and into enmity with God; an intention can be pinned on another by those set against them.

observations.text: His purpose is before the ages and not from works: "because of his own purpose and grace, which he gave us in Christ Jesus before the ages began" (2Ti 1:9); "in order that God's purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of him who calls" (Rom 9:11); "according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will" (Eph 1:11); "the mystery of his will, according to his purpose, which he set forth in Christ" (Eph 1:9); "the eternal purpose that he has realized in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Eph 3:11); "whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood" (Rom 3:25).
observations.meaning: God's purpose precedes the person and works, and is set forth in Christ.

claims.text: No verse read makes the spirit the subject of "to sin". But the spirit is morally judged: haughty before a fall (Pro 16:18), "spirit was not faithful" (Psa 78:8), hardened by God (Deu 2:30), needing to be made "right" (Psa 51:10), with or without deceit (Psa 32:2), defiled with the body (2Co 7:1). The part Scripture judges most is the heart (D §3.4, §9.2, §11.1–3; C §9.2). The original itself listed Pro 16:18 and Deu 2:30, then set them aside

tell.section: The heart thinks, attends and remembers

claims.text: Scripture locates the source of evil chiefly in the heart: "out of the heart come evil thoughts" (Mat 15:19; Mar 7:21); "the heart is deceitful above all things" (Jer 17:9); sin "engraved on the tablet of their heart" (Jer 17:1). The vice-list catalogue is not yet read (D §11.1, §11.7). Added 2026-10-01: Gen 6:5's "intention" is *yēṣer*, the formed inclination of the heart. It must be read with Gen 8:21, where the same evil inclination is the ground of God's forbearance

blocks.section: Breath lent, and held by God
blocks.text:
## Breath lent, and held by God

Life is held in the breath, and the breath is God's to give and to take back.
- "In his hand is the life of every living thing and the breath of all mankind" (Job 12:10).
- Daniel tells a king who had praised idols that he had not honoured "the God in whose hand is your breath, and whose are all your ways" (Daniel 5:23).
- "If he should set his heart to it and gather to himself his spirit and his breath, all flesh would perish together, and man would return to dust" (Job 34:14–15).
- "When you take away their breath, they die and return to their dust. When you send forth your Spirit, they are created" (Psalm 104:29–30).
- "No man has power to retain the spirit, or power over the day of death" (Ecclesiastes 8:8).
- "When his breath departs, he returns to the earth; on that very day his plans perish" (Psalm 146:4). Thinking goes when the breath goes. "Man is like a breath; his days are like a passing shadow" (Psalm 144:4), and the Lord "knows the thoughts of man, that they are but a breath" (Psalm 94:11).

People say the same of their own lives. "Remember that my life is a breath; my eye will never again see good" (Job 7:7). James asks, "What is your life? For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes." He draws from it a way of speaking about tomorrow: "Instead you ought to say, 'If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that.'" (James 4:14–15). Section 10.7 follows that.

God holds both ends. "I kill and I make alive; I wound and I heal" (Deuteronomy 32:39). "The Lord kills and brings to life; he brings down to Sheol and raises up" (1 Samuel 2:6). When a letter asked the king of Israel to heal a man of leprosy, he tore his clothes: "Am I God, to kill and to make alive …?" (2 Kings 5:7). And between the two ends, he keeps alive:
- "that he may deliver their soul from death and keep them alive in famine" (Psalm 33:19)
- "He does not keep the wicked alive, but gives the afflicted their right" (Job 36:6)
- Joseph to his brothers: "you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive" (Genesis 50:20)
- Moses joins it to the fear of God: "to fear the Lord our God, for our good always, that he might preserve us alive" (Deuteronomy 6:24)

The breath does more than keep a body going. "But it is the spirit in man, the breath of the Almighty, that makes him understand" (Job 32:8). "The spirit of man is the lamp of the Lord, searching all his innermost parts" (Proverbs 20:27). There the word the ESV renders "spirit" is *nəšāmâ* ("breath"). Words come out on it too. Job asks a friend, "With whose help have you uttered words, and whose breath has come out from you?" (Job 26:4). Not everything breathed out is good: "a false witness breathes out lies" (Proverbs 14:5). Section 10.5 follows that.

The breath can fail in a person who is still alive. After his vision Daniel says, "no strength remains in me, and no breath is left in me" (Daniel 10:17). Zion is pictured "gasping for breath, stretching out her hands" (Jeremiah 4:31). The psalm's last word gives the breath its purpose: "Let everything that has breath praise the Lord!" (Psalm 150:6).

God gives this frailty as a reason for holding back his anger: "I will not contend forever, nor will I always be angry; for the spirit would grow faint before me, and the breath of life that I made" (Isaiah 57:16). A psalm says what the holding back did, and why: "Yet he, being compassionate, atoned for their iniquity and did not destroy them; he restrained his anger often and did not stir up all his wrath. He remembered that they were but flesh, a wind that passes and comes not again" (Psalm 78:38–39). The people lived because his wrath was not stirred. And a whole life can be felt as lived under that anger: "For all our days pass away under your wrath; we bring our years to an end like a sigh" (Psalm 90:9). Chapter 13 follows this.

In this, humans and animals share one lot: "They all have the same breath, and man has no advantage over the beasts" (Ecclesiastes 3:19). The flood fell on "all flesh in which is the breath of life" (Genesis 6:17), and "Everything on the dry land in whose nostrils was the breath of life died" (7:22).

## Living before God

The opening of this chapter said that life is lived before God. Scripture shows it in an oath that people swore by life itself.

"As the Lord lives" is its commonest form, in 39 verses. In six of them a second life is joined to it, the life of the one spoken to. David to Jonathan: "But truly, as the Lord lives and as your soul lives, there is but a step between me and death" (1 Samuel 20:3). Elisha, three times, to Elijah: "As the Lord lives, and as you yourself live, I will not leave you" (2 Kings 2:2). Ittai to David: "wherever my lord the king shall be, whether for death or for life, there also will your servant be" (2 Samuel 15:21). I read the oath as placing a promise before the living God and binding the speaker to it by life.

Sometimes the oath names what God has done for the one who swears:
- "As the Lord lives, who has redeemed my soul out of every adversity" (1 Kings 1:29)
- "As the Lord, the God of Israel, lives, before whom I stand" (1 Kings 17:1)
- Job, in his complaint: "As God lives, who has taken away my right, and the Almighty, who has made my soul bitter" (Job 27:2)

The words of the oath stay the same, but the heart that speaks them does not. David, his anger "greatly kindled", swore, "As the Lord lives, the man who has done this deserves to die" (2 Samuel 12:5). Saul swore that Jonathan should die, and the people swore back, "As the Lord lives, there shall not one hair of his head fall to the ground" (1 Samuel 14:45). Gehazi swore it on his way to take what his master had refused: "As the Lord lives, I will run after him and get something from him" (2 Kings 5:20). So the oath is judged by how it is sworn. "Though they say, 'As the Lord lives,' yet they swear falsely" (Jeremiah 5:2). It is to be sworn "in truth, in justice, and in righteousness" (Jeremiah 4:2). Section 10.5 follows the oath as speech.

God swears by his own life, and the oath carries both what he wants and what he will do. "As I live, declares the Lord God, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live" (Ezekiel 33:11). "As I live, declares the Lord God, I will not be inquired of by you" (Ezekiel 20:3). Paul quotes it of the end: "As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God" (Romans 14:11).

The one before whom life is lived is called "the living God". The name sets him against idols: "But the Lord is the true God; he is the living God and the everlasting King" (Jeremiah 10:10); "you turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God" (1 Thessalonians 1:9). Habakkuk mocks the other side: "Woe to him who says to a wooden thing, Awake; to a silent stone, Arise! Can this teach? Behold, it is overlaid with gold and silver, and there is no breath at all in it. But the Lord is in his holy temple; let all the earth keep silence before him" (Habakkuk 2:19–20). What has no breath cannot be woken, and the one who calls on it "trusts in his own creation" (2:18). Before the living God, the answer is silence.

The inner being turns toward him, or away from him:
- "My soul thirsts for God, for the living God" (Psalm 42:2)
- "my heart and flesh sing for joy to the living God" (Psalm 84:2)
- "lest there be in any of you an evil, unbelieving heart, leading you to fall away from the living God" (Hebrews 3:12)
- "It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God" (Hebrews 10:31)

His life is praised as well as sworn by: "The Lord lives, and blessed be my rock" (2 Samuel 22:47). Section 10.9 follows this.

Scripture counts a life in days, and says what the days are for. Israel was gathered "so that they may learn to fear me all the days that they live on the earth, and that they may teach their children so" (Deuteronomy 4:10). The king "shall read in it all the days of his life, that he may learn to fear the Lord his God" (17:19). The Passover was kept "that all the days of your life you may remember the day when you came out of the land of Egypt" (16:3). The psalmists give the length of their lives to praise: "I will praise the Lord as long as I live" (Psalm 146:2); "that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life" (Psalm 27:4). And a life can be summed at its end. Jacob said to Pharaoh, "Few and evil have been the days of the years of my life" (Genesis 47:9). Sections 10.2, 10.3 and 10.9 follow these.

The world where life is lived has its own name, "the land of the living". There the goodness of God is looked for: "I believe that I shall look upon the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living!" (Psalm 27:13); "You are my refuge, my portion in the land of the living" (Psalm 142:5). Hezekiah, told he would die, mourned that he would leave it: "I shall not see the Lord, the Lord in the land of the living" (Isaiah 38:11). Abigail says to David that his life "shall be bound in the bundle of the living in the care of the Lord your God" (1 Samuel 25:29).

## What death is

Death is the breath gone. "When you take away their breath, they die and return to their dust" (Psalm 104:29). Of the widow's son, Scripture says "there was no breath left in him" (1 Kings 17:17).

It is the end of a life's way. David on his deathbed: "I am about to go the way of all the earth" (1 Kings 2:2). Abraham "breathed his last and died in a good old age, an old man and full of years, and was gathered to his people" (Genesis 25:8).

It comes to everyone. "What man can live and never see death? Who can deliver his soul from the power of Sheol?" (Psalm 89:48). The psalmist asks it inside a plea about God's anger: "How long will your wrath burn like fire? Remember how short my time is!" (89:46–47; 10.9). "Your fathers, where are they? And the prophets, do they live forever?" (Zechariah 1:5). Living forever was withheld at the very start, "lest he reach out his hand and take also of the tree of life and eat, and live forever" (Genesis 3:22). And Job asks: "If a man dies, shall he live again? All the days of my service I would wait, till my renewal should come" (Job 14:14).

A death can go unmissed: of Jehoram, *"he departed with no one's regret"* (2 Chronicles 21:20). The word is the desire word: no one wanted him back.

Joab sent a wise woman of Tekoa to David with a staged plea: "Joab put the words in her mouth" (2 Samuel 14:3). In it she says: "We must all die; we are like water spilled on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again. But God will not take away life, and he devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast" (14:14). Death falls alike on those the world would set apart:
- "How the wise dies just like the fool!" (Ecclesiastes 2:16)
- "a time to be born, and a time to die" (Ecclesiastes 3:2)
- "it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment" (Hebrews 9:27)

The same death is met in different ways. "One dies in his full vigor, being wholly at ease and secure"; "Another dies in bitterness of soul, never having tasted of prosperity" (Job 21:23, 25). Nothing goes with the dead: "For when he dies he will carry nothing away; his glory will not go down after him" (Psalm 49:17); "When the wicked dies, his hope will perish" (Proverbs 11:7). No one knows when it will come: "I am old; I do not know the day of my death" (Genesis 27:2). Yet the Preacher can write that "the day of death" is better "than the day of birth" (Ecclesiastes 7:1). Asaph, who says "I was envious" of the wicked, noticed that "they have no pangs until death" (Psalm 73:3–4).

The law names what a death can leave unfinished. A man who has built a house, planted a vineyard or betrothed a wife is sent home from the battle, "lest he die in the battle and another man dedicate it … enjoy its fruit … take her" (Deuteronomy 20:5–7). I read the law as weighing a life by what it has begun.

What lies beyond death is not shown to a person. God asks Job, "Have the gates of death been revealed to you, or have you seen the gates of deep darkness?" (Job 38:17).

blocks.section: What death is > Death in the living
blocks.text:
### Death in the living

Scripture also speaks of death inside a living person:
- **The heart can die first.** Nabal's "heart died within him, and he became as a stone" ten days before he died (below).
- **The living can be called dead.** Paul writes to living people, "you, who were dead in your trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh" (Colossians 2:13; also Ephesians 2:5).
- **A person can be called alive and be dead.** "You have the reputation of being alive, but you are dead" (Revelation 3:1). "She who is self-indulgent is dead even while she lives" (1 Timothy 5:6). Paul speaks of people "alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them, due to their hardness of heart" (Ephesians 4:18).
- **The mind can be set on it.** "For to set the mind on the flesh is death, but to set the mind on the Spirit is life and peace" (Romans 8:6).
- **A person can abide in it.** "Whoever does not love abides in death" (1 John 3:14). And "worldly grief produces death" (2 Corinthians 7:10).
- **A person can cry out under it.** "Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?" (Romans 7:24).
- **A church can be near it.** "strengthen what remains and is about to die" (Revelation 3:2).
- **Works and faith can be dead.** "repentance from dead works" (Hebrews 6:1); the blood of Christ will "purify our conscience from dead works to serve the living God" (9:14); "faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead" (James 2:17).
- **It can lie behind a fair outside.** "you are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful, but within are full of dead people's bones and all uncleanness" (Matthew 23:27).
- **A people can die while it lives.** Ephraim "incurred guilt through Baal and died" (Hosea 13:1). False teachers are "twice dead, uprooted" (Jude 12).
- **Inner things can perish.** "the hope of the godless shall perish" (Job 8:13). "My endurance has perished; so has my hope from the Lord" (Lamentations 3:18). "Our bones are dried up, and our hope is lost" (Ezekiel 37:11). "Courage shall fail both king and officials" (Jeremiah 4:9); the word behind "courage" is *lēḇ* ("heart"), and the verb is *ʾāḇaḏ* ("perish"). "The wisdom of their wise men shall perish" (Isaiah 29:14). "Truth has perished; it is cut off from their lips" (Jeremiah 7:28). "A bribe corrupts the heart" (Ecclesiastes 7:7), with the same verb.

The verses name what brings it, each in its own place:
- trespasses and sins (Ephesians 2:1), "the uncircumcision of your flesh" (Colossians 2:13)
- self-indulgence (1 Timothy 5:6)
- works that look alive: "I know your works. You have the reputation of being alive" (Revelation 3:1)
- not loving (1 John 3:14)
- the mind set on the flesh (Romans 8:6)
- sin taking its opportunity through the commandment: "It was sin, producing death in me through what is good" (Romans 7:13)
- worldly grief (2 Corinthians 7:10)
- the letter: "the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life" (2 Corinthians 3:6)
- hating wisdom: "all who hate me love death" (Proverbs 8:36)

No verse gathers these into one list, and I do not join them into one.

The verses also name the way out. "Truly, truly, I say to you, an hour is coming, and is now here, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live" (John 5:25); "whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me … has passed from death to life" (5:24). God "made alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses" (Colossians 2:13). To believers: "Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you" (Ephesians 5:14). The lost son "came to himself" and went home, and his father calls it coming alive (Luke 15:17–24). John gives a sign that it has happened: "We know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers" (1 John 3:14). "Made alive", below, follows this.

One person can bring it on another. "And so by your knowledge this weak person is destroyed, the brother for whom Christ died" (1 Corinthians 8:11); "By what you eat, do not destroy the one for whom Christ died" (Romans 14:15). Section 10.10 follows that.

The living can also feel themselves among the dead. "like one set loose among the dead, like the slain that lie in the grave, like those whom you remember no more" (Psalm 88:5). "For the enemy has pursued my soul; he has crushed my life to the ground; he has made me sit in darkness like those long dead" (Psalm 143:3). "among those in full vigor we are like dead men" (Isaiah 59:10). "He has made me dwell in darkness like the dead of long ago" (Lamentations 3:6). It is on "those dwelling in the region and shadow of death" that "a light has dawned" (Matthew 4:16).

## Sleep and waking

Scripture speaks of death as sleep. And it gives its hope against death in the same picture: waking.

The books of Kings and Chronicles tell the deaths of kings this way, 36 times: "Then David slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David" (1 Kings 2:10). The sleep is with the fathers: the king lies down with those who went before him.

Job sets a man beside a tree. "For there is hope for a tree, if it be cut down, that it will sprout again" (Job 14:7). The man has no such hope in himself: "so a man lies down and rises not again; till the heavens are no more he will not awake or be roused out of his sleep" (14:12). Job does not stop at the fact. In the next breath he turns to God: "Oh that you would hide me in Sheol, that you would conceal me until your wrath be past, that you would appoint me a set time, and remember me!" And he pictures what he cannot see: "You would call, and I would answer you; you would long for the work of your hands" (14:13, 15). The despair and the asking stand together in one speech. I read "till the heavens are no more" as setting a limit on the not-waking. Job does not draw it out, and I leave it there.

The sleep can be laid on as judgment. Of Babylon the Lord says, "While they are inflamed I will prepare them a feast and make them drunk, that they may become merry, then sleep a perpetual sleep and not wake" (Jeremiah 51:39). The merriment itself leads into the sleep.

In one household a death is spoken of as not waking. Gehazi laid Elisha's staff on the dead boy, "but there was no sound or sign of life. Therefore he returned to meet him and told him, 'The child has not awakened.'" (2 Kings 4:31). Elisha "shut the door behind the two of them and prayed to the Lord". Then "the flesh of the child became warm", and "the child sneezed seven times, and the child opened his eyes" (4:33–35). The return of life is told as a waking.

Jesus speaks of death as sleep. "the girl is not dead but sleeping. And they laughed at him" (Matthew 9:24); Luke adds, "knowing that she was dead" (Luke 8:53). Of Lazarus he says, "Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I go to awaken him." The disciples hear it as rest: "Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will recover." So "Jesus told them plainly, 'Lazarus has died'" (John 11:11–14). The picture had to be said plainly before they understood it. At his own death, "many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep were raised" (Matthew 27:52).

Paul uses the same word of those who die believing, and he uses it to speak to grief. "But we do not want you to be uninformed, brothers, about those who are asleep, that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope." "God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep" (1 Thessalonians 4:13–14). The living "will not precede those who have fallen asleep" (4:15). Of the five hundred who saw the risen Christ, "most of whom are still alive, though some have fallen asleep" (1 Corinthians 15:6). He does not forbid the grief. He sets it apart from grief that has no hope. The hope rests on a rising: "Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep" (1 Corinthians 15:20). Without that, "those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished" (15:18).

Even an ordinary waking is credited to God. David fled from Absalom while "many are saying of my soul, 'There is no salvation for him in God.'" He writes, "I lay down and slept; I woke again, for the Lord sustained me. I will not be afraid of many thousands of people who have set themselves against me all around" (Psalm 3:2, 5–6). The waking releases the fear. Another psalm wakes to God's presence: "I awake, and I am still with you" (Psalm 139:18).

When life is in danger, the picture is turned toward God. Each of these calls on God to wake comes where the psalmist's life is at stake:
- "let him trample my life to the ground … awake for me" (Psalm 7:5–6)
- "Rescue me from their destruction, my precious life from the lions! … Awake and rouse yourself for my vindication" (Psalm 35:17, 23)
- "Yet for your sake we are killed all the day long … Awake! Why are you sleeping, O Lord? Rouse yourself!" (Psalm 44:22–23)
- "For behold, they lie in wait for my life … Awake, come to meet me, and see!" (Psalm 59:3–4)
- "stir up your might and come to save us!" (Psalm 80:2), in a psalm that asks, "give us life" (80:18)

I read these as speaking from how it feels when God does not act. Scripture also says, "he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep" (Psalm 121:4). Both are stated. I leave them side by side. Paul quotes the cry of Psalm 44 and answers it: "No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us" (Romans 8:36–37).

And the dead will wake. "Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt" (Daniel 12:2). The waking is not the same for all. Isaiah sets two kinds of dead side by side: "They are dead, they will not live; they are shades, they will not arise" (Isaiah 26:14), and "You who dwell in the dust, awake and sing for joy!" (26:19). For the psalmist, waking means seeing God: "when I awake, I shall be satisfied with your likeness" (Psalm 17:15). These verses are followed below, in "The body raised" and "Life, and judgment". Job's "he will not awake" stands beside them, and I do not reconcile the two.

blocks.section: The body raised > Believed, questioned, denied
blocks.text:
### Believed, questioned, denied

The raising of the dead is not only told. It is met, and the verses show how people met it.
- **Denied.** Luke notes that "the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit" (Acts 23:8). They brought Jesus a woman who had been married to seven brothers: "In the resurrection, therefore, of the seven, whose wife will she be?" (Matthew 22:28). He named the cause of their error: "You are wrong, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God" (22:29). He answered from God's own words to Moses, "I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob" (Mark 12:26), and Luke adds, "Now he is not God of the dead, but of the living, for all live to him" (Luke 20:38).
- **Questioned, and understood later.** Coming down the mountain, the disciples "kept the matter to themselves, questioning what this rising from the dead might mean" (Mark 9:10). At the empty tomb, "as yet they did not understand the Scripture, that he must rise from the dead" (John 20:9). The understanding came afterwards. "When therefore he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this, and they believed the Scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken" (John 2:22). "Then he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures" (Luke 24:45). Paul still writes, "Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead" (2 Timothy 2:8).
- **Known, and believed.** Martha knew the teaching: "I know that he will rise again in the resurrection on the last day" (John 11:24). Jesus turned it to himself, "I am the resurrection and the life", and asked her, "Do you believe this?" She answered, "Yes, Lord; I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who is coming into the world" (11:25–27).
- **Mocked, put off, thought incredible.** At Athens, "when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked. But others said, 'We will hear you again about this'" (Acts 17:32). Paul asks, "Why is it thought incredible by any of you that God raises the dead?" (Acts 26:8). He says he is on trial "with respect to the hope and the resurrection of the dead" (23:6).
- **Faith resting on it.** Paul puts the question to believers: "how can some of you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?" (1 Corinthians 15:12). He lets everything rest on it: "if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins" (15:17); "If in Christ we have hope in this life only, we are of all people most to be pitied" (15:19). Teaching that "the resurrection has already happened" is "upsetting the faith of some" (2 Timothy 2:18).
- **Feared.** The chief priests had the tomb sealed, "lest his disciples go and steal him away and tell the people, 'He has risen from the dead'" (Matthew 27:64). When Herod heard of Jesus he said, "John, whom I beheaded, has been raised" (Mark 6:16), and "he was perplexed" (Luke 9:7). I read Herod's word as his conscience speaking, because it names the beheading.
- **A sign that moves people.** When John asked from prison, "Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?", part of the answer was that "the dead are raised up" (Matthew 11:3, 5). After Lazarus was raised, "the chief priests made plans to put Lazarus to death as well, because on account of him many of the Jews were going away and believing in Jesus" (John 12:10–11).

### Christ first

"But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep" (1 Corinthians 15:20). "For as by a man came death, by a man has come also the resurrection of the dead" (15:21). "For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive. But each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then at his coming those who belong to Christ" (15:22–23). He is "the firstborn from the dead" (Colossians 1:18). "God raised the Lord and will also raise us up by his power" (1 Corinthians 6:14). Peter says death could not keep him: "God raised him up, loosing the pangs of death, because it was not possible for him to be held by it" (Acts 2:24). He and Paul read the psalm of him: "For you will not abandon my soul to Hades, or let your Holy One see corruption" (Acts 2:27). "For David, after he had served the purpose of God in his own generation, fell asleep and was laid with his fathers and saw corruption, but he whom God raised up did not see corruption" (Acts 13:36–37).

The Gospels show his risen body. They do not define it.
- **He could be touched, and he ate.** When the disciples "thought they saw a spirit", he said, "See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me, and see. For a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have" (Luke 24:37, 39). They gave him broiled fish, "and he took it and ate before them" (24:42–43). The apostles "ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead" (Acts 10:41). To Thomas he said, "put out your hand, and place it in my side" (John 20:27).
- **He came and went.** With "the doors being locked … Jesus came and stood among them" (John 20:19). At Emmaus "their eyes were opened, and they recognized him. And he vanished from their sight" (Luke 24:31).
- **He was not known at once.** On the road, "their eyes were kept from recognizing him" (Luke 24:16). Mary "saw Jesus standing, but she did not know that it was Jesus" (John 20:14). At the lake, "the disciples did not know that it was Jesus" (21:4).

Paul also writes, "flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable" (1 Corinthians 15:50). Scripture states both: flesh and bones that can be touched, and flesh and blood that cannot inherit. I leave them side by side.

## The heart speaks to itself

The heart is the place where a person talks without a voice. Scripture says, over and over, that someone "said in his heart":

- Abraham laughed and "said to himself" (Genesis 17:17).
- Esau planned murder in his heart (Genesis 27:41).
- The fool "says in his heart, 'There is no God'" (Psalm 14:1).
- "Beware lest you say in your heart, 'My power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth'" (Deuteronomy 8:17).
- Babylon is told that she says "in your heart, 'I am, and there is no one besides me'" (Isaiah 47:8).

Many of these sentences are verdicts. When I gathered them together, they fell into a few kinds.

- **About God.** "There is no God" (Psalm 14:1). "God has forgotten, he has hidden his face, he will never see it" (Psalm 10:11). "The Lord will not do good, nor will he do ill" (Zephaniah 1:12).
- **About myself.** "I shall not be moved; throughout all generations I shall not meet adversity" (Psalm 10:6). "I will ascend to heaven" (Isaiah 14:13). "Who will bring me down to the ground?" (Obadiah 3). "I sit as a queen, I am no widow, and mourning I shall never see" (Revelation 18:7; 10.15).
- **Taking the credit.** "My power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth" (Deuteronomy 8:17). "It is because of my righteousness that the Lord has brought me in to possess this land" (Deuteronomy 9:4).
- **Fear.** "These nations are greater than I. How can I dispossess them?" (Deuteronomy 7:17). "Now I shall perish one day by the hand of Saul" (1 Samuel 27:1).
- **Enquiry.** The Preacher uses his inner speech to test life: "I said in my heart, 'Come now, I will test you with pleasure; enjoy yourself.' But behold, this also was vanity" (Ecclesiastes 2:1).

And what the heart fails to say can be as telling as what it says: "They do not say in their hearts, 'Let us fear the Lord our God, who gives the rain in its season'" (Jeremiah 5:24).

Scripture does not leave these sentences alone. It forbids some ("Do not say in your heart", Deuteronomy 9:4) and answers others, and the sentences lead to deeds. Chapter 10 follows that path. Even God is said to speak in his heart (Genesis 8:21; Chapter 11).

The same inner speech can be turned toward God. Hannah "was speaking in her heart; only her lips moved, and her voice was not heard" (1 Samuel 1:13). Abraham's servant says, "Before I had finished speaking in my heart, behold, Rebekah came out" (Genesis 24:45). The prayer was complete, and answered, before a word was spoken aloud. The opposite is true as well: "They do not cry to me from the heart, but they wail upon their beds" (Hosea 7:14).

blocks.section: The heart thinks, attends and remembers
blocks.text:
## The heart thinks, attends and remembers

Much of what we would call the mind, Scripture calls the heart. Here I am concerned with the heart as the *place* of thinking. What thinking itself does (arising, weighing, devising, meditating) I take up in Chapter 10.4.

- **It plans.** "The heart of man plans his way, but the Lord establishes his steps" (Proverbs 16:9). "Many are the plans in the mind [heart] of a man, but it is the purpose of the Lord that will stand" (Proverbs 19:21).
- **It understands.** Solomon asks for "an understanding mind" (1 Kings 3:9). The Hebrew is a *hearing heart*. The prophets speak of people who will not "understand with their hearts" (Isaiah 6:10; Matthew 13:15).
- **It pays attention.** To pay attention is literally to *set the heart*. Haggai's "Consider your ways" (Haggai 1:5) is literally *set your heart on your ways*. The Preacher "applied my heart to seek and to search out" (Ecclesiastes 1:13). The failure is its opposite: "it burned him up, but he did not take it to heart" (Isaiah 42:25).
- **It remembers and holds.** "I have stored up your word in my heart" (Psalm 119:11). Mary "treasured up all these things, pondering them in her heart" (Luke 2:19). Mary's second treasuring comes straight after a saying she "did not understand" (2:50–51). Earlier, at the angel's greeting, she "was greatly troubled at the saying, and tried to discern what sort of greeting this might be" (Luke 1:29). Daniel, alarmed by his vision, "kept the matter in my heart" (Daniel 7:28).
- **It watches what people do with power.** "All this I observed while applying my heart to all that is done under the sun, when man had power over man to his hurt" (Ecclesiastes 8:9).

## The heart and anger

Anger is mostly described by what it does: a face falls, a hand strikes, a king gives an order. When the verses do name the heart in an anger, they give it a part to play, and the part differs from verse to verse. In the narratives, the angry person's own heart is rarely named. In Proverbs, Job and Ecclesiastes it is named often, and there anger is something to be held, kept or removed.

The heart is named **just before** the anger, in the state it was in when the anger came.
- Haman "went out that day joyful and glad of heart. But when Haman saw Mordecai in the king's gate, that he neither rose nor trembled before him, he was filled with wrath against Mordecai" (Esther 5:9).
- "But when he was strong, he grew proud, to his destruction" (2 Chronicles 26:16). The Hebrew has *his heart was lifted up*. Three verses later Uzziah's anger at the priests breaks out with leprosy (26:19).

The heart is where anger is **kept and planned**.
- "The godless in heart cherish anger" (Job 36:13).
- "With perverted heart devises evil, continually sowing discord" (Proverbs 6:14).
- Esau "hated Jacob because of the blessing", and "Esau said to himself" (in his heart), "then I will kill my brother Jacob" (Genesis 27:41).

But the heart is also where anger is **taken to counsel**. Nehemiah was "very angry" at the outcry of the poor, and "I took counsel with myself, and I brought charges against the nobles" (Nehemiah 5:6–7). The Hebrew is *my heart took counsel*. The anger went into the heart and came out as a charge brought in the open.

It can **rage against God**. "When a man's folly brings his way to ruin, his heart rages against the Lord" (Proverbs 19:3).

It **carries vexation**, and can be cleared of it. "All his days are full of sorrow, and his work is a vexation. Even in the night his heart does not rest" (Ecclesiastes 2:23). "Sorrow is better than laughter, for by sadness of face the heart is made glad" (7:3). "Remove vexation from your heart, and put away pain from your body" (11:10).

It is **what must not faint** before another's anger. When the kings came against Jerusalem, "the heart of Ahaz and the heart of his people shook as the trees of the forest shake before the wind" (Isaiah 7:2). The word to Ahaz was: "Be careful, be quiet, do not fear, and do not let your heart be faint because of these two smoldering stumps of firebrands, at the fierce anger of Rezin" (7:4).

The angry can **read another's heart wrongly**. Eliab, angry at David on the battlefield: "I know your presumption and the evil of your heart, for you have come down to see the battle" (1 Samuel 17:28). The chapter shows David was sent by his father with food (17:17–18, 20).

Under God's anger, the verses give the heart several roles, each in its own verses.
- **The heart that provokes it.** "And the Lord was angry with Solomon, because his heart had turned away from the Lord" (1 Kings 11:9). "Do not harden your hearts, as at Meribah" (Psalm 95:8). "They made their hearts diamond-hard lest they should hear the law … Therefore great anger came from the Lord of hosts" (Zechariah 7:12). "Because of your hard and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath" (Romans 2:5).
- **The heart that turns it.** "Now it is in my heart to make a covenant with the Lord, the God of Israel, in order that his fierce anger may turn away from us" (2 Chronicles 29:10). "But Hezekiah humbled himself for the pride of his heart … so that the wrath of the Lord did not come upon them" (2 Chronicles 32:26). Josiah was heard "because your heart was penitent" (2 Kings 22:19).
- **The heart that is called to be torn, or cut.** "Return to me with all your heart … and rend your hearts and not your garments" (Joel 2:12–13). "Circumcise yourselves to the Lord; remove the foreskin of your hearts … lest my wrath go forth like fire" (Jeremiah 4:4).
- **The heart that does not take it in.** "It set him on fire all around, but he did not understand; it burned him up, but he did not take it to heart" (Isaiah 42:25).
- **The heart that rejoices** when God's anger acts for it: "You shall see, and your heart shall rejoice … and the hand of the Lord shall be known to his servants, and he shall show his indignation against his enemies" (Isaiah 66:14).

In two places the heart named is the other person's. Jesus "looked around at them with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart" (Mark 3:5). And at Stephen's speech, "when they heard these things they were enraged, and they ground their teeth at him" (Acts 7:54). The Greek of "enraged" is *sawn through in their hearts*: the word reached the heart before the stones were thrown.

God's own heart is named with his anger too. That is set out in 10.13 (Hosea 11:8; Jeremiah 23:20; Isaiah 63:4).

blocks.section: The heart is hidden, and God sees it
blocks.text:
## The heart is hidden, and God sees it

"The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?" (Jeremiah 17:9). "The heart knows its own bitterness, and no stranger shares its joy" (Proverbs 14:10). Other people cannot fully see into it, and often its owner cannot either. But "man looks on the outward appearance, but the Lord looks on the heart" (1 Samuel 16:7). The word corrects a prophet. Samuel had looked on Eliab and "thought, 'Surely the Lord's anointed is before him'" (16:6). The one sent to choose formed his thought from what he saw. God is the one who "knows the secrets of the heart" (Psalm 44:21). "You discern my thoughts from afar" (Psalm 139:2). He knows the heart's leaning before it acts: "I know what they are inclined to do even today" (Deuteronomy 31:21). He tests it and weighs it: "the Lord weighs the heart" (Proverbs 21:2). People try to hide what the heart holds, and Isaiah answers them: "Ah, you who hide deep from the Lord your counsel … and who say, 'Who sees us? Who knows us?' You turn things upside down!" (Isaiah 29:15–16). Section 10.11 follows hiding and disclosing.

The heart can lead a person away from life itself. "Take care, brothers, lest there be in any of you an evil, unbelieving heart, leading you to fall away from the living God" (Hebrews 3:12). Paul traces being "alienated from the life of God" to "the ignorance that is in them, due to their hardness of heart" (Ephesians 4:18). Chapter 2 ("Living before God", "Death in the living") gives the setting.

The heart is tied to life and death in plain words. "The lips of the righteous feed many, but fools die for lack of sense" (Proverbs 10:21). The word for "sense" there is *heart*. "Make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit! Why will you die, O house of Israel?" (Ezekiel 18:31). And what is believed in the heart is that God raised Jesus "from the dead" (Romans 10:9). Of the heart after death, I have found nothing (Chapter 2, "Soul, spirit and heart at death").

## The human spirit

What does a person's own spirit do, and what happens to it?

**It is troubled and anxious.** Pharaoh's "spirit was troubled" by his dreams (Genesis 41:8). Daniel: "my spirit within me was anxious, and the visions of my head alarmed me" (Daniel 7:15). Jesus was "troubled in his spirit" (John 13:21). Paul's "spirit was provoked within him" at the idols of Athens (Acts 17:16).

**It is crushed, and it faints.** "By sorrow of heart the spirit is crushed" (Proverbs 15:13). "A man's spirit will endure sickness, but a crushed spirit who can bear?" (Proverbs 18:14). "My spirit faints within me" (Psalm 143:4). Israel "did not listen to Moses, because of their broken spirit and harsh slavery" (Exodus 6:9). A broken spirit can keep a person from even hearing good news. Job: "My spirit is broken; my days are extinct; the graveyard is ready for me" (Job 17:1).

**It revives, with food, drink and good news.** After three days without food, the Egyptian servant was given food, "and when he had eaten, his spirit revived" (1 Samuel 30:12). Samson drank, and "his spirit returned, and he revived" (Judges 15:19). When Jacob heard that Joseph was alive and saw the wagons, "the spirit of their father Jacob revived" (Genesis 45:27). In each case, food or drink came first.

**It knows.** "It is the spirit in man, the breath of the Almighty, that makes him understand" (Job 32:8). "Who knows a person's thoughts except the spirit of that person, which is in him?" (1 Corinthians 2:11). The spirit is where a person knows themselves. Jesus "perceiv[ed] in his spirit" what others were thinking (Mark 2:8).

**It is lowly or proud, and it is judged.** "Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall" (Proverbs 16:18). The next verse chooses the company: "It is better to be of a lowly spirit with the poor than to divide the spoil with the proud" (16:19). "One's pride will bring him low, but he who is lowly in spirit will obtain honor" (Proverbs 29:23). "Blessed are the poor in spirit" (Matthew 5:3). The verse places the poverty in the spirit, not in what a person has, and the next blessing is on "those who mourn, for they shall be comforted" (5:4). God dwells "with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit" (Isaiah 57:15). God looks to "he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word" (Isaiah 66:2). Israel was "a generation whose heart was not steadfast, whose spirit was not faithful to God" (Psalm 78:8). The psalm's blessed man is "the one whose transgression is forgiven" (Psalm 32:1), the man "against whom the Lord counts no iniquity, and in whose spirit there is no deceit" (32:2). The no-deceit stands beside his confession: "I acknowledged my sin to you, and I did not cover my iniquity" (32:5). David prays for "a right spirit" (Psalm 51:10). Paul calls for cleansing "from every defilement of body and spirit" (2 Corinthians 7:1). And "the Lord weighs the spirit" (Proverbs 16:2).

This matters because it is often said that the human spirit never sins. It is true that I found no verse where "the spirit" is the subject of the verb "to sin". But the spirit is certainly judged. It is proud or lowly, faithful or unfaithful, deceitful or clean, and it needs renewing.

**It is ruled, or it runs loose.** "Whoever is slow to anger is better than the mighty, and he who rules his spirit than he who takes a city" (Proverbs 16:32). "A man without self-control is like a city broken into and left without walls" (Proverbs 25:28). Self-control is the rule of one's own spirit. Without it, a person is a city with no walls. Anger and the spirit are often named together: "Be not quick in your spirit to become angry" (Ecclesiastes 7:9). And a prophet carrying God's word could say, "I went in bitterness in the heat of my spirit, the hand of the Lord being strong upon me" (Ezekiel 3:14). Chapter 10.1 follows how anger rises and is governed, and 10.13 gives the full account of anger.

**It is gentle, and it is under the person.** "restore him in a spirit of gentleness" (Galatians 6:1). "Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love in a spirit of gentleness?" (1 Corinthians 4:21). "a gentle and quiet spirit, which in God's sight is very precious" (1 Peter 3:4). "the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets. For God is not a God of confusion but of peace" (1 Corinthians 14:32–33): the one who speaks governs what moves in him. And every spirit has one Father: "Shall we not much more be subject to the Father of spirits and live?" (Hebrews 12:9). Humility is in 10.14.

**In anger it is held back, heated, pressed and embittered.** The wisdom sayings speak of the spirit in an anger as something kept cool or let run: "the patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit" (Ecclesiastes 7:8), and "he who has a cool spirit is a man of understanding" (Proverbs 17:27). "He who has a hasty temper exalts folly" (Proverbs 14:29) is literally short of spirit. In the accounts, the spirit is named in other ways.
- **Provoked:** Paul's "spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols" (Acts 17:16). What followed was reasoning: "So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews" (17:17).
- **Pressed until it speaks:** Elihu "burned with anger" (Job 32:2), waited, and then said, "the spirit within me constrains me" (32:18), and "I must speak, that I may find relief" (32:20).
- **Embittered, with the lips rash:** at Meribah "they made his spirit bitter, and he spoke rashly with his lips" (Psalm 106:33). The verse does not say whether the spirit is Moses' or God's.
- **Receiving God's anger:** "the arrows of the Almighty are in me; my spirit drinks their poison" (Job 6:4).
- **What would faint,** and so is the reason God's anger is held back: "For I will not contend forever, nor will I always be angry; for the spirit would grow faint before me, and the breath of life that I made" (Isaiah 57:16). Moses pleaded on the same ground: "O God, the God of the spirits of all flesh, shall one man sin, and will you be angry with all the congregation?" (Numbers 16:22).

**It is stirred, and it is hardened.** "The Lord stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia" (Ezra 1:1). The returning exiles were "everyone whose spirit God had stirred" (Ezra 1:5). Not everyone went; the stirred ones rose. Haggai shows what came before the stirring. The people "obeyed the voice of the Lord … And the people feared the Lord", and they were told "I am with you". Then "the Lord stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel … and the spirit of all the remnant of the people. And they came and worked on the house" (Haggai 1:12–14). The same chapter had them sowing much and harvesting little, clothed and not warm (1:6; 10.6). The spirit is stirred toward destroying too: "the God of Israel stirred up the spirit of Pul king of Assyria" after his people "broke faith" (1 Chronicles 5:25–26), and "the spirit of the kings of the Medes" against Babylon (Jeremiah 51:11). 13.1 (*Stirring*) gathers what the verses say of God in this. And of Sihon: "the Lord your God hardened his spirit and made his heart obstinate" (Deuteronomy 2:30), the same verse saying that he "would not let us pass by him". Nebuchadnezzar's spirit hardened itself with his pride: "when his heart was lifted up and his spirit was hardened so that he dealt proudly, he was brought down" (Daniel 5:20).

**It is willing.** "The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak" (Matthew 26:41). At the tabernacle, "everyone whose spirit moved him" came and brought (Exodus 35:21), and the next verse calls them "of a willing heart" (35:22). David asks for a willing spirit in the same prayer as a clean heart, a right spirit and God's Holy Spirit: "Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me … take not your Holy Spirit from me … uphold me with a willing spirit" (Psalm 51:10–12). The verse does not say whose spirit the willing spirit is. Verse 10 has "a right spirit within me" and verse 11 "your Holy Spirit", but verse 12 has neither "my" nor "your". What it says is that the willing spirit is asked of God, and that God upholds it. 10.7 (*Willing*) gives the account. Caleb "has a different spirit and has followed me fully" (Numbers 14:24).

**It is present where the body is not.** "Though absent in body, I am present in spirit" (1 Corinthians 5:3; Colossians 2:5).

The verbs in these verses are many: the spirit is moved, stirred, fervent ("fervent in spirit", Romans 12:11), willing, crushed, revived and ruled.

The human spirit is spoken of as kept alive by God. Job: "You have granted me life and steadfast love, and your care has preserved my spirit" (Job 10:12). Hezekiah, recovered: "in all these is the life of my spirit" (Isaiah 38:16; Chapter 2).

blocks.section: Flesh in the New Testament: one word, several values
blocks.text:
## Flesh in the New Testament: one word, several values

In the New Testament, flesh can still simply mean human life in the body.

- "The Word became flesh and dwelt among us" (John 1:14).
- "In the days of his flesh, Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears" (Hebrews 5:7).
- "The life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God" (Galatians 2:20).
- "If I am to live in the flesh, that means fruitful labor for me" (Philippians 1:22).
- "A thorn was given me in the flesh" (2 Corinthians 12:7).

But in Paul, and in Peter and John, flesh also becomes something else: **a way the inner person is set**, with its own desires and its own mind.

- "The desires of the flesh are against the Spirit, and the desires of the Spirit are against the flesh" (Galatians 5:17).
- "To set the mind on the flesh is death, but to set the mind on the Spirit is life and peace" (Romans 8:6).
- "I know that nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh. For I have the desire to do what is right, but not the ability to carry it out" (Romans 7:18).
- "I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin" (Romans 7:25).
- "The passions of the flesh … wage war against your soul" (1 Peter 2:11).
- "The desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride of life" (1 John 2:16).

The same letters say what is to be done with these desires. "Walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh" (Galatians 5:16). "Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires" (5:24). "Put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires" (Romans 13:14). Peter speaks of living "for the rest of the time in the flesh no longer for human passions but for the will of God" (1 Peter 4:2). In that verse "the flesh" is simply life in the body, and the passions are what it is no longer lived for. The same desires can be used on others. False teachers "entice by sensual passions of the flesh those who are barely escaping from those who live in error" (2 Peter 2:18); they "indulge in the lust of defiling passion and despise authority" (2:10). And flesh can be an outward mark to boast in: "It is those who want to make a good showing in the flesh who would force you to be circumcised", and "they desire to have you circumcised that they may boast in your flesh" (Galatians 6:12–13).
Jude sets the same acts together: "relying on their dreams, defile the flesh, reject authority, and blaspheme the glorious ones" (Jude 8). Against them he sets the archangel, who "did not presume to pronounce a blasphemous judgment, but said, 'The Lord rebuke you'" (9; 13.2). They "blaspheme all that they do not understand" (10).

Here flesh is spoken of as having desires and a mind: it wants, it sets its mind, it judges "according to the flesh" (John 8:15), and it boasts "according to the flesh" (2 Corinthians 11:18).

The same word can change value within a single speech. In John 6, Jesus says, "the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh" (6:51), and "whoever feeds on my flesh … has eternal life" (6:54). When the disciples take offence, he says, "It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is no help at all. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life" (6:63). Within a dozen verses, flesh is the gift of life and "no help at all".

blocks.section: Lines that are often drawn, but that I cannot find
blocks.text:
## Lines that are often drawn, but that I cannot find

Several confident distinctions are often taught. When I read the verses in their places, they did not hold up. Here they are, one by one.

**"The soul sins; the human spirit never does."** It is true that "the soul who sins shall die" (Ezekiel 18:4), but there the soul means the *person*, the one who answers for the sin. And while I find no verse where "the spirit" is the subject of the verb "to sin", the spirit is plainly judged. It is "haughty" before a fall (Proverbs 16:18). It was "not faithful to God" (Psalm 78:8). It is hardened (Deuteronomy 2:30). It needs to be made "right" (Psalm 51:10). It has or lacks "deceit" (Psalm 32:2). It needs cleansing from "defilement" (2 Corinthians 7:1). If Scripture has a *moral centre*, it is the heart (Chapter 12). The spirit stands beside it, not above it.

**"Animals have souls but not spirits."** The animals are "living creatures", the same phrase as the man in Genesis 2:7. But they also have "the breath of life". The flood came on "all flesh in which is the breath of life" (Genesis 6:17; 7:15), and there the word is *rûaḥ*. "They all have the same breath" (Ecclesiastes 3:19). There is "the spirit of the beast" (Ecclesiastes 3:21). "When you take away their breath, they die" (Psalm 104:29). What marks the man in Genesis 2:7 is not that he has breath and they do not. It is that **God himself breathed it into him**.

**"The soul faces the self; the spirit faces God."** The soul is the part that thirsts for God, lifts itself to God, waits for him and blesses him (Chapter 5). The spirit is anxious, provoked, hot-tempered and crushed (Chapter 6). Each faces both ways.
