**"The soul goes to Sheol; the spirit goes to God."** The verses usually cited speak of the soul being *delivered from* Sheol ("you will not abandon my soul to Sheol", Psalm 16:10; "you have brought up my soul from Sheol", Psalm 30:3). Psalm 30:3 is about a living person rescued from death. Peter reads Psalm 16:10 of Christ, "not abandoned to Hades" (Acts 2:31). Neither sends the soul one way and the spirit another, and the verses that name Sheol or Hades speak of the soul and never of the spirit. And Ecclesiastes leaves the spirit's destination as a question: "Who knows whether the spirit of man goes upward?" (Ecclesiastes 3:21). See Chapter 2.

**"Spirit first, soul second, body third."** Scripture does not rank the inner words. It lists them in different orders for different purposes (Chapter 3). It gives God a soul as readily as a spirit: "my soul shall not abhor you" (Leviticus 26:11), "my soul delights" (Isaiah 42:1). It brings a dead child's life back as soul ("the life of the child came into him again", 1 Kings 17:22) as readily as spirit ("her spirit returned", Luke 8:55).

blocks.section: From a thought to a deed
blocks.text:
## From a thought to a deed

Read side by side, the verses trace a path.

1. **Thoughts arise.** "To you, O king, as you lay in bed came thoughts of what would be after this" (Daniel 2:29). "Why do doubts arise in your hearts?" (Luke 24:38).
2. **They lodge.** "How long shall your wicked thoughts lodge within you?" (Jeremiah 4:14).
3. **They weigh and judge.** "We esteemed him stricken, smitten by God, and afflicted" (Isaiah 53:4).
4. **They take the shape of a plan.** "He plots trouble while on his bed" (Psalm 36:4).
5. **They reach the tongue, the lips and the eyes.** "Your tongue plots destruction" (Psalm 52:2). "Whoever winks his eyes plans dishonest things; he who purses his lips brings evil to pass" (Proverbs 16:30).
6. **They reach the hand and the feet.** "Woe to those who devise wickedness and work evil on their beds! When the morning dawns, they perform it, because it is in the power of their hand" (Micah 2:1). "A heart that devises wicked plans, feet that make haste to run to evil" (Proverbs 6:18). "Their feet run to evil … their thoughts are thoughts of iniquity" (Isaiah 59:7).

No single verse lists these six steps. The order is my reading of many verses together. But the stories show the path being walked.
- David "said in his heart, 'Now I shall perish one day by the hand of Saul. There is nothing better for me than that I should escape to the land of the Philistines'" (1 Samuel 27:1). And he went.
- Jeroboam "said in his heart, 'Now the kingdom will turn back to the house of David'" (1 Kings 12:26). Two verses later, "the king took counsel and made two calves of gold" (12:28). A private sentence became a nation's idolatry.
- The tenants in the parable reason it through together: "they said to themselves, 'This is the heir. Let us kill him, so that the inheritance may be ours'" (Luke 20:14).

The same path runs toward good.
- "When I think on my ways, I turn my feet to your testimonies" (Psalm 119:59). The thinking reaches the feet.
- Joshua is told to meditate on the law day and night "so that you may be careful to do according to all that is written in it" (Joshua 1:8).

There can be a pause on the path, and the pause matters: "The heart of the righteous ponders how to answer, but the mouth of the wicked pours out evil things" (Proverbs 15:28).

**What lodges is not always a plan.** Thoughts that lodge can also act back on the person who holds them. "My thoughts answer me, because of my haste within me" (Job 20:2). "My thoughts greatly alarmed me, and my color changed, but I kept the matter in my heart" (Daniel 7:28). Daniel's thoughts stayed with him, but they did not move on toward a deed. He kept them. So the second step can be a lodging that plots, or a keeping that waits.

blocks.section: The path can start with a feeling
blocks.text:
## The path can start with a feeling

The path above begins with a thought. Scripture also traces one that begins with a feeling, and anger shows it most clearly. Saul is the clearest case.
1. **Something is heard.** The women sing, "Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands" (1 Samuel 18:7).
2. **Anger rises.** "And Saul was very angry, and this saying displeased him" (18:8).
3. **It becomes a reckoning.** "They have ascribed to David ten thousands, and to me they have ascribed thousands, and what more can he have but the kingdom?" (18:8).
4. **It watches.** "And Saul eyed David from that day on" (18:9).
5. **It reaches the hand.** "Saul hurled the spear" (18:11).
6. **It becomes a plan.** "Now Saul thought to make David fall by the hand of the Philistines" (18:25).

Esau's path is the same. He "hated Jacob because of the blessing", then "said to himself … 'then I will kill my brother Jacob'" (Genesis 27:41), and the plan kept the anger warm: he "comforts himself about you by planning to kill you" (27:42).

This path can be broken, and Scripture shows where. God speaks to Cain at the second step: "Why are you angry …? … sin is crouching at the door. Its desire is for you, and you must rule over it" (Genesis 4:6–7). Nehemiah, very angry, stops at the third: "I took counsel with myself, and I brought charges against the nobles" (Nehemiah 5:7). And for Esau, time and forgetting broke it: "Esau ran to meet him and embraced him" (Genesis 33:4).

## The path runs back

The path does not end at the deed. What was devised comes back to the one who devised it.
- Haman's "evil plan that he had devised against the Jews should return on his own head" (Esther 9:25).
- "He makes a pit, digging it out, and falls into the hole that he has made. His mischief returns upon his own head" (Psalm 7:15–16).
- "Woe to those who devise wickedness and work evil on their beds!" (Micah 2:1). And two verses later, "behold, against this family I am devising disaster" (2:3). The deviser meets the same verb coming back, with God as its subject.
- Anger poured out comes back. "Woe to him who makes his neighbors drink — you pour out your wrath and make them drunk … The cup in the Lord's right hand will come around to you" (Habakkuk 2:15–16). Provoking God harms the provoker: "Is it not themselves, to their own shame?" (Jeremiah 7:19).
- It comes back for good too: "The plans of the diligent lead surely to abundance" (Proverbs 21:5). "Commit your work to the Lord, and your plans will be established" (Proverbs 16:3).

## Where I am answerable

The commands meet this path from the second step onward.
- "Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts" (Isaiah 55:7).
- "Let none of you devise evil against another in your heart" (Zechariah 7:10).
- "Do not say in your heart … 'It is because of my righteousness'" (Deuteronomy 9:4).
- "Take every thought captive to obey Christ" (2 Corinthians 10:5).
- "Wash your heart from evil" (Jeremiah 4:14).

I have found no command about what first arises. But what arises is not neutral. "Every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually" (Genesis 6:5). "Out of the heart of man, come evil thoughts" (Mark 7:21). The commands address what lodges, what is planned, what is said and what is done.

Scripture does more than command. It also answers the sentence the heart speaks. "If you say in your heart, 'These nations are greater than I. How can I dispossess them?' you shall not be afraid of them but you shall remember what the Lord your God did to Pharaoh and to all Egypt" (Deuteronomy 7:17–18). The answer to a fearful inner sentence is a remembered act of God.

## How the activities connect

Each section that follows ends by naming the activities it touches. Taken together so far, they look like this:

- **Hearing feeds thinking.** What is heard and remembered is what the heart then ponders (10.2 → 10.4).
- **Thinking passes into speaking**, and speaking is heard, by people and by God (10.4 → 10.5 → 10.2, 10.9).
- **Thinking passes into choosing and into the deed** (10.4 → 10.7, and the path above).
- **Thinking and feeling move each other.** "His thoughts alarmed him; his limbs gave way, and his knees knocked together" (Daniel 5:6) (10.4 ↔ 10.1).
- **Wanting drives thinking.** The rich man's planning serves his wanting (Luke 12:17–19) (10.6 → 10.4).
- **Thinking stands under right and wrong**, and its own thoughts accuse or excuse it (Romans 2:15) (10.4 → 10.8).
- **Thinking happens together**, and shared reasoning can become a shared deed (10.4 → 10.10).
- **Hearing kindles feeling.** "I was very angry when I heard their outcry" (Nehemiah 5:6) (10.2 → 10.1).
- **Feeling drives thinking.** Anger reckons: "what more can he have but the kingdom?" (1 Samuel 18:8) (10.1 → 10.4).
- **Feeling is released in speech**, or turned away by it. "A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger" (Proverbs 15:1) (10.1 ↔ 10.5).
- **Remembering and forgetting decide how long a feeling stays** (10.3 ↔ 10.1).
- **Feeling between people becomes strife** (10.1 → 10.10).
- **Thinking acts back on itself.** Thoughts answer, alarm and weary the one who thinks them (Job 20:2; Daniel 7:28; Psalm 73:16) (10.4 → 10.4, 10.1).
- **Fear drives hiding.** "I was afraid, because I was naked, and I hid myself" (Genesis 3:10) (10.1 → 10.11).
- **What is hidden is drawn out by speech.** "Tell me now what you have done; do not hide it from me" (Joshua 7:19) (10.11 ↔ 10.5).
- **What goes out comes back.** The plan returns on the head of the one who made it (Esther 9:25; Micah 2:1–3) (10.0, the path above).

**Every activity can change character.** The same act of thinking is discretion in one person and an evil device in another. It is a plan against that is meant to bring people back, or a plot against the messenger (Jeremiah 18:11–18). What changes it is not the act itself. The verses point to its direction, the company it keeps, the state of the heart it rises from, its pace, and whether it is brought before God. Chapter 10.4 shows this for thinking, and Chapter 11 (§4) gathers it across all the activities.

This picture is not finished. As I read more widely, I expect it to grow, and to correct itself.

## How a feeling rises

Very often, something is seen or heard first.
- "The men were indignant and very angry, because he had done an outrageous thing in Israel" (Genesis 34:7). They had just heard of it.
- "I was very angry when I heard their outcry and these words" (Nehemiah 5:6).
- "When Haman saw that Mordecai did not bow down or pay homage to him, Haman was filled with fury" (Esther 3:5).
- Paul's "spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols" (Acts 17:16).

What is perceived may not even be true. Potiphar heard his wife's story, "his anger was kindled", and Joseph went to prison (Genesis 39:19–20). The officials "were enraged at Jeremiah" over a charge he had just called "a lie" (Jeremiah 37:14–15). The feeling acts on what it believes it has seen.

Anger often rises where a will is blocked:
- Balaam beats his donkey, and says why: "Because you have made a fool of me" (Numbers 22:29).
- Naaman: "Naaman was angry and went away, saying, 'Behold, I thought that he would surely come out to me'" (2 Kings 5:11).
- Nebuchadnezzar is refused, and "the expression of his face was changed" (Daniel 3:19).

It rises where a heart that was lifted up is checked. Uzziah "when he was strong, he grew proud" (2 Chronicles 26:16). When the priests withstood him, "Uzziah was angry" (26:19). The king's anger burned when "the heart of the king was merry with wine" and his queen refused him (Esther 1:10–12). Chapter 11 follows this threshold further.

And anger rises on behalf of someone else. Jonathan "rose from the table in fierce anger … for he was grieved for David" (1 Samuel 20:34). When Jesus saw the children turned away, "he was indignant" (Mark 10:14).

Before the king's merry heart gave its command, the feast had set every guest free: "There is no compulsion", "to do as each man desired" (Esther 1:8, 10).

# 10.2 Knowing and hearing

Knowing belongs chiefly to the heart, as Chapter 4 showed. To pay attention is to set the heart. To understand is to have a *hearing heart*. To remember is to keep a thing in the heart. The spirit knows the self from within: "who knows a person's thoughts except the spirit of that person, which is in him?" (1 Corinthians 2:11). The soul receives what is known as something good to taste: "knowledge will be pleasant to your soul" (Proverbs 2:10).

**Hearing is the main way in.** The ear receives, and the heart keeps it or refuses it. "All my words that I shall speak to you receive in your heart, and hear with your ears" (Ezekiel 3:10). "Making your ear attentive to wisdom and inclining your heart to understanding" (Proverbs 2:2). When the heart is hard, hearing stops: "Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he would not listen" (Exodus 7:13). "They made their hearts diamond-hard lest they should hear the law" (Zechariah 7:12). A crushed spirit can block hearing as well. Israel "did not listen to Moses, because of their broken spirit and harsh slavery" (Exodus 6:9).

A refusal to hear can stand on a reading of the past. The survivors in Egypt told Jeremiah, "As for the word that you have spoken to us in the name of the Lord, we will not listen to you" (Jeremiah 44:16). Their reason was what they remembered: "For then we had plenty of food, and prospered, and saw no disaster. But since we left off making offerings to the queen of heaven and pouring out drink offerings to her, we have lacked everything" (44:17–18). They had seen the ruin (44:2; 10.13, *Seen and not taken in*) and read it the other way. I read the refusal as resting on their own account of cause and effect.

What is heard moves everything inside. Rahab says, "As soon as we heard it, our hearts melted, and there was no spirit left in any man because of you" (Joshua 2:11). Good news works the other way: "Like cold water to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a far country" (Proverbs 25:25). And hearing is a kind of eating: "Listen diligently to me, and eat what is good, and delight yourselves in rich food. Incline your ear, and come to me; hear, that your soul may live" (Isaiah 55:2–3).

Sometimes hearing is not enough, and the inner being needs to *see*. Jacob's heart went numb at the news that Joseph was alive. His spirit revived only when he saw the wagons (Genesis 45:26–27).

Understanding has a source that Scripture names in the breath: "it is the spirit in man, the breath of the Almighty, that makes him understand" (Job 32:8; Chapter 2). And hearing God himself was a matter of life. "Did any people ever hear the voice of a god speaking out of the midst of the fire, as you have heard, and still live?" (Deuteronomy 4:33). Section 10.9 follows this.

**Hearing goes both ways.** The ear is the way in, and it is also where what goes out arrives. God hears what people say: "You have heard their taunts, O Lord, all their plots against me" (Lamentations 3:61). "Then those who feared the Lord spoke with one another. The Lord paid attention and heard them" (Malachi 3:16). And refusing to hear goes with devising. "I am bringing disaster upon this people, the fruit of their devices, because they have not paid attention to my words" (Jeremiah 6:19). Jeremiah's enemies plot against him with these words: "let us not pay attention to any of his words" (Jeremiah 18:18).

What a person listens to shows what he is: *"An evildoer listens to wicked lips, and a liar gives ear to a mischievous tongue"* (Proverbs 17:4).

Who speaks can decide whether a word is heard. In the Preacher's example a poor, wise man "by his wisdom delivered the city. Yet no one remembered that poor man. But I say that wisdom is better than might, though the poor man's wisdom is despised and his words are not heard" (Ecclesiastes 9:15–16). His wisdom had saved them. I read the verse as saying that what was seen in him was his poverty, and that was why he was forgotten and not heard (10.3).

Hearing can be taken away, and then wanted. *"Behold, the days are coming, declares the Lord God, when I will send a famine on the land—not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the Lord. They shall wander from sea to sea … to seek the word of the Lord, but they shall not find it. In that day the lovely virgins and the young men shall faint for thirst"* (Amos 8:11–13). The famine is not of the word but of hearing it. The bodily thirst comes in the same day.

Before Samuel, *"the word of the Lord was rare in those days; there was no frequent vision"* (1 Samuel 3:1). The word for *rare* is the word for *precious*. When the call came, the boy did not know it: *"Samuel did not yet know the Lord, and the word of the Lord had not yet been revealed to him"* (3:7). Three times he ran to Eli, until *"Eli perceived that the Lord was calling the boy"* and taught him the answer, *"Speak, Lord, for your servant hears"* (3:8–9). The old priest, whose eyes were growing dim (3:2), knew the voice the boy could not yet place. I read hearing that had to be learned, in a time when the word was rare.

Hearing can stop at a single word. Paul tells the crowd of his vision in the temple: *"Make haste and get out of Jerusalem quickly, because they will not accept your testimony about me"* (Acts 22:18). He objected that they knew his past: *"Lord, they themselves know that in one synagogue after another I imprisoned and beat those who believed in you"* (22:19). The answer was *"Go, for I will send you far away to the Gentiles"* (22:21). Then *"Up to this word they listened to him. Then they raised their voices and said, 'Away with such a fellow from the earth! For he should not be allowed to live'"* (22:22). They heard him through the persecution and the vision; the word "Gentiles" ended their hearing. Paul had thought his past would make them listen; the Lord had said it would not.

Ears can be closed to a word that is still being spoken. "To whom shall I speak and give warning, that they may hear? Behold, their ears are uncircumcised, they cannot listen; behold, the word of the Lord is to them an object of scorn; they take no pleasure in it" (Jeremiah 6:10). The act is a hearing that does not happen. "Cannot listen" is followed by what they do with the word instead: they scorn it. Taking no pleasure in it is the measure of the scorn. I read the uncircumcised ears as hearing that lacks the mark of belonging to him. The one who must speak is left holding it: "Therefore I am full of the wrath of the Lord; I am weary of holding it in" (6:11).

Words that are heard can be pictured as tools. The Preacher *"sought to find words of delight, and uprightly he wrote words of truth"* (Ecclesiastes 12:10). *"The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails firmly fixed are the collected sayings; they are given by one Shepherd. My son, beware of anything beyond these"* (12:11–12). A goad drives an animal on; a nail holds something in place. I read the figure as two works of the same words on the hearer: they move him, and they fix in him. Delight is in the search for the words, and the words are given by one Shepherd.

What is heard can also kindle. "I was very angry when I heard their outcry and these words" (Nehemiah 5:6). And when what is heard lowers the hearers' standing or exposes their guilt, rage can refuse to hear any more. Stephen's hearers "were enraged, and they ground their teeth at him … But they cried out with a loud voice and stopped their ears and rushed together at him" (Acts 7:54, 57). James puts hearing first for this very reason: "let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger; for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God" (James 1:19–20).

The same words, read aloud, brought fear to some and none to others. When the scroll of Jeremiah's words was read, the officials "heard all the words, they turned one to another in fear" (Jeremiah 36:16). The king cut it up column by column and burned it, and "neither the king nor any of his servants who heard all these words was afraid, nor did they tear their garments" (36:23–24).

Understanding can itself be dread: "it will be sheer terror to understand the message" (Isaiah 28:19; Chapter 13). And some hold the word in awe: "Princes persecute me without cause, but my heart stands in awe of your words" (Psalm 119:161). Section 10.9 follows those who tremble at his word.

Some things are only understood later. Of God's anger, Jeremiah says, "In the latter days you will understand it clearly" (Jeremiah 23:20). Chapter 13 follows how people read, and misread, what has happened to them.

God also says what knowing him is. Of Josiah: "He judged the cause of the poor and needy; then it was well. Is not this to know me? declares the Lord" (Jeremiah 22:16). It is said against his son, who built "by unrighteousness" and kept back his neighbour's wages (22:13): "But you have eyes and heart only for your dishonest gain, for shedding innocent blood, and for practicing oppression and violence" (22:17). Knowing God is named here in a deed done for the poor, and set against a heart and eyes given to gain (10.6).

Knowing has a beginning, and Scripture names it. "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge; fools despise wisdom and instruction" (Proverbs 1:7). "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom" (Proverbs 9:10; Psalm 111:10). To man God said, "Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to turn away from evil is understanding" (Job 28:28). It also runs the other way. The one who seeks wisdom "as for hidden treasures" is told, "then you will understand the fear of the Lord and find the knowledge of God" (Proverbs 2:4–5). And it can be refused: "Because they hated knowledge and did not choose the fear of the Lord" (Proverbs 1:29). The fear of God is also learned by hearing (10.9).

Learning to fear God takes a life. Israel was gathered "so that they may learn to fear me all the days that they live on the earth, and that they may teach their children so" (Deuteronomy 4:10). The ear decides much: "The ear that listens to life-giving reproof will dwell among the wise" (Proverbs 15:31). God can open the ear himself. In a dream "he opens the ears of men and terrifies them with warnings, that he may turn man aside from his deed and conceal pride from a man" (Job 33:16–17). Chapter 2 ("Living before God", "Delivered from death") gives the setting.

Wisdom, refused, says: "I also will laugh at your calamity; I will mock when terror strikes you" (Proverbs 1:26). And "whoever listens to me will dwell secure and will be at ease, without dread of disaster" (1:33).

What is known is also kept and returned to. Remembering feeds thinking: "I remember the days of old; I meditate on all that you have done; I ponder the work of your hands" (Psalm 143:5).

Hearing can be woken. "The Lord God has given me the tongue of those who are taught, that I may know how to sustain with a word him who is weary. Morning by morning he awakens; he awakens my ear to hear as those who are taught. The Lord God has opened my ear, and I was not rebellious; I turned not backward" (Isaiah 50:4–5). The order is the verses' own: the ear is woken before the tongue sustains anyone, and it is woken each morning. The next verse goes on to "I gave my back to those who strike" (50:6), so the woken ear is no shelter from suffering. An angel wakes a prophet too, and the first thing said is "What do you see?" (Zechariah 4:1–2; 13.2).

What is known can be known in heart and soul. Joshua, near death: "you know in your hearts and souls, all of you, that not one word has failed of all the good things that the Lord your God promised concerning you. All have come to pass for you; not one of them has failed" (Joshua 23:14). This is knowing from experience. He turns it into a warning straight away: "But just as all the good things that the Lord your God promised concerning you have been fulfilled for you, so the Lord will bring upon you all the evil things" (23:15). The faithfulness they know from the good is the same faithfulness that stands behind the warnings.

Receiving a word can wait on being willing. "and if you are willing to accept it, he is Elijah who is to come. He who has ears to hear, let him hear" (Matthew 11:14–15). The Bereans "received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so. Many of them therefore believed" (Acts 17:11–12). Paul calls a saying "trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost" (1 Timothy 1:15). The other way is also named: scoffers "following their own sinful desires … deliberately overlook this fact" (2 Peter 3:3, 5). I read the willing, or the unwilling, as standing before the hearing in these verses.

## Perplexity

Perplexity is knowing that cannot close. Something has been seen or heard, and the person cannot yet say what it means. The Greek words are *aporeō*, "to be at a loss, perplexed", and *diaporeō*, "to be greatly perplexed"; Daniel's Aramaic has *shevash*, "to be perplexed".

It rises when what is seen or heard goes beyond what the person can make sense of.
- An empty tomb: "While they were perplexed about this, behold, two men stood by them in dazzling apparel" (Luke 24:4).
- Their own languages spoken by Galileans: "all were amazed and perplexed, saying to one another, 'What does this mean?'" (Acts 2:12).
- A vision: "Peter was inwardly perplexed as to what the vision that he had seen might mean" (Acts 10:17).
- Jesus's word that one of them would betray him: "The disciples looked at one another, uncertain of whom he spoke" (John 13:22).
- Writing on a wall that no one could read: "his lords were perplexed" (Daniel 5:9).

What perplexity does shows in those same verses. It asks aloud ("What does this mean?", Acts 2:12). It looks at others (John 13:22). It stays inside ("inwardly perplexed", Acts 10:17, literally *in himself*). Festus, "being at a loss how to investigate these questions", passed the question on to someone else (Acts 25:20).

It can sit beside other feelings in one person. "Herod feared John, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man, and he kept him safe. When he heard him, he was greatly perplexed, and yet he heard him gladly" (Mark 6:20). Fear, knowledge, perplexity and gladness are all there, and the perplexity did not stop him listening. Paul's perplexity comes from love: "my little children, for whom I am again in the anguish of childbirth … I am perplexed about you" (Galatians 4:19–20). And Paul sets a limit to it: "perplexed, but not driven to despair" (2 Corinthians 4:8). In Greek the second word is the first one made stronger. He is at a loss, but not utterly at a loss.

In several of these scenes, perplexity ends when someone comes.
- The two men at the tomb (Luke 24:4).
- To the perplexed chief priests, "someone came and told them, 'Look! The men whom you put in prison are standing in the temple and teaching the people'" (Acts 5:24–25).
- At Peter's gate, the men from Cornelius, and then the Spirit: "the Spirit said to him, 'Behold, three men are looking for you'" (Acts 10:17, 19).
- Peter "lifted up his voice" to the crowd (Acts 2:14).
- The queen named Daniel, in whom "an excellent spirit, knowledge, and understanding to interpret dreams, explain riddles, and solve problems were found" (Daniel 5:12).

blocks.section: Remembering as a cure, and remembering as hope
blocks.text:
## Remembering as a cure, and remembering as hope

So remembering is commanded.
- **Against self-righteousness:** "Remember and do not forget how you provoked the Lord your God to wrath in the wilderness" (Deuteronomy 9:7). It comes straight after "Do not say in your heart … 'It is because of my righteousness'" (9:4).
- **Against fear:** "you shall not be afraid of them but you shall remember what the Lord your God did to Pharaoh and to all Egypt" (Deuteronomy 7:18).
- **Against the pride of having:** "You shall remember the Lord your God, for it is he who gives you power to get wealth" (Deuteronomy 8:18).
- **Before old age:** "Remember also your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come" (Ecclesiastes 12:1). The days that follow are pictured with trembling and terrors (12:3–5; 10.12).
- **Kept in a song**, so it will not be lost: "this song shall confront them as a witness (for it will live unforgotten in the mouths of their offspring)" (Deuteronomy 31:21).

Remembering also rescues. The psalmist fears that God's anger has shut him out: "Has God forgotten to be gracious? Has he in anger shut up his compassion?" (Psalm 77:9). His answer is not a reply from heaven but an act of memory: "I will remember the deeds of the Lord; yes, I will remember your wonders of old" (77:11). The poet of Lamentations does the same in the middle of ruin. "My soul continually remembers it and is bowed down within me. But this I call to mind, and therefore I have hope: The steadfast love of the Lord never ceases" (Lamentations 3:20–22). One remembering bows the soul down, and another lifts it.

## God remembers

God remembers too, and his remembering changes things.
- He remembers what we are: "he knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust" (Psalm 103:14). "He remembered that they were but flesh, a wind that passes and comes not again" (Psalm 78:39). In that psalm this is his reason for holding back his anger.
- He is asked to remember mercy inside his anger: "in wrath remember mercy" (Habakkuk 3:2).
- He is asked not to remember sin: "Do not remember against us our former iniquities" (Psalm 79:8).
- He stops remembering when a person turns, either way. Of the wicked who turns: "None of the transgressions that he has committed shall be remembered against him" (Ezekiel 18:22). Of the righteous who turns to injustice: "None of the righteous deeds that he has done shall be remembered" (18:24).
- Job asks to be hidden "until your wrath be past" and then "remember me!" (Job 14:13).
- He keeps a book of remembrance of those who feared him (Malachi 3:16).
- And he remembers in judgment: "God remembered Babylon the great, to make her drain the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath" (Revelation 16:19).

## Where thoughts come from

They come from the heart. "For from within, out of the heart of man, come evil thoughts" (Mark 7:21). "The heart of man plans his way, but the Lord establishes his steps" (Proverbs 16:9).

They are not always chosen. Often they simply **arise**, and often at night.
- "To you, O king, as you lay in bed came thoughts of what would be after this, and he who reveals mysteries made known to you what is to be" (Daniel 2:29).
- "Amid thoughts from visions of the night, when deep sleep falls on men" (Job 4:13).
- Jesus asks his frightened disciples, "Why are you troubled, and why do doubts arise in your hearts?" (Luke 24:38).
- Of Gog: "thoughts will come into your mind, and you will devise an evil scheme" (Ezekiel 38:10). The thought arrives first, and the devising follows it. 10.10 follows where that scheme was aimed.

What arises has also been **shaped from outside**.
- God fills craftsmen "with skill" (Exodus 35:35) "to devise artistic designs" (35:32).
- Instruction forms thinking: "discretion will watch over you, understanding will guard you" (Proverbs 2:11).
- Thinking can also be darkened. People who knew God "became futile in their thinking, and their foolish hearts were darkened" (Romans 1:21). "The god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers" (2 Corinthians 4:4). The enemy has thoughts of his own, and the word for them is the word for ours: "we are not ignorant of his designs" (2 Corinthians 2:11). The serpent's cunning can lead thoughts "astray from a sincere and pure devotion to Christ" (2 Corinthians 11:3). Yet the same mind can be guarded: "the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus" (Philippians 4:7).

A thought can be answered by God. To the elders who came "to inquire of the Lord" (Ezekiel 20:1), he names what is in them: "What is in your mind shall never happen—the thought, 'Let us be like the nations, like the tribes of the countries, and worship wood and stone.'" And he answers it with an oath by his own life: "As I live, declares the Lord God, surely with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm and with wrath poured out I will be king over you" (20:32–33; 13.1).

## The inclination: a shaped thing

The word behind "every *intention* of the thoughts of his heart" (Genesis 6:5) is *yēṣer*. It is the same word Isaiah uses for what a potter makes: "the thing formed say of him who formed it, 'He has no understanding'" (Isaiah 29:16). And it is the word in "he knows our *frame*; he remembers that we are dust" (Psalm 103:14).

The inclination in Genesis 6:5 is "only evil continually". The ESV renders the same word "mind" in a promise: "You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you" (Isaiah 26:3).

The word can be turned upside down from either end. In Isaiah, the thing formed says its maker has no understanding. In Habakkuk, the maker trusts the thing he formed: "its maker trusts in his own creation when he makes speechless idols!" (Habakkuk 2:18). And God's knowing of my frame does not end in contempt. The verse before says, "As a father shows compassion to his children, so the Lord shows compassion to those who fear him" (Psalm 103:13).

## What thinking does

**It designs.** The verb for devising is used of the craftsmen who worked the cherubim "skillfully" into the tabernacle curtains (Exodus 26:1), and of people who plot. One word, *mᵊzimmāh*, covers both: "discretion will watch over you" (Proverbs 2:11), and "a man of evil devices he condemns" (Proverbs 12:2).

The same skill is put to different uses:
- The tabernacle craftsmen were given it for God's house (Exodus 35:35). Huram-abi, sent to Solomon for the temple, was trained "to do all sorts of engraving and execute any design that may be assigned him" (2 Chronicles 2:14). His skill was to carry out a design another gave him.
- King Uzziah's engineers turned it to war: "he made machines, invented by skillful men … And his fame spread far, for he was marvelously helped, till he was strong" (2 Chronicles 26:15). The next verse: "But when he was strong, he grew proud, to his destruction" (26:16).
- Those "at ease in Zion" (Amos 6:1) turned it on themselves: they "like David invent for themselves instruments of music" (6:5).

**It reckons**, giving things their worth. People reckon wrongly.
- Judah "thought she was a prostitute" (Genesis 38:15).
- Eli watched Hannah praying silently and "took her to be a drunken woman" (1 Samuel 1:13).
- A whole people looked at the servant of the Lord and "esteemed him not … we esteemed him stricken, smitten by God, and afflicted" (Isaiah 53:3–4).
- A price can be set on a person, and called lordly in irony: "Then the Lord said to me, 'Throw it to the potter'—the lordly price at which I was priced by them" (Zechariah 11:13). It was thirty pieces of silver (11:12). Matthew reads it of the silver Judas brought back when he "changed his mind": "the price of him on whom a price had been set by some of the sons of Israel" (Matthew 27:3, 9).
- Opponents reckon the worst: "some who suspect us of walking according to the flesh" (2 Corinthians 10:2).
- People reckon by the surface: "Even a fool who keeps silent is considered wise" (Proverbs 17:28). Even a good act can be reckoned by its manner: "Whoever blesses his neighbor with a loud voice, rising early in the morning, will be counted as cursing" (27:14).
- A people at ease can be made to reckon itself: "Pass over to Calneh, and see … Are you better than these kingdoms? Or is their territory greater than your territory" (Amos 6:2), said to those "at ease in Zion" (6:1) who "put far away the day of disaster" (6:3).
- A father can reckon his own daughters as strangers. Rachel and Leah: "Are we not regarded by him as foreigners? For he has sold us" (Genesis 31:15).
- What is precious can be reckoned cheap: "The precious sons of Zion, worth their weight in fine gold, how they are regarded as earthen pots, the work of a potter's hands!" (Lamentations 4:2).
- When a land breaks down, regard for people goes with it: "Covenants are broken; cities are despised; there is no regard for man" (Isaiah 33:8). The Medes are named by what they do not value: they "have no regard for silver and do not delight in gold" (13:17), and the next verse says "they will have no mercy" (13:18).

Being reckoned is felt from the inside.
- "Yet for your sake we are killed all the day long; we are regarded as sheep to be slaughtered" (Psalm 44:22).
- "I am counted among those who go down to the pit; I am a man who has no strength" (Psalm 88:4). The verse before says, "my soul is full of troubles" (88:3).
- A people can reckon itself apart. Balaam, sent to curse, sees "a people dwelling alone, and not counting itself among the nations!" (Numbers 23:9).
- Being reckoned trustworthy carries a charge. Nehemiah appointed treasurers "for they were considered reliable, and their duty was to distribute to their brothers" (Nehemiah 13:13).
- A man can be reckoned worthy by others and reckon himself not. The elders said of the centurion, "He is worthy to have you do this for him, for he loves our nation" (Luke 7:4–5). He sent word, "Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy to have you come under my roof. Therefore I did not presume to come to you. But say the word, and let my servant be healed" (7:6–7). Jesus "marveled at him" (7:9).

God reckons truly.
- Abraham "believed the Lord, and he counted it to him as righteousness" (Genesis 15:6).
- The nations "are accounted as the dust on the scales" (Isaiah 40:15). Yet the same God "takes thought for me" (Psalm 40:17).

Jesus took the wrong reckoning on himself: "this Scripture must be fulfilled in me: 'And he was numbered with the transgressors'" (Luke 22:37). And reckoning is not mine to turn toward myself: "Not that we are sufficient in ourselves to claim anything as coming from us, but our sufficiency is from God" (2 Corinthians 3:5).

Reckoning is not only about judging. In the law it serves **release**: the man who sold himself "shall calculate with his buyer from the year when he sold himself to him until the year of jubilee" (Leviticus 25:50), and pay his way free. And there are times when reckoning is laid aside because there is trust: "they did not ask for an accounting from the men into whose hand they delivered the money … for they dealt honestly" (2 Kings 12:15).

The Greek word carries this on. "I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us" (Romans 8:18). And faith is itself a reckoning: Abraham "considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead" (Hebrews 11:19). Paul says the same of Abraham before his own body: "He did not weaken in faith when he considered his own body, which was as good as dead (since he was about a hundred years old), or when he considered the barrenness of Sarah's womb" (Romans 4:19).

Reckoning from what God has done can answer a fear of dying. Manoah said, "We shall surely die, for we have seen God." His wife answered, "If the Lord had meant to kill us, he would not have accepted a burnt offering and a grain offering at our hands, or shown us all these things" (Judges 13:22–23). Chapter 2 follows the fear of dying.

**It likens.** The Hebrew *dāmāh* means both "to be like" and "to think".
- Mordecai warns Esther, "Do not think to yourself that in the king's palace you will escape any more than all the other Jews" (Esther 4:13).
- Worshippers say, "We have thought on your steadfast love, O God, in the midst of your temple" (Psalm 48:9).
- Love likens: "I compare you, my love, to a mare among Pharaoh's chariots" (Song of Songs 1:9).
- Comfort tries to liken, and sometimes cannot: "What can I say for you, to what compare you, O daughter of Jerusalem? What can I liken to you, that I may comfort you …? For your ruin is vast as the sea; who can heal you?" (Lamentations 2:13).

- Lament likens the self truly: "I am like a desert owl of the wilderness" (Psalm 102:6).
- God himself teaches by likening: "through the prophets gave parables" (Hosea 12:10).

Likening can go badly wrong. God says, "you thought that I was one like yourself" (Psalm 50:21). Chapter 12 follows this further.

**It murmurs.** *Hāgāh* is the word for meditating, and it is not silent. "On his law he meditates day and night" (Psalm 1:2). "I remember you upon my bed, and meditate on you in the watches of the night" (Psalm 63:6). But the same word devises and plots: "their hearts devise violence" (Proverbs 24:2). And it can "meditate treachery all day long" (Psalm 38:12). Chapter 10.5 picks up its sense of uttering.

**It reasons, inside and between.** The Greek word for reasoning is used for a single heart talking to itself and for people talking together, with no change of word.
- Inside: a thought can be a whole sentence. "In the pride of his face the wicked does not seek him; all his thoughts are, 'There is no God'" (Psalm 10:4). Jesus perceived "that they thus questioned within themselves" (Mark 2:8). The rich man "thought to himself, 'What shall I do, for I have nowhere to store my crops?'" (Luke 12:17).
- Between: "What were you discussing on the way?" (Mark 9:33).

**It can be troubled.** Mary "was greatly troubled at the saying, and tried to discern what sort of greeting this might be" (Luke 1:29). She is trying to understand. The disciples' worried reasoning about bread is different. "Why are you discussing the fact that you have no bread? Do you not yet perceive or understand? Are your hearts hardened?" (Mark 8:17). Jesus connects it with a hard heart and "little faith" (Matthew 16:8).

Thinking can weigh answers by their cost, not by their truth. Asked by what authority he acted, Jesus asked in return, "The baptism of John, from where did it come? From heaven or from man?" "And they discussed it among themselves, saying, 'If we say, From heaven, he will say to us, Why then did you not believe him? But if we say, From man, we are afraid of the crowd'" (Matthew 21:25–26). They answered, "We do not know" (21:27). Both answers were weighed against what each would cost them (10.12, 10.11).

A wrong expectation can be what a teaching answers. Jesus told the parable of the nobleman and the minas "because he was near to Jerusalem, and because they supposed that the kingdom of God was to appear immediately" (Luke 19:11).

## When thinking changes character

Again and again in these words I found the same thought becoming something else.

**One word, three faces: *mᵊzimmāh*.**
- In the young it is discretion: "to give prudence to the simple, knowledge and discretion to the youth" (Proverbs 1:4). It "will watch over you" (2:11).
- In the wicked it is an evil device, joined to arrogance: "In arrogance the wicked hotly pursue the poor; let them be caught in the schemes that they have devised" (Psalm 10:2). It sits beside a short temper: "A man of quick temper acts foolishly, and a man of evil devices is hated" (Proverbs 14:17).
- In God it is purpose: "no purpose of yours can be thwarted" (Job 42:2). His anger serves it, and it is understood only later: "The anger of the Lord will not turn back until he has executed and accomplished the intents of his heart. In the latter days you will understand it clearly" (Jeremiah 23:20).

**One passage, three plans: Jeremiah 18.**
- God says, "Behold, I am shaping disaster against you and devising a plan against you. Return, every one from his evil way" (18:11). Even this plan is open: "if that nation … turns from its evil, I will relent of the disaster that I intended to do to it" (18:8).
- The people answer, "We will follow our own plans, and will every one act according to the stubbornness of his evil heart" (18:12).
- Then they turn on the messenger: "Come, let us make plots against Jeremiah" (18:18).

God's plan is *against*, and in the same breath he says "Return" (Jeremiah 18:11). The people's plans are, in their own words, "the stubbornness of his evil heart" (18:12). The word "against" is the same in God's plan and in their plot.

**What it keeps company with.** Plans fail alone and stand with counsel: "Without counsel plans fail, but with many advisers they succeed" (Proverbs 15:22). "Commit your work to the Lord, and your plans will be established" (16:3). The same togetherness can go the other way: "All who hate me whisper together about me; they imagine the worst for me" (Psalm 41:7).

**The state it rises from.** Paul names the order of cause in so many words: people are "darkened in their understanding … due to their hardness of heart" (Ephesians 4:18). A hard heart makes for dark thinking. Ease does it too: "In the thought of one who is at ease there is contempt for misfortune; it is ready for those whose feet slip" (Job 12:5). A comfortable mind looks down on those who fall.

**Its pace.** "The plans of the diligent lead surely to abundance, but everyone who is hasty comes only to poverty" (Proverbs 21:5). Haste is named again in Job 20:2 (below).

**Where it is done.** Thinking alone can stall. "When I thought how to understand this, it seemed to me a wearisome task, until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end" (Psalm 73:16–17). The bed, as I show below, is a place that holds both ways of thinking.

**Reasoning that becomes a quarrel.** The Greek word for inner reasoning is also the word for a quarrel. The disciples' reasoning about greatness became an argument: "An argument arose among them as to which of them was the greatest. But Jesus, knowing the reasoning of their hearts, took a child" (Luke 9:46–47). Paul uses the word for dispute: "Do all things without grumbling or disputing" (Philippians 2:14). And he uses it beside anger: men are to pray "lifting holy hands without anger or quarreling" (1 Timothy 2:8).

**Imagination that makes gods.** The power to design can be turned to making a god: "we ought not to think that the divine being is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by the art and imagination of man" (Acts 17:29).

None of these is a rule I have laid on the verses. They are what the verses themselves put beside the change. Chapter 11 gathers them across all the activities.

## When anger thinks

Anger does not stay a feeling. It starts to reckon, and it reckons badly.
- It reads another's heart, and misreads it. Eliab, angry at his young brother, says, "I know your presumption and the evil of your heart" (1 Samuel 17:28). The reader knows David came because his father sent him.
- It calculates the future. "They have ascribed to David ten thousands, and to me they have ascribed thousands, and what more can he have but the kingdom?" (1 Samuel 18:8). Seventeen verses later it has become a plan: "Now Saul thought to make David fall by the hand of the Philistines" (18:25).
- It soothes itself with a plan. "Your brother Esau comforts himself about you by planning to kill you" (Genesis 27:42).
- Rage and plotting stand in one line: "Why do the nations rage, and the peoples plot in vain?" (Psalm 2:1). The apostles read that psalm over what was done to Jesus (Acts 4:25–27).

But zeal can also be reckoned rightly. When Phinehas acted with God's own jealousy, "that was counted to him as righteousness from generation to generation forever" (Psalm 106:31). This is the same reckoning word that was used of Abraham's faith.

## The night and the bed

The bed is where several kinds of thinking happen.
- People plot there: "He plots trouble while on his bed" (Psalm 36:4).
- Unbidden thoughts come there, and God's revealing with them (Daniel 2:29).
- The psalmist meditates on God there (Psalm 63:6).
- The angry are told: "ponder in your own hearts on your beds, and be silent" (Psalm 4:4).

Night thoughts are not all the same. For Nebuchadnezzar they became revelation, because God made them known and Daniel interpreted them (Daniel 2:29–30). For Belshazzar, with no one to read the writing, they only frightened: "his thoughts alarmed him" (Daniel 5:6), until the queen pointed to the one who could "show the interpretation" (5:12). And a night thought can be claimed as revelation and still be wrong. Eliphaz tells of "thoughts from visions of the night" (Job 4:13). At the end God says to him, "you have not spoken of me what is right" (Job 42:7).

What fills the heart in the night shows by morning. "Woe to those who devise wickedness and work evil on their beds! When the morning dawns, they perform it" (Micah 2:1).

## What is devised comes back

What a person devises does not stay where it was sent. It returns to the one who devised it.
- Haman's "evil plan that he had devised against the Jews should return on his own head" (Esther 9:25).
- "Let them be caught in the schemes that they have devised" (Psalm 10:2).
- "He makes a pit, digging it out, and falls into the hole that he has made. His mischief returns upon his own head" (Psalm 7:15–16).
- "I am bringing disaster upon this people, the fruit of their devices" (Jeremiah 6:19).
- The law makes it so for the false witness: "you shall do to him as he had meant to do to his brother" (Deuteronomy 19:19).
- "He catches the wise in their own craftiness, and the schemes of the wily are brought to a quick end" (Job 5:13).

Micah shows it in the words themselves. "Woe to those who devise wickedness and work evil on their beds!" (Micah 2:1). Two verses later, "Therefore thus says the Lord: behold, against this family I am devising disaster" (2:3). The same verb comes back to them, now with God as its subject.

It comes back for good as well. "The plans of the diligent lead surely to abundance" (Proverbs 21:5). The wicked who forsakes "his thoughts" finds that God "will abundantly pardon" (Isaiah 55:7).

## Small, passing, and wholly seen

Human thought is real, and it is also small. "The Lord — knows the thoughts of man, that they are but a breath" (Psalm 94:11).

And none of it is hidden.
- "You discern my thoughts from afar" (Psalm 139:2).
- "The Lord searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought" (1 Chronicles 28:9).
- He knows the inclination before it is acted on: "I know what they are inclined to do even today" (Deuteronomy 31:21).
- Jesus "perceived their thoughts" (Luke 5:22).
- What is hidden will be brought out. Simeon says the child is set for a sign "so that thoughts from many hearts may be revealed" (Luke 2:34–35).

The same psalm that says God knows my thoughts uses the same word for his thoughts: "How precious to me are your thoughts, O God! How vast is the sum of them!" (Psalm 139:17).

God thinks too, and his thinking is not like mine. "The Lord takes thought for me" (Psalm 40:17). "For I know the plans I have for you, declares the Lord, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope" (Jeremiah 29:11). In the plea that Joab put in a woman's mouth to move David (2 Samuel 14:3), she says of God that "he devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast" (14:14). "My thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways" (Isaiah 55:8). Chapter 11 returns to this.

## Connections

- **From hearing (10.2):** what is heard and remembered becomes the material of thought (Psalm 143:5).
- **Into speaking (10.5):** murmuring becomes uttering.
- **Into choosing and the deed (10.7, and the path in 10.0):** devising becomes doing, and what is devised comes back. Looking ahead, weighing first and holding a purpose are in 10.7 (*Planning*).
- **Against another (10.10):** plotting, and the one it is aimed at (*Plotting against another*).
- **From remembering (10.3):** what is remembered is meditated on.
- **With feeling (10.1):** anger reckons and plots (1 Samuel 18:8, 25). "his thoughts alarmed him; his limbs gave way" (Daniel 5:6). "When the cares of my heart are many, your consolations cheer my soul" (Psalm 94:19). A quick temper and evil devices stand side by side (Proverbs 14:17).
- **From wanting (10.6):** the rich man's thinking serves his wanting (Luke 12:17–19).
- **Under right and wrong (10.8):** "their conflicting thoughts accuse or even excuse them" (Romans 2:15).
- **With others (10.10):** reasoning together, and reasoning that becomes a quarrel.
- **Before God (10.9):** reckoned by him, seen by him, and brought to him (Psalm 73:17; 139:23).
- **Across all the activities (Chapter 11 §4):** what changes the character of an activity.

blocks.section: The tongue, the lips and the eyes devise
blocks.text:
## The tongue, the lips and the eyes devise

Several verses give the tongue, the lips and the eyes the verbs of planning.
- "Your tongue plots destruction, like a sharp razor, you worker of deceit" (Psalm 52:2).
- "They do not speak peace, but against those who are quiet in the land they devise words of deceit" (Psalm 35:20).
- "Whoever winks his eyes plans dishonest things; he who purses his lips brings evil to pass" (Proverbs 16:30).
- "All who hate me whisper together about me; they imagine the worst for me" (Psalm 41:7).
- Jeremiah's enemies: "Come, let us make plots against Jeremiah … let us strike him with the tongue" (Jeremiah 18:18).

## Speech is heard

Every word that goes out is heard, and Scripture follows it there.

By God, in both directions:
- "You have heard their taunts, O Lord, all their plots against me" (Lamentations 3:61).
- "Then those who feared the Lord spoke with one another. The Lord paid attention and heard them, and a book of remembrance was written before him of those who feared the Lord and esteemed his name" (Malachi 3:16).

The plots of enemies and the talk of the faithful both reach him. Before any of it is spoken, he knows it: "Even before a word is on my tongue, behold, O Lord, you know it altogether" (Psalm 139:4).

By people: Esau's private sentence about killing his brother did not stay private. "The words of Esau her older son were told to Rebekah" (Genesis 27:42).

What is heard can also set another speaking. "When the chief baker saw that the interpretation was favorable, he said to Joseph, 'I also had a dream'" (Genesis 40:16). He spoke on the strength of the other man's outcome. His own was death (40:19).

## Through the eye

Desire can take hold in the heart before anything is done. Jesus says, "everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart" (Matthew 5:28). The way in is the eye, and he goes straight on: "If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out and throw it away" (5:29). Proverbs warns a son in the same order, heart and eyes: "Do not desire her beauty in your heart, and do not let her capture you with her eyelashes" (Proverbs 6:25). The Preacher uses the hunter's picture for the other side of that capture: "the woman whose heart is snares and nets, and whose hands are fetters. He who pleases God escapes her, but the sinner is taken by her" (Ecclesiastes 7:26). He names it as his own finding, after he had "turned my heart to know and to search out" (7:25). The escape he names is not strength of will but pleasing God.

The first look of desire in Scripture comes in the same order. God had made trees "pleasant to the sight and good for food" (Genesis 2:9). Then "when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took of its fruit and ate" (3:6). "Good for food" is word for word the same in both verses, and "pleasant" and "desired" are the same Hebrew word. The tree really was what she saw. What changed the look was whose word governed it: the tree was the one God had withheld. Three acts stand in that verse in order: she saw, she desired, she took. The verse states the order. It does not say that every desire runs that way.

A law case starts in the same place: *"you see among the captives a beautiful woman, and you desire to take her to be your wife"* (Deuteronomy 21:11). Its end, when the delight is gone, is in 10.1 (*Delight*). In Ezekiel the look is at pictures: *"She saw men portrayed on the wall, the images of the Chaldeans"*, and she *"lusted after the Assyrians … all of them desirable young men"* (Ezekiel 23:14, 12).

The servant of Isaiah is the opposite case: *"he had no form or majesty that we should look at him, and no beauty that we should desire him. He was despised and rejected by men"* (Isaiah 53:2–3). The woman's look at the tree found something "to be desired" and took it. This look found nothing to desire and turned away. I read that the one who *"has borne our griefs"* (53:4) is the one the desiring eye passed over.

The eye can also give. "Whoever has a bountiful eye will be blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor" (Proverbs 22:9). "Bountiful" is literally "good": a good eye. The same book warns against "the bread of a man who is stingy" (23:6, *Possessions*), literally one with an evil eye. I read the eye here as the way a person looks on another's need, and the look moves the hand that shares (10.10).

Before that, the first seeing in Scripture is God's: "And God saw that it was good" (Genesis 1:21, 25), and of everything, "very good" (1:31). 13.4 takes that up.

The heart is also where desire can be held. Paul speaks of the man who "is firmly established in his heart, being under no necessity but having his desire under control, and has determined this in his heart" (1 Corinthians 7:37). Timothy is told to "flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace, along with those who call on the Lord from a pure heart" (2 Timothy 2:22).

## Coveting

The commandment always names the neighbour's thing: *"You shall not covet your neighbor's house; you shall not covet your neighbor's wife, or his male servant, or his female servant, or his ox, or his donkey, or anything that is your neighbor's"* (Exodus 20:17). Deuteronomy uses two verbs, "covet" for the wife and "desire" for the house and the rest (Deuteronomy 5:21). I read coveting as wanting defined by a relationship: it is wanting what is another's. Paul gives the answer as a love for the same neighbour: *"You shall not covet," and any other commandment, are summed up in this word: "You shall love your neighbor as yourself"* (Romans 13:9).

Coveting runs in the order the woman's look did: seeing, desiring, taking. Achan says it himself: *"when I saw among the spoil a beautiful cloak from Shinar, and 200 shekels of silver, and a bar of gold weighing 50 shekels, then I coveted them and took them. And see, they are hidden in the earth inside my tent"* (Joshua 7:21; 10.11). He adds the fourth act, hiding. Micah adds the night and the power: *"Woe to those who devise wickedness and work evil on their beds! When the morning dawns, they perform it, because it is in the power of their hand. They covet fields and seize them, and houses, and take them away"* (Micah 2:1–2). The covetous wish is planned in bed and done when there is power to do it.

David's look runs in the same order, and the verses name no desire at all. It was "the time when kings go out to battle … But David remained at Jerusalem" (2 Samuel 11:1). "He saw from the roof a woman bathing; and the woman was very beautiful. And David sent and inquired about the woman" (11:2–3). "So David sent messengers and took her" (11:4). Seeing, asking and taking are all there. The wanting is not named, only done. The taking is done by a king's word: he sends, and messengers bring her, as Micah said of those who take "because it is in the power of their hand" (Micah 2:1). Nathan later named the act as despising "the word of the Lord, to do what is evil in his sight" (2 Samuel 12:9). I read the power to send as closing the gap between the look and the taking.

The command itself names the desire, and sin uses the naming: *"I would not have known what it is to covet if the law had not said, 'You shall not covet.' But sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, produced in me all kinds of covetousness"* (Romans 7:7–8). I read the command as making the desire known, and sin as using that very knowledge to multiply it.

Coveting can be put as a fair offer. Ahab to Naboth: "Give me your vineyard, that I may have it for a vegetable garden, because it is near my house, and I will give you a better vineyard for it; or, if it seems good to you, I will give you its value in money" (1 Kings 21:2). The want is dressed as an exchange. Naboth's refusal is not about the price: "The Lord forbid that I should give you the inheritance of my fathers" (21:3). The want, refused, goes into the body: Ahab "lay down on his bed and turned away his face and would eat no food" (21:4; 10.1). I read the courtesy of the offer as covering a want that could not bear a no.

What is coveted can be a snare: *"You shall not covet the silver or the gold that is on them or take it for yourselves, lest you be ensnared by it"* (Deuteronomy 7:25). Proverbs sets taking against growing: *"Whoever is wicked covets the spoil of evildoers, but the root of the righteous bears fruit"* (Proverbs 12:12). And Paul shows the opposite lived: *"I coveted no one's silver or gold or apparel. You yourselves know that these hands ministered to my necessities … 'It is more blessed to give than to receive'"* (Acts 20:33–35). The hands that might have taken work, and give.

Simon wanted an authority that was God's to give, and thought it could be bought. "Now when Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles' hands, he offered them money, saying, 'Give me this power also'" (Acts 8:18–19). Peter named what was in him: "you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money!", "your heart is not right before God", and "I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity" (8:20–23; Chapter 4).

Coveting can add until it leaves the coveter alone. "Woe to those who join house to house, who add field to field, until there is no more room, and you are made to dwell alone in the midst of the land." The answer is sworn: "Surely many houses shall be desolate, large and beautiful houses, without inhabitant" (Isaiah 5:8–9).

## Thirst answered

Twice in John people ask for the gift and mean the thing itself. The woman at the well: "Sir, give me this water, so that I will not be thirsty or have to come here to draw water" (John 4:15). The crowd, who had followed Jesus "because you ate your fill of the loaves" (6:26): "Sir, give us this bread always" (6:34). Both times the answer moves from the thing to a person: "I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst" (6:35). The want is real, and it is not refused. It is met by coming and believing, acts toward someone, and not by a supply.

The water is pictured as a spring: "Everyone who drinks of this water will be thirsty again, but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again. The water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life" (John 4:13–14). Jeremiah has the opposite: "they have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed out cisterns for themselves, broken cisterns that can hold no water" (Jeremiah 2:13; Chapter 2). A cistern holds what is poured into it, and a broken one loses it. A spring wells up from within. One is a want that must be filled again and again. The other is a want met at its source, and the source is "in him".

The thirst is answered with water: "let the one who is thirsty come; let the one who desires take the water of life without price" (Revelation 22:17). God hears the desire: "O Lord, you hear the desire of the afflicted; you will strengthen their heart" (Psalm 10:17). He gives it: "You have given him his heart's desire and have not withheld the request of his lips" (Psalm 21:2). A desire met reaches the whole person: "a desire fulfilled is a tree of life" (Proverbs 13:12), and "A desire fulfilled is sweet to the soul, but to turn away from evil is an abomination to fools" (13:19). And God himself satisfies it: "You open your hand; you satisfy the desire of every living thing" (Psalm 145:16). The creatures' thirst is met the same way (13.4).

At the feast the offer is made aloud, and the water now flows outward: *"Jesus stood up and cried out, 'If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water.'"* John adds, *"Now this he said about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive"* (John 7:37–39; Chapter 6). At the well the spring wells up *"in him"*. At the feast rivers flow *"out of his heart"*. I read a want that is met and then becomes a source for others.

The one who offered the water thirsted: *"After this, Jesus, knowing that all was now finished, said (to fulfill the Scripture), 'I thirst.'"* He was given sour wine, and then he said, *"It is finished"* (John 19:28–30). The psalm puts the thirst beside the want of comfort: *"I looked for pity, but there was none, and for comforters, but I found none. They gave me poison for food, and for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink"* (Psalm 69:20–21). He says "I thirst" knowing what it fulfils. I read the want spoken, not hidden, and answered with sour wine.

The want can be aimed at righteousness, and then it is called blessed: *"Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied"* (Matthew 5:6). God's answer to plain thirst is given with its reason. *"When the poor and needy seek water, and there is none, and their tongue is parched with thirst, I the Lord will answer them; I the God of Israel will not forsake them"* (Isaiah 41:17). *"They shall not hunger or thirst, neither scorching wind nor sun shall strike them, for he who has pity on them will lead them, and by springs of water will guide them"* (Isaiah 49:10). The end is said in nearly the same words: *"They shall hunger no more, neither thirst anymore; the sun shall not strike them, nor any scorching heat. For the Lamb in the midst of the throne will be their shepherd, and he will guide them to springs of living water, and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes"* (Revelation 7:16–17). The thirst and the tears are answered together.

A thirst met can be forgotten. *"You gave them bread from heaven for their hunger and brought water for them out of the rock for their thirst … But they and our fathers acted presumptuously and stiffened their neck"*; they *"were not mindful of the wonders that you performed among them"* (Nehemiah 9:15–17). Isaiah sets the same memory beside the wicked: *"They did not thirst when he led them through the deserts; he made water flow for them from the rock … There is no peace, says the Lord, for the wicked"* (Isaiah 48:21–22). I read a want met so fully that it was no longer felt, and the giver forgotten with it (10.3).

Thirst also comes as judgment, and the verses name the inner ground each time. Joyless service in plenty: *"Because you did not serve the Lord your God with joyfulness and gladness of heart, because of the abundance of all things, therefore you shall serve your enemies whom the Lord will send against you, in hunger and thirst"* (Deuteronomy 28:47–48). A choice of what he did not delight in: *"you did what was evil in my eyes and chose what I did not delight in"* (Isaiah 65:12), so *"my servants shall drink, but you shall be thirsty … my servants shall sing for gladness of heart, but you shall cry out for pain of heart and shall wail for breaking of spirit"* (65:13–14). The outward thirst is matched by pain of heart and a broken spirit. Drink without regard: those who *"run after strong drink"* (5:11) and *"do not regard the deeds of the Lord"* (5:12) end *"parched with thirst"*, and the lack named is knowledge: *"my people go into exile for lack of knowledge"* (Isaiah 5:13). The drinkers end thirsty.

Hunger and thirst can be borne for others. *"To the present hour we hunger and thirst, we are poorly dressed and buffeted and homeless, and we labor, working with our own hands. When reviled, we bless; when persecuted, we endure"* (1 Corinthians 4:11–12). Paul's longer list ends *"in hunger and thirst, often without food, in cold and exposure. And, apart from other things, there is the daily pressure on me of my anxiety for all the churches"* (2 Corinthians 11:27–28). The bodily wants are listed and passed over. The weight he names last is inside, and it is for others.

A bodily want can be the setting of a vision. Peter *"became hungry and wanted something to eat, but while they were preparing it, he fell into a trance"* (Acts 10:10), and saw a sheet let down full of animals (10:11–12). The verses do not say why it came then.

## Being chosen

The verb a person uses to choose is also used when God chooses a person. Then the one who chooses is God. In these verses the inner life of the one chosen is not what made them chosen. It is what the choosing is for, and what follows from it.

**The choosing comes first.** When God chooses, the verses put the inner life of the chosen after the choosing, as its purpose:
- *"my servant whom I have chosen, that you may know and believe me and understand that I am he"* (Isaiah 43:10). The witnesses he chose are *"the people who are blind, yet have eyes, who are deaf, yet have ears"* (43:8).
- *"he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him"* (Ephesians 1:4).
- *"has not God chosen those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith"* (James 2:5).
- *"Blessed is the one you choose and bring near"* (Psalm 65:4) comes straight after *"When iniquities prevail against me, you atone for our transgressions"* (65:3).

One verse names God's choosing and a person's belief together: *"God chose you as the firstfruits to be saved, through sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth"* (2 Thessalonians 2:13). It does not say how the two fit.

When people choose a person, the order is the other way. The gathering in Jerusalem was told to *"pick out from among you seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom"* (Acts 6:3), and they chose Stephen, *"a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit"* (6:5). They chose by what was already seen in him. It was seen in him to the end: *"full of the Holy Spirit"*, he prayed for those who stoned him, *"Lord, do not hold this sin against them"* (7:55, 60).

**What the chosen are moved to.** The verses set an inner response beside being chosen. Twice they name the choosing as its ground.
- **Celebrating.** David, rebuked by Michal for dancing before the ark: *"It was before the Lord, who chose me above your father and above all his house … and I will celebrate before the Lord"* (2 Samuel 6:21). Her measure was the eyes of the servants (6:20). His was the Lord. Being chosen had not kept him from being angry, afraid and unwilling when Uzzah died (6:8–10).
- **Not fearing.** *"Fear not, O Jacob my servant, Jeshurun whom I have chosen"* (Isaiah 44:2). The ground is who chose him: *"the Lord who made you, who formed you from the womb and will help you"*.
- **Satisfaction.** *"We shall be satisfied with the goodness of your house, the holiness of your temple!"* (Psalm 65:4).
- **Joy and singing.** *"So he brought his people out with joy, his chosen ones with singing"* (Psalm 105:43).
- **Gladness that another asks to share.** *"that I may rejoice in the gladness of your nation"* (Psalm 106:5). He asks it while confessing *"Both we and our fathers have sinned"* (106:6).

**What the chosen are called to.** Being chosen is given as the ground of commands:
- **Be strong and do it.** *"the Lord has chosen you to build a house for the sanctuary; be strong and do it"* (1 Chronicles 28:10), with *"serve him with a whole heart and with a willing mind, for the Lord searches all hearts"* (28:9).
- **Put on.** *"Put on then, as God's chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience"* (Colossians 3:12). What is put on is turned toward others: *"as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive"* (3:13); *"above all these put on love"* (3:14).
- **Stand firm.** *"stand firm and hold to the traditions that you were taught by us"* (2 Thessalonians 2:15).
- **Confirm it.** *"be all the more diligent to confirm your calling and election, for if you practice these qualities you will never fall"* (2 Peter 1:10). The qualities are added one to another, from faith to love (1:5–7). The effort follows what was given first: *"His divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness"* (1:3).
- **Remember.** *"Remember the wondrous works that he has done … children of Jacob, his chosen ones!"* (Psalm 105:5–6); *"Remember these things, O Jacob … you will not be forgotten by me"* (Isaiah 44:21).

**Standing for others.** The chosen can stand between God and people who have turned from him. After the calf, *"he said he would destroy them—had not Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach before him, to turn away his wrath from destroying them"* (Psalm 106:23). The psalm calls Moses chosen at the very point where he stands for people who *"forgot God, their Savior"* (106:21). It also says what those people did to him. They *"were jealous of Moses"* (106:16), and later *"they made his spirit bitter, and he spoke rashly with his lips"* (106:33). Standing for them did not keep him from being embittered by them. The anger he turned away is taken up in 10.13.

**Faith, and the truth.** Several verses name faith, and knowing the truth, for the chosen:
- *"the faith of God's elect and their knowledge of the truth, which accords with godliness"* (Titus 1:1)
- *"rich in faith"* (James 2:5)
- *"belief in the truth"* (2 Thessalonians 2:13)

For people already chosen, Paul prays for *"the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope to which he has called you"* (Ephesians 1:18). Faith is shown in what it does: *"faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead"* (James 2:17).

**Being chosen is not a guarantee.** The verses say plainly that the chosen can fail:
- **A condition.** *"if you forsake him, he will cast you off forever"* (1 Chronicles 28:9).
- **Forgetting and despising.** The chosen people *"soon forgot his works"* and *"despised the pleasant land, having no faith in his promise"* (Psalm 106:13, 24). "Despised" is the refusing verb of Isaiah 7:15.
- **Not calling.** *"Yet you did not call upon me, O Jacob; but you have been weary of me, O Israel!"* (Isaiah 43:22).
- **Blindness.** Whoever lacks the qualities is *"so nearsighted that he is blind, having forgotten that he was cleansed from his former sins"* (2 Peter 1:9).

The way back is the Lord's remembering: *"For their sake he remembered his covenant"* (Psalm 106:45); *"I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins"* (Isaiah 43:25).

**Set against others.** In each passage the chosen stand beside others who choose otherwise, or cannot see:
- the idol-maker, whose heart is shut *"so that they cannot understand"* (Isaiah 44:18)
- those who *"refused to love the truth"* and *"had pleasure in unrighteousness"* (2 Thessalonians 2:10, 12)
- those who *"profess to know God, but they deny him by their works"* (Titus 1:16)
- an assembly that seats the rich and sends the poor to stand, having *"become judges with evil thoughts"* (James 2:4). God chose the poor: *"But you have dishonored the poor man"* (2:6).
- kings who *"are of one mind"* with the beast, against *"those with him"*, who *"are called and chosen and faithful"* (Revelation 17:13–14)

## Holding a choice

A choice spoken is not yet a choice carried out, and the verses say so in several ways.
- **It binds the one who made it.** *"You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen the Lord"* (Joshua 24:22).
- **Choosing is not the same as being able.** *"You are not able to serve the Lord, for he is a holy God"* (Joshua 24:19). Joshua says this to people who have just chosen, and they answer *"No, but we will serve the Lord"* (24:21).
- **It is held by keeping it in view, and by clinging.** *"I have chosen the way of faithfulness; I set your rules before me. I cling to your testimonies, O Lord"* (Psalm 119:30–31). The verb for "cling" is the one used a few verses earlier: *"My soul clings to the dust"* (119:25). The one verb is used of the soul clinging to the dust and of the one who chose clinging to God's testimonies.
- **It is held by keeping and holding fast.** *"who keep my Sabbaths, who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant"* (Isaiah 56:4). The choice stands between a keeping and a holding on.
- **It is held while waiting.** *"May integrity and uprightness preserve me, for I wait for you"* (Psalm 25:21). The psalm ends still waiting and in trouble. The right choice has not ended the trouble.
- **Readiness has to be completed.** *"so that your readiness in desiring it may be matched by your completing it"* (2 Corinthians 8:11).
- **Those God has chosen are told to make it firm.** *"be all the more diligent to confirm your calling and election"* (2 Peter 1:10). See *Being chosen*.
- **It is held as a purpose set ahead.** *"I have purposed that my mouth will not transgress"* (Psalm 17:3). See *Planning*.
- **It can be guarded by another.** Mary *"sat at the Lord's feet and listened to his teaching"* (Luke 10:39). Martha asked Jesus to send her to help (10:40). He named what Mary was doing a choice, and kept it for her: *"Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her"* (10:42).

The choice at Shechem held for a time: *"Israel served the Lord all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the elders who outlived Joshua and had known all the work that the Lord did for Israel"* (Joshua 24:31). The verse ties those years to people who had known the work the choice was made from. It gives the timing; it does not give the cause.

## Planning

A choice settles a direction. A plan carries it ahead, into a time that has not yet come. Scripture gives the inner being this power plainly. Of the builders at Babel God says, *"this is only the beginning of what they will do. And nothing that they propose to do will now be impossible for them"* (Genesis 11:6). The words for it are the words for thinking: to devise, to reckon, to purpose (10.4). They are used for a woman buying a field, a king counting his soldiers, a sailor looking for a beach, and a man plotting on his bed. This section is about the looking ahead itself. Plans made against another person are in 10.10. The next section, *Willing*, is about how a person answers what others put forward. The two often appear in the same passage.

The place of it is the heart: *"The heart of man plans his way, but the Lord establishes his steps"* (Proverbs 16:9). In that one verse the plan is the person's own, and the steps are not. I read the rest of what the verses say about planning inside that verse.

**Weighing first.** Jesus asks his hearers to look ahead before they begin. "For which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it?" (Luke 14:28).
