In the light of a king's face there is life, and his favor is like the clouds that bring the spring rain" (Proverbs 16:14–15). In Jesus' parable the king uses that power to release: "And out of pity for him, the master of that servant released him and forgave him the debt" (Matthew 18:27). The same servant then refused his fellow servant, and the master's anger followed (18:33–34; 10.13).

## Loyalty and honour

Loyalty between people was sworn by life. Ittai to David: "As the Lord lives, and as my lord the king lives, wherever my lord the king shall be, whether for death or for life, there also will your servant be" (2 Samuel 15:21). Elisha to Elijah: "As the Lord lives, and as you yourself live, I will not leave you" (2 Kings 2:2). David's lament says it of Saul and Jonathan: "In life and in death they were not divided" (2 Samuel 1:23). Chapter 2 ("Living before God") gives the oath.

Delight in a person can stand against a father. *"And Saul spoke to Jonathan his son and to all his servants, that they should kill David. But Jonathan, Saul's son, delighted much in David"* (1 Samuel 19:1). The writer names him "Saul's son" just where he stands against Saul. The delight acts. Jonathan warns David (19:2). He stands beside his father in the field (19:3). He speaks well of David: *"Let not the king sin against his servant David"* (19:4). And he reminds Saul of Saul's own joy: *"You saw it, and rejoiced"* (19:5). Saul listens and swears that David shall not be put to death (19:6). Jonathan's bond is named twice: his soul *"knit to the soul of David"* (18:1, above), and here, in the danger, his delight. Saul's turn had begun with a saying that *"displeased him"*, and *"Saul eyed David from that day on"* (18:8–9). I read delight and displeasure about one man, in a son and a father, with the look on the side of displeasure (10.6, *Jealousy and envy*).

Honour is joined to life: "Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land" (Exodus 20:12). And patience with others is named as glory: "Good sense makes one slow to anger, and it is his glory to overlook an offense" (Proverbs 19:11).

A duty can be refused, and the law makes the refusal public. "And if the man does not wish to take his brother's wife, then his brother's wife shall go up to the gate to the elders" (Deuteronomy 25:7). "If he persists, saying, 'I do not wish to take her,' then his brother's wife shall go up to him in the presence of the elders and pull his sandal off his foot and spit in his face" (25:8–9), and "the name of his house shall be called in Israel, 'The house of him who had his sandal pulled off'" (25:10). The act is refusing to build up a dead brother's house. The law does not force the wanting; it names the refusal.

Loyalty can be called for over a body. Joab killed Amasa as he greeted him: "Is it well with you, my brother?" (2 Samuel 20:9). Then one of his men "took his stand by Amasa and said, 'Whoever favors Joab, and whoever is for David, let him follow Joab'" (20:11). "And anyone who came by, seeing him, stopped" (20:12). Once the body was covered, "all the people went on after Joab" (20:13). The act is following. I read that the sight held them, and the covering let them go on.

A people's approval can read a king's heart. David mourned Abner, wept at the grave, and swore not to eat till sunset (2 Samuel 3:31–35). "And all the people took notice of it, and it pleased them, as everything that the king did pleased all the people. So all the people and all Israel understood that day that it had not been the king's will to put to death Abner the son of Ner" (2 Samuel 3:36–37). They watched what he did, were pleased, and understood what he had not willed (10.2).

When David came back over the Jordan, three men met him. Ziba and his men "crossed the ford to bring over the king's household and to do his pleasure" (2 Samuel 19:18). Shimei fell down before him: "Let not my lord hold me guilty or remember how your servant did wrong … For your servant knows that I have sinned" (19:19–20). Mephibosheth had not cared for his feet or beard or clothes since the king left (19:24). Slandered by Ziba, he did not argue his cause: "my lord the king is like the angel of God; do therefore what seems good to you … What further right have I, then, to cry to the king?" (19:27–28). When the land was divided, he said, "Oh, let him take it all, since my lord the king has come safely home" (19:30). I read his loyalty in what he gives up: the king's return is what he holds to, not the land.

Shelter given to guests can be held above one's own. Lot to the men of Sodom: "I beg you, my brothers, do not act so wickedly. Behold, I have two daughters who have not known any man. Let me bring them out to you, and do to them as you please. Only do nothing to these men, for they have come under the shelter of my roof" (Genesis 19:7–8). The verse gives his reason, the shelter of his roof. The men answer, "This fellow came to sojourn, and he has become the judge!" (19:9). The verses record the offer and the reason, and do not weigh them.

Another person's will to take can be met by giving. "And if anyone would sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well … Give to the one who begs from you, and do not refuse the one who would borrow from you" (Matthew 5:40–42). One's own wish is made the measure of what is done to others: "So whatever you wish that others would do to you, do also to them, for this is the Law and the Prophets" (Matthew 7:12; Luke 6:31). I read the wish here as turned outward: what a person wants for himself becomes the measure of what he does for another.

Loyalty can be held even to death, and it can fail there. The spies promise Rahab, "Our life for yours even to death!" (Joshua 2:14). Thomas: "Let us also go, that we may die with him" (John 11:16). Peter says he is "ready to go with you both to prison and to death", and is told he will deny him (Luke 22:33–34). Chapter 2 ("Dying to the Lord") gives these.

Loyalty can fail at its post. David called across to Saul's guard: "Why then have you not kept watch over your lord the king? For one of the people came in to destroy the king your lord. This thing that you have done is not good. As the Lord lives, you deserve to die, because you have not kept watch over your lord, the Lord's anointed" (1 Samuel 26:15–16). David had refused to strike Saul himself (26:9–11). He showed the spear and the jar as proof and asked Saul, "Why does my lord pursue after his servant? For what have I done? What evil is on my hands?" (26:18).

Honour can be yielded. Joab, about to take Rabbah, sent for David: "encamp against the city and take it, lest I take the city and it be called by my name" (2 Samuel 12:28). The crown of the city's king "was placed on David's head" (12:30).

Honour can be shown upward by the one on the throne. When Bathsheba came, "the king rose to meet her and bowed down to her. Then he sat on his throne and had a seat brought for the king's mother, and she sat on his right" (1 Kings 2:19). He promised, "Make your request, my mother, for I will not refuse you" (2:20). Then he refused it (2:22; 10.5).

### Hiding from God

In each scene where a person hides from God, something of God is perceived first: a sound (Genesis 3:10), God naming himself (Exodus 3:6), "the terror of the Lord, and … the splendor of his majesty" (Isaiah 2:10), "the face of him who is seated on the throne, and … the wrath of the Lamb" (Revelation 6:16).
- Adam hid because he knew he was naked (Genesis 3:10).
- Moses "hid his face, for he was afraid to look at God" (Exodus 3:6), and no wrong is named.
- At the end, people call "to the mountains and rocks, 'Fall on us and hide us'", for "who can stand?" (Revelation 6:16–17).

Job names the one condition on which he will not hide: "Only grant me two things, then I will not hide myself from your face: withdraw your hand far from me, and let not dread of you terrify me" (Job 13:20–21). In his words, it is the dread that makes a person hide.

None of it works. "Can a man hide himself in secret places so that I cannot see him? declares the Lord. Do I not fill heaven and earth?" (Jeremiah 23:24). "There is no gloom or deep darkness where evildoers may hide themselves" (Job 34:22). Isaiah names what the attempt does: "Ah, you who hide deep from the Lord your counsel … and who say, 'Who sees us? Who knows us?' You turn things upside down! Shall the potter be regarded as the clay" (Isaiah 29:15–16).

That nothing is hidden from God is the same fact for everyone, and it falls very differently.
- For the one who suffers it is comfort: "O Lord, all my longing is before you; my sighing is not hidden from you" (Psalm 38:9).
- For the one being made it is wonder: "My frame was not hidden from you, when I was being made in secret" (Psalm 139:15), and the psalmist answers, "my soul knows it very well" (139:14).
- For the one who has done wrong it is judgement: "I know Ephraim, and Israel is not hidden from me; for now, O Ephraim, you have played the whore" (Hosea 5:3).

### The hidden trap

In the Psalms a purpose is hidden in order to catch someone. "They hold fast to their evil purpose; they talk of laying snares secretly, thinking, 'Who can see them?'" (Psalm 64:5). The next verse says where the purpose was hidden first: "For the inward mind and heart of a man are deep" (64:6).

A friendly word can be the cover. *"Come and let us meet together"*, Sanballat wrote, *"But they intended to do me harm"* (Nehemiah 6:2). Jeremiah did not see it at all: *"I did not know it was against me they devised schemes"* (Jeremiah 11:19). The psalmist names the arrogant who *"have hidden a trap for me"* (Psalm 140:5). 10.10 (*Plotting against another*) follows what passes between them.

The one it is set for prays out of his weakness. "When my spirit faints within me, you know my way! In the path where I walk they have hidden a trap for me" (Psalm 142:3). "No one cares for my soul" (142:4). It is worse when it comes from those he had prayed for: "Yet they have dug a pit for my life. Remember how I stood before you to speak good for them" (Jeremiah 18:20).

And the trap turns. "In the net that they hid, their own foot has been caught" (Psalm 9:15). The soul the pit was dug for (Psalm 35:7) is the soul that rejoices: "Then my soul will rejoice in the Lord" (35:9). The one taken "out of the net they have hidden for me" says, "Into your hand I commit my spirit" (Psalm 31:4–5).

## Dread laid on others

Fear does not stay with single persons. It falls on peoples and on creatures. In most of these verses God lays it; in Esther no giver is named. The verses say what it led to.
- "The fear of you and the dread of you shall be upon every beast of the earth" (Genesis 9:2).
- "a terror from God fell upon the cities that were around them, so that they did not pursue the sons of Jacob" (Genesis 35:5).
- "Put them in fear, O Lord! Let the nations know that they are but men!" (Psalm 9:20).
- "that their hearts may melt, and many stumble. At all their gates I have given the glittering sword" (Ezekiel 21:15). The melting heart is what the sword is given for (*Fear in the body*, above).

The same dread came to different peoples and ended in different ways.
- **Rahab:** "as soon as we heard it, our hearts melted, and there was no spirit left in any man because of you, for the Lord your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath" (Joshua 2:11).
- **Moab:** "Moab was in great dread of the people, because they were many", and Balak sent for Balaam: "Come now, curse this people for me, since they are too mighty for me" (Numbers 22:3, 6).
- **The peoples in Esther's day:** where the king's second edict reached, "there was gladness and joy among the Jews … And many from the peoples of the country declared themselves Jews, for fear of the Jews had fallen on them" (Esther 8:17). The verse gives fear as the only reason. This dread did not send the peoples away, nor set them against the Jews; it brought many of them over to the name of those they feared. On the day itself, "no one could stand against them, for the fear of them had fallen on all peoples" (9:2; 10.10).

A people can itself be made a horror to others. "I will make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth, to be a reproach, a byword, a taunt, and a curse" (Jeremiah 24:9). "Everyone who passes by it will be horrified and will hiss because of all its wounds" (Jeremiah 19:8). The feeling is in those who pass by. The verses give the reasons in the people's own deeds: "The Lord could no longer bear your evil deeds" (Jeremiah 44:22). The same root, held by the prophet, is his own grief for them: "dismay has taken hold on me" (Jeremiah 8:21).

One phrase passes through many mouths. Jeremiah gave it as a name: "The Lord does not call your name Pashhur, but Terror on Every Side" (Jeremiah 20:3). Then he heard it whispered against himself: "For I hear many whispering. Terror is on every side! 'Denounce him! Let us denounce him!' say all my close friends" (20:10). He answered: "But the Lord is with me as a dread warrior" (20:11). A psalmist heard "the whispering of many" and "terror on every side" (Psalm 31:13), and answered in his own words: "But I trust in you, O Lord; I say, 'You are my God'" (31:14).

Job's friends say that terrors chase the wicked: "Terrors frighten him on every side, and chase him at his heels" (Job 18:11). They say it of Job. God's own verdict stands over them: "you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has" (Job 42:7).

# 10.13 Anger

Scripture never defines anger. It describes what anger does, and it uses the same words for God and for people.
- **It is kindled, burns and is poured.** "So the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel" (Judges 2:20). "At this the king became enraged, and his anger burned within him" (Esther 1:12). "My anger and my wrath will be poured out on this place" (Jeremiah 7:20).
- **It is set off by something heard or seen,** on both sides. "When the Lord heard it, his anger was kindled" (Numbers 11:1). "As soon as his master heard the words that his wife spoke to him … his anger was kindled" (Genesis 39:19). "When Haman saw Mordecai in the king's gate … he was filled with wrath" (Esther 5:9).
- **It moves, and it has a span.** "Wrath has gone out against you from the Lord" (2 Chronicles 19:2). "For his anger is but for a moment, and his favor is for a lifetime" (Psalm 30:5). Edom "kept his wrath forever" (Amos 1:11).
- **It is felt in the body.** "So Cain was very angry, and his face fell" (Genesis 4:5). "There is no soundness in my flesh because of your indignation" (Psalm 38:3).
- **It is drunk.** "You who have drunk from the hand of the Lord the cup of his wrath" (Isaiah 51:17).

The same pictures are used for God and for people. Where the verses mark a difference, they mark it in restraint: "I will not execute my burning anger … for I am God and not a man" (Hosea 11:9).

The verses do say what human anger does not do: "the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God" (James 1:20). And they name anger by its absence: "lifting holy hands without anger or quarreling" (1 Timothy 2:8). Love "is not irritable or resentful" (1 Corinthians 13:5).

blocks.section: A person's anger > Anger in the body
blocks.text:
### Anger in the body

Anger shows, and the verses see it in the teeth.
- "The wicked man sees it and is angry; he gnashes his teeth and melts away" (Psalm 112:10).
- "The wicked plots against the righteous and gnashes his teeth at him" (Psalm 37:12).
- At Stephen's speech, "they were enraged, and they ground their teeth at him" (Acts 7:54). The Greek of "enraged" is *sawn through in their hearts* (Chapter 4). The heart and the teeth are named in one sentence.
- Enemies gloat with it: "All your enemies rail against you; they hiss, they gnash their teeth, they cry: 'We have swallowed her!'" (Lamentations 2:16). Mockers do the same: "like profane mockers at a feast, they gnash at me with their teeth" (Psalm 35:16).
- Job says it of God's anger as he feels it: "He has torn me in his wrath and hated me; he has gnashed his teeth at me" (Job 16:9). It is how the anger looks to the one under it (*Living under God's anger*, below).

The face carries it too. *ʾAph*, anger's own Hebrew word, is also the nostril and the face (Chapter 11). Fear shows in the hands (10.12, *Fear in the body*). The weeping and gnashing of teeth at the judgment is in Chapter 2.

blocks.section: A person's anger > What it does next
blocks.text:
### What it does next

What follows the anger is where the cases differ. The verses follow it into what the person does.
- **The hand acts at once.** Moses "threw the tablets out of his hands and broke them" (Exodus 32:19). Balaam "struck the donkey with his staff" (Numbers 22:27).
- **Where there is power, a command.** Pharaoh "put them in custody" (Genesis 40:3). Nebuchadnezzar "commanded that all the wise men of Babylon be destroyed" (Daniel 2:12). Herod "sent and killed all the male children in Bethlehem" (Matthew 2:16). "A king's wrath is like the growling of a lion" (Proverbs 19:12).
- **Killing.** "For in their anger they killed men" (Genesis 49:6). God asked Cain, "Why are you angry, and why has your face fallen?" (Genesis 4:6), and Cain "rose up against his brother Abel and killed him" (4:8).
- **A watching eye, and a plot.** "And Saul eyed David from that day on" (1 Samuel 18:9). Sanballat and Tobiah "all plotted together" (Nehemiah 4:8). "The wicked plots against the righteous and gnashes his teeth at him" (Psalm 37:12).
- **Rage that wants to kill at once.** The council heard the apostles and "were enraged and wanted to kill them" (Acts 5:33). This is not a plan laid in advance: the wish follows the rage straight away. Gamaliel, "a teacher of the law held in honor by all the people", stopped it by having the men put outside for a little while: "take care what you are about to do with these men" (5:34–35). Plotting is in 10.10.
- **The face falls, and the body withdraws.** Cain's face fell (Genesis 4:5). Jonathan "ate no food the second day of the month" (1 Samuel 20:34).
- **Counsel, and then a charge.** Nehemiah: "I took counsel with myself, and I brought charges against the nobles" (Nehemiah 5:7).
- **Silence, and waiting.** Absalom "spoke to Amnon neither good nor bad" (2 Samuel 13:22). Two years later he had him killed.
- **Prayer.** "And Samuel was angry, and he cried to the Lord all night" (1 Samuel 15:11). The verses give what was behind it: Saul and the people "spared Agag and the best … and would not utterly destroy them" (15:9), and God said, "he has turned back from following me" (15:11).
- **Fear.** After Uzzah was struck, David was angry, and "David was afraid of the Lord that day" (2 Samuel 6:9).
- **Speech that must come out.** Elihu, angry and long silent: "I must speak, that I may find relief" (Job 32:20). Moses at Meribah: "they made his spirit bitter, and he spoke rashly with his lips" (Psalm 106:33).
- **Mercy.** Saul, after the Spirit came on him in anger and the victory was won, said, "Not a man shall be put to death this day" (1 Samuel 11:13).
- **Staying outside.** The elder brother "refused to go in" (Luke 15:28).
- **Strife.** "A hot-tempered man stirs up strife" (Proverbs 15:18). "One given to anger causes much transgression" (Proverbs 29:22).
- **Separation.** Paul and Barnabas: "there arose a sharp disagreement, so that they separated from each other" (Acts 15:39).

Some of these end in harm, and some in counsel, prayer or mercy. The verses do not say anger always leads to one place. They follow each person to where it led.

## Those who carry it out

Some people carry out God's anger, and the verses judge how they do it.
- **Assyria is the rod, and has its own heart:** "Woe to Assyria, the rod of my anger … But he does not so intend, and his heart does not so think; but it is in his heart to destroy" (Isaiah 10:5, 7). He boasts, "By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom" (10:13), and the Lord "will punish the speech of the arrogant heart of the king of Assyria and the boastful look in his eyes" (10:12). "Shall the axe boast over him who hews with it …?" (10:15).
- **Babylon goes too far:** "I gave them into your hand; you showed them no mercy" (Isaiah 47:6). "While I was angry but a little, they furthered the disaster" (Zechariah 1:15).
- **Israel's army goes past the commission:** "you have killed them in a rage that has reached up to heaven" (2 Chronicles 28:9).
- **Saul is judged for not carrying it out:** "Because you did not obey the voice of the Lord and did not carry out his fierce wrath against Amalek, therefore the Lord has done this thing to you this day" (1 Samuel 28:18).
- **The governing authority:** "he is the servant of God, an avenger who carries out God's wrath on the wrongdoer. Therefore one must be in subjection, not only to avoid God's wrath but also for the sake of conscience" (Romans 13:4–5).

## What changes it

The verses show anger changing character with its circumstances.
- **Who is angry.** The same words are used for God and for people, and "for I am God and not a man" (Hosea 11:9) is said in restraint.
- **Whether what sets it off is true.** Potiphar acted on a lie (Genesis 39:19).
- **For whom it burns.** For the widow and fatherless (Exodus 22:24); for the children (Mark 10:14); for one wronged (2 Samuel 12:5).
- **What it is joined with in the verse.** Jealousy (Deuteronomy 6:15); grief, "with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart" (Mark 3:5); the Spirit (1 Samuel 11:6); hatred, "the anger and envy that you showed because of your hatred" (Ezekiel 35:11); fear, "he shall be afraid and withdraw, and shall turn back and be enraged" (Daniel 11:30); compassion set against it (Hosea 11:8–9).
- **Time.** God's "for a moment" (Psalm 30:5) and "finished" (Revelation 15:1); a man's wrath kept "forever" (Amos 1:11); "do not let the sun go down on your anger" (Ephesians 4:26).
- **Power.** The ruler's anger becomes a command (Daniel 2:12).
- **The one who carries it out,** and their own heart (Isaiah 10:7).
- **One and many** (Numbers 16:22; Joshua 7:1).
- **What meets it.** A soft answer, a servants' question, a father who comes out, a counsellor (Proverbs 15:1; 2 Kings 5:13; Luke 15:28; Acts 5:34–35). Or no one: "I looked, but there was no one to help" (Isaiah 63:5).
- **Correction with or without the anger:** "Correct me, O Lord, but in justice; not in your anger" (Jeremiah 10:24).
- **The measure:** "storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath" (Romans 2:5).
- **The same root, rendered as another movement.** *ʿEbrāh* is wrath and pride (Proverbs 21:24). *Kāʿas* is provoking God and Hannah's grief (1 Samuel 1:16). *Ḥēmāh* is wrath and venom (Psalm 140:3). *Paroxysmos* is a sharp disagreement and stirring up to love (Acts 15:39; Hebrews 10:24). *Thymos* is God's wrath and Babylon's passion (Revelation 14:8, 10): "For all nations have drunk the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality" (18:3).

Chapter 11 (§4) gathers what changes the character of a word across all the activities. These are anger's part in it.

## Submitting

**To God.** "Submit yourselves therefore to God" (James 4:7), in the same breath as "Humble yourselves before the Lord" (4:10). James draws no line between them.

Not submitting is told in two ways:
- **Building one's own righteousness:** "seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to God's righteousness" (Romans 10:3).
- **Inability:** "the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God, for it does not submit to God's law; indeed, it cannot" (Romans 8:7). The way out named is the Spirit (8:9).

**To one another, for a reason that faces God.** Submission among people is almost never told without its ground:

| Verse | The ground given |
| --- | --- |
| Ephesians 5:21 | *"out of reverence for Christ"* |
| 1 Peter 2:13 | *"for the Lord's sake"* |
| Romans 13:5 | *"for the sake of conscience"* |
| 1 Peter 2:19 | *"mindful of God"* |
| 1 Peter 3:5 | *"the holy women who hoped in God"* |
| Hebrews 13:17 | the leaders *"are keeping watch over your souls, as those who will have to give an account"* |

Where the passage goes on, it lays a duty on the other side:
- "Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her" (Ephesians 5:25)
- "do not be harsh with them" (Colossians 3:19)
- the elders are "not domineering over those in your charge" (1 Peter 5:3)

**Under wrong.** "be subject to your masters with all respect, not only to the good and gentle but also to the unjust. For this is a gracious thing, when, mindful of God, one endures sorrows while suffering unjustly … because Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example" (1 Peter 2:18–21). Hagar was sent back to a mistress who had dealt harshly with her: "Return to your mistress and submit to her", with "the Lord has listened to your affliction" (Genesis 16:6–11).

**One's own spirit.** "the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets. For God is not a God of confusion but of peace" (1 Corinthians 14:32–33). The one who speaks governs what moves in him.

**The limit.** "to them we did not yield in submission even for a moment, so that the truth of the gospel might be preserved for you" (Galatians 2:5). To false brothers who would bring others into slavery, refusing is the right act. Its ground is given too.

blocks.section: Given, then held as one's own
blocks.text:
## Given, then held as one's own

The clearest thing the verses say about pride is where it comes from. In account after account a person is given something, and the heart rises on it.
- **Strength.** Uzziah "was marvelously helped, till he was strong. But when he was strong, he grew proud, to his destruction" (2 Chronicles 26:15–16).
- **Healing.** Hezekiah was healed and given a sign, and gifts were brought "so that he was exalted in the sight of all nations". Then: "But Hezekiah did not make return according to the benefit done to him, for his heart was proud" (2 Chronicles 32:23–25).
- **Majesty.** "The Most High God gave Nebuchadnezzar your father kingship and greatness and glory and majesty … But when his heart was lifted up and his spirit was hardened so that he dealt proudly, he was brought down from his kingly throne" (Daniel 5:18–20).
- **Wealth.** "By your great wisdom in your trade you have increased your wealth, and your heart has become proud in your wealth" (Ezekiel 28:5).
- **Beauty and height.** Of the great tree God says, "I made it beautiful", and then, "its heart was proud of its height" (Ezekiel 31:9–10). Chapter 12 follows the king of Tyre's beauty the same way.

The law saw it coming: "then your heart be lifted up, and you forget the Lord your God … Beware lest you say in your heart, 'My power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth.' You shall remember the Lord your God, for it is he who gives you power to get wealth" (Deuteronomy 8:14, 17–18). Paul says it as a question: "What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?" (1 Corinthians 4:7).

So the standing in these verses is real. It was given. Pride holds it as if it had not been given. I read that this is the line the verses draw. It does not run between having height and having none. It runs between height that is one's own by nature, height that is given, and height that is taken as one's own.

**It credits its own hand.** The king of Assyria says, "By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom, for I have understanding" (Isaiah 10:13). In the same passage he is the rod in the Lord's hand: "Shall the axe boast over him who hews with it?" (10:5, 15). Nebuchadnezzar: "Is not this great Babylon, which I have built by my mighty power … for the glory of my majesty?" (Daniel 4:30). I read pride here as crediting to itself what was done through it.

**It gives itself the glory.** The great city "glorified herself and lived in luxury" (Revelation 18:7). The Greek verb is the one used where people give glory to God: "so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven" (Matthew 5:16). Here she is the one who gives the glory and the one who receives it. What it brings her is in *Where it ends*, below.

**The same word can name an honour God gives.** "He chose our heritage for us, the pride of Jacob whom he loves" (Psalm 47:4). To a city "forsaken and hated": "I will make you majestic forever, a joy from age to age" (Isaiah 60:15). "The Lord is restoring the majesty of Jacob" (Nahum 2:2). Israel's triumph is the Lord himself: "the sword of your triumph" (Deuteronomy 33:29). Where God chooses, gives or restores it, the word is honour. And what was given can be turned. God's own sanctuary became "the pride of your power, the delight of your eyes, and the yearning of your soul" (Ezekiel 24:21). His beautiful ornament "they used for pride, and they made their abominable images … of it" (Ezekiel 7:20).

## Pride over another

Pride is seldom alone in these verses. It stands over someone.
- **The poor.** "In arrogance the wicked hotly pursue the poor" (Psalm 10:2). "Whoever mocks the poor insults his Maker" (Proverbs 17:5). The mocking reaches past the poor man to the one who made him.
- **The widow.** "The Lord tears down the house of the proud but maintains the widow's boundaries" (Proverbs 15:25).
- **The needy left unaided.** "Behold, this was the guilt of your sister Sodom: she and her daughters had pride, excess of food, and prosperous ease, but did not aid the poor and needy" (Ezekiel 16:49). Pride is listed with plenty and ease, and with what was not done.
- **The righteous.** Lips "which speak insolently against the righteous in pride and contempt" (Psalm 31:18). "The insolent utterly deride me … The insolent smear me with lies … The insolent have dug pitfalls for me" (Psalm 119:51, 69, 85). Against each, the one who bears it holds to the law: "but I do not turn away from your law" (119:51).
- **With the heart closed.** "They close their hearts to pity; with their mouths they speak arrogantly" (Psalm 17:10).
- **Against love.** "'Knowledge' puffs up, but love builds up" (1 Corinthians 8:1). "Love … does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant" (13:4). Conceit goes with provoking and envying: "Let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another" (Galatians 5:26).
- **Where mourning belongs.** "And you are arrogant! Ought you not rather to mourn?" (1 Corinthians 5:2).

It is also felt from below. "Our soul has had more than enough of the scorn of those who are at ease, of the contempt of the proud" (Psalm 123:4). The psalm's answer is to look elsewhere: "our eyes look to the Lord our God, till he has mercy upon us" (123:2). Section 10.10 follows pride between people.

blocks.section: 1. The inner being is acted upon as much as it acts
blocks.text:
## 1. The inner being is acted upon as much as it acts

I expected the heart, soul and spirit to be mainly the doers in the verses. Very often they are the ones being done to.

- **God turns and puts things into hearts.** "The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the Lord; he turns it wherever he will" (Proverbs 21:1). "Blessed be the Lord … who put such a thing as this into the heart of the king" (Ezra 7:27).
- **God stirs spirits.** "The Lord stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia" (Ezra 1:1).
- **God hardens.** "The Lord hardened the heart of Pharaoh king of Egypt" (Exodus 14:8). "The Lord your God hardened his spirit and made his heart obstinate" (Deuteronomy 2:30).
- **Dread is laid on, given, and comes upon.** "The Lord your God will lay the fear of you and the dread of you on all the land that you shall tread" (Deuteronomy 11:25). In the curse, "the Lord will give you there a trembling heart and failing eyes and a languishing soul" (Deuteronomy 28:65). And the verbs make the dread the one that acts: "dread came upon me" (Job 4:14); "trembling has seized the godless" (Isaiah 33:14); "Trembling took hold of them there" (Psalm 48:6); "a great trembling fell upon them" (Daniel 10:7).
- **Others steal, sway and turn hearts.** Absalom told each man who came with a case, "See, your claims are good and right, but there is no man designated by the king to hear you" (2 Samuel 15:3), and so "Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel" (15:6). Solomon's "wives turned away his heart after other gods" (1 Kings 11:4).
- **Things are poured in.** "Satan filled your heart" (Acts 5:3). "God's love has been poured into our hearts" (Romans 5:5).
- **Skill and laws are put in, and minds are blinded.** God fills craftsmen "with skill" to devise (Exodus 35:35). He promises, "I will put my laws into their minds, and write them on their hearts" (Hebrews 8:10). And other powers act on thinking too: "the god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers" (2 Corinthians 4:4).

Kings' hearts are "unsearchable" to their subjects (Proverbs 25:3), yet in God's hand they are like water.

Enticement shows the same thing. The same verb is used for being drawn by several very different enticers. Job asks whether "my heart has been enticed toward a woman" (Job 31:9). False teachers "entice unsteady souls" (2 Peter 2:14). In the heavenly council a spirit offers, "I will entice him", and becomes "a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets" (1 Kings 22:21–22). And God says of unfaithful Israel, "Therefore, behold, I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak tenderly to her" (Hosea 2:14), literally *to her heart*. Then he makes "the Valley of Achor a door of hope" (2:15).

On the night Israel left, "the mind [heart] of Pharaoh and his servants was changed toward the people, and they said, 'What is this we have done, that we have let Israel go from serving us?'" (Exodus 14:5). Then the Lord hardened his heart, "and he pursued" (14:8). The heart had already changed (14:5) before the Lord hardened it (14:8). And I have found no text in which God hardens his own heart.

blocks.section: 2. Thresholds: the merry heart and the sad heart
blocks.text:
## 2. Thresholds: the merry heart and the sad heart

In a number of stories, **a heart made merry with food and wine comes just before a decisive event**.

- Amnon: "Mark when Amnon's heart is merry with wine … then kill him" (2 Samuel 13:28).
- King Ahasuerus: "when the heart of the king was merry with wine, he commanded … to bring Queen Vashti", and when she refused, "his anger burned within him" (Esther 1:10–12).
- The Philistines: "when their hearts were merry, they said, 'Call Samson'", and the house fell (Judges 16:25–30).
- Gibeah: "as they were making their hearts merry, behold, the men of the city … surrounded the house" (Judges 19:22).
- Boaz: "when Boaz had eaten and drunk, and his heart was merry", Ruth came to him and asked him to be her redeemer (Ruth 3:7–9).
- Nabal: "Nabal's heart was merry within him, for he was very drunk". The next morning, "his heart died within him" (1 Samuel 25:36–37).
- Haman leaves Esther's banquet "joyful and glad of heart", sees Mordecai, and builds a gallows (Esther 5:9–14). Between the glad heart and the gallows comes anger: "he was filled with wrath against Mordecai" (5:9), and "all this is worth nothing to me, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king's gate" (5:13).

The same threshold is reached by other roads. Uzziah's heart was lifted by strength, not wine: "when he was strong, he grew proud". When the priests withstood him, "Uzziah was angry" (2 Chronicles 26:16, 19).

What follows in these stories is murder, anger, catastrophe, outrage, redemption, a dead heart and a gallows. The rich fool says the same words to his soul: "Soul … relax, eat, drink, be merry". The next line: "Fool! This night your soul is required of you" (Luke 12:19–20).

There is a counter-pattern: **the sad heart at the feast**. Hannah would not eat. Her husband asked, "why is your heart sad?" After the meal she rose and prayed, and she went away with her face "no longer sad" (1 Samuel 1:8–18). Nehemiah stood before the king "when wine was before him", and the king asked, "Why is your face sad …? This is nothing but sadness of the heart". Nehemiah prayed, then asked, and was given what he asked (Nehemiah 2:1–5). The sad heart at a feast is also a threshold. But what enters there is prayer, and what follows is a gift.

Some refuse the threshold. "Daniel resolved [set on his heart] that he would not defile himself with the king's food, or with the wine that he drank" (Daniel 1:8). Uriah would not go home and feast while the ark and the army camped in the field: "As you live, and as your soul lives, I will not do this thing" (2 Samuel 11:11).

Solomon's people "went to their homes joyful and glad of heart for all the goodness that the Lord had shown" (1 Kings 8:66). The Preacher commands the merry heart and gives God's approval as the reason: "Go, eat your bread with joy, and drink your wine with a merry heart, for God has already approved what you do" (Ecclesiastes 9:7). And eating can carry the soul the other way across the threshold: the angel's bread carried Elijah from wanting to die to walking forty days to Horeb (1 Kings 19:5–8).

## 4. One word, opposite values

Again and again I found a single word for an inner state that is good in one place and bad in another. What decides is not the word but **what the inner being is yielding to, or holding firm against**.

- **A tender heart.** It melts before an enemy and spreads fear to others (Deuteronomy 20:8). But Josiah's heart "was penitent [tender]" before God's word, and God answered him with peace (2 Kings 22:19–20). The same softness is cowardice in one place and repentance in the other.
- **A strong heart.** "Be strong, and let your heart take courage; wait for the Lord!" (Psalm 27:14). With Absalom, the same verb gives his servants the nerve to kill: "be courageous and be valiant" (2 Samuel 13:28). With Pharaoh it is hardening: "I will harden his heart" (Exodus 4:21), literally *strengthen*.
- **A guarded heart.** "Keep your heart with all vigilance" (Proverbs 4:23). Three chapters later the same word describes the adulteress, "wily [guarded] of heart" (Proverbs 7:10).
- **Crushing.** Crushed by an enemy, the spirit collapses (Psalm 143:3–4). Offered to God, a crushed spirit is the very sacrifice he wants: "a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise" (Psalm 51:17).
- **Loving and hating one's own soul** (Chapter 5).
- **Devising.** The same Hebrew verb describes the craftsmen who worked cherubim "skillfully" into the tabernacle curtains (Exodus 26:1) and those who plot. One word for planning means "discretion" (Proverbs 2:11), "evil devices" (Proverbs 12:2), and God's own purpose: "no purpose of yours can be thwarted" (Job 42:2).
- **Planning against.** God says, "I am … devising a plan against you. Return" (Jeremiah 18:11), and the people say, "Come, let us make plots against Jeremiah" (18:18). The word and the "against" are the same. One plan is meant to bring people back, and the other is meant to silence the one who calls them.
- **Purposing.** The verb for purposing (*zāmam*) is the psalmist's resolve: "I have purposed that my mouth will not transgress" (Psalm 17:3). It is the wicked man's plot: "The wicked plots against the righteous" (Psalm 37:12). It is the wise woman's weighing: "She considers a field and buys it" (Proverbs 31:16). And it is God's fixed purpose: "I have purposed; I have not relented" (Jeremiah 4:28). I read the change as following whom it is aimed at: one's own mouth, another's harm, one's own household, or a whole land.
- **Willing.** The Hebrew word for being willing (*ʾāḇâ*) is almost always a "no". It is the guard's refusal to kill the priests (1 Samuel 22:17), David refusing the water for the men's sake (2 Samuel 23:17), Amnon refusing Tamar's plea (2 Samuel 13:14), and Israel refusing God's rest (Isaiah 30:15). God himself is "not willing to destroy" (2 Kings 8:19), and "will not be willing to forgive" the man who blesses himself in his stubbornness (Deuteronomy 29:20). The Greek word runs from Pilate "wishing to satisfy the crowd" (Mark 15:15) to God "not wishing that any should perish" (2 Peter 3:9). Each passage gives the reason: faith, honour, force, fear, grief, covenant, love, a self-blessing heart. I read the change as following what is refused, and for whose sake (10.7, *Willing*).
- **Planning ahead.** The same looking ahead is a king's honest count of his strength (Luke 14:31) and sailors' guess "on the chance that somehow" (Acts 27:12). It is a man's "aim in life" (2 Timothy 3:10) and a plot "to put him to death" (John 11:53). I read the verses as setting the difference beside how much the planner can see. The king can count, the sailors cannot see the reef, and over all of it "the Lord establishes his steps" (Proverbs 16:9).
- **Reckoning.** People misreckon: "we esteemed him stricken" (Isaiah 53:4). God reckons faith "as righteousness" (Genesis 15:6). The law reckons in order to release (Leviticus 25:50). Love refuses to reckon at all: it "is not … resentful" (1 Corinthians 13:5).
- **Likening.** Comparing is how love praises ("I compare you, my love", Song of Songs 1:9), how comfort reaches out (Lamentations 2:13), and how worship ends ("who in the skies can be compared to the Lord?", Psalm 89:6). It is also how pride rises: "I will make myself like the Most High" (Isaiah 14:14).
- **Reasoning.** The Greek word is Mary's honest pondering (Luke 1:29), the disciples' anxious circling (Mark 8:17), and a quarrel (Philippians 2:14; 1 Timothy 2:8).
- **The nose.** The Hebrew word for anger, *ʾaph*, is the nostril where God breathed in life (Genesis 2:7), the face bowed in worship (2 Chronicles 7:3), and the face lifted in pride (Psalm 10:4). It can be given a ring in love (Ezekiel 16:12) or a hook for raging (2 Kings 19:28). "Long of nostrils" is patience, in God and in the wise (Exodus 34:6; Proverbs 14:29).
- **Anger.** Jesus's anger heals (Mark 3:5). A crowd's anger stops its ears and kills (Acts 7:57–58). "Be angry and do not sin" (Ephesians 4:26).
- **Vexation.** It is provocation done to another (1 Samuel 1:6), suffering borne (1:16), and "Sorrow is better than laughter, for by sadness of face the heart is made glad" (Ecclesiastes 7:3).
- **Provoking.** Love "is not irritable" (1 Corinthians 13:5), with the same word that tells believers to "stir up one another to love and good works" (Hebrews 10:24).
- **Overflow.** One Hebrew word, *ʿebrah*, is the overflow of anger and the overflow of pride. God offers it to Job with irony: "Pour out the overflowings of your anger, and look on everyone who is proud and abase him" (Job 40:11). And "'Scoffer' is the name of the arrogant, haughty man who acts with arrogant pride" (Proverbs 21:24), where the word is the same.
- **Lifted up.** One Hebrew word names the heart that grew proud when Uzziah was strong (2 Chronicles 26:16) and Jehoshaphat's heart, "courageous in the ways of the Lord" (2 Chronicles 17:6). One family of words is God's majesty and human pride (Exodus 15:7; Jeremiah 48:29). And the boast moves: "Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom" (Jeremiah 9:23), "but let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me" (9:24). What differs is where the height comes from, and which way it faces (10.15).
- **Glory.** The verb that gives glory to God (Matthew 5:16) is the great city's own: she "glorified herself" (Revelation 18:7). The noun is the glory some take "in their shame" (Philippians 3:19), and two verses later the glory of the body to come, "like his glorious body" (3:21). The same word names glory taken where it does not belong and glory given (10.15).
- **Storm.** The same storm word, *sāʿar*, is the angry king's mind ("the mind of the king of Syria was greatly troubled", 2 Kings 6:11) and the suffering city ("O afflicted one, storm-tossed and not comforted", Isaiah 54:11).
- **Denouncing.** "How can I curse whom God has not cursed?" (Numbers 23:8). But "Whoever says to the wicked, 'You are in the right,' will be cursed by peoples, abhorred by nations" (Proverbs 24:24). The word is empty when it goes against God's verdict, and it lands when it follows justice.
- **A creed.** "Slow to anger" is used in worship, in pleading, in confession, in Jonah's complaint, in praise, in wonder, in announcing judgment, and as the ground for returning (Chapter 10.9).
- **Mourning.** Aaron is forbidden to mourn "lest … wrath come" (Leviticus 10:6). When the wrath has come, mourning is commanded (Jeremiah 4:8).
- **God's hand.** The "mighty hand" brought Israel out (Deuteronomy 6:21) and later fought "against you … in anger" (Jeremiah 21:5).
- **Fear.** One word, *yārēʾ*, "to fear", names the fear that drives a person away from God and the fear of God that keeps a person from sin. In one sentence Moses takes the first away and sets the second in its place: "Do not fear, for God has come to test you, that the fear of him may be before you, that you may not sin" (Exodus 20:20). The same people, with the same word, are afraid of Egypt and then fear the Lord (Exodus 14:10, 31). Turned round, the word describes the one who is feared: "the great and awesome God, who keeps covenant and steadfast love" (Nehemiah 1:5). Beside a choice it has three more faces. It is learned at a feast in the place God chose: "that you may learn to fear the Lord your God always" (Deuteronomy 14:23). It falls on those who hear of presumption punished: "all the people shall hear and fear and not act presumptuously again" (17:13). And it comes as terror on people who resisted God's choice once he made it plain: "Are we all to perish?" (Numbers 17:13). Section 10.1 sets out the word, and 10.7 the faces beside a choice.
- **"Do not fear."** God says it with a reason, and the reason is himself: "for I am with you" (Isaiah 41:10). Joseph says it and refuses to stand in God's place (Genesis 50:19, 21). Jael says it before the tent peg (Judges 4:18). The words are the same. What they are for is not.
- **Trembling and dread.** The Hebrew words for trembling and dread are rendered as fear, and also as "Be angry" (Psalm 4:4), "deeply moved" (2 Samuel 18:33), a heart that "trembled for the ark of God" (1 Samuel 4:13), and "your heart shall thrill and exult" (Isaiah 60:5). I read them as naming one inner stirring, which its situation turns into fear, anger, grief, care or joy (10.1).
- **"None shall make you afraid."** It is promised peace: "I will give peace in the land, and you shall lie down, and none shall make you afraid" (Leviticus 26:6). The same Hebrew phrase is used of desolation: "The cities of Aroer are deserted; they will be for flocks, which will lie down, and none will make them afraid" (Isaiah 17:2). One phrase describes rest for a people and the emptiness left when they are gone.
- **Care.** The Greek *merimnaō*, "to be anxious, to care", is rebuked when it is about my own food and clothing (Matthew 6:25) and praised when it is "genuinely concerned for your welfare" (Philippians 2:20). The Hebrew *dāʾag*, "to be anxious, to dread", is dread of what may come (Jeremiah 38:19), a father's worry for his son (1 Samuel 10:2), and sorrow for sin: "I am sorry for my sin" (Psalm 38:18). Section 10.1 sets this out.
- **Hiding.** The Hebrew *sātar*, "to hide", is God hiding a person in safety and God hiding his face, four verses apart (Psalm 27:5, 9), and a sinner asking God to hide his face from his sins (Psalm 51:9). A treasure is hidden "in his joy", and a talent hidden because "I was afraid" (Matthew 13:44; 25:25). Sections 10.9 and 10.11.
- **Murmuring.** The Hebrew *rāgan* is the people's complaint "in your tents" against God (Deuteronomy 1:27) and the whisperer's words that separate friends (Proverbs 16:28) (10.5).
- **Remembering.** It bows the soul down and it gives hope, in two consecutive verses (Lamentations 3:20–21; Chapter 10.3).
- **The bed.** It is the same place, but what happens there goes either way. "He plots trouble while on his bed" (Psalm 36:4). "I remember you upon my bed, and meditate on you in the watches of the night" (Psalm 63:6).
- **"Good" or "evil" in your eyes.** Joshua leaves the choice to the people's own sight: "if it is evil in your eyes to serve the Lord, choose this day" (Joshua 24:15). The king honours an old man's sight: "whatever seems good to you" (2 Samuel 19:38). In Isaiah the measure is the Lord's: "you did what was evil in my eyes" (Isaiah 65:12). Section 10.7 sets this out.
- **Knowing good and evil.** It is the child's knowing "how to refuse the evil and choose the good" (Isaiah 7:15). It is Barzillai's palate at eighty, with the same words: "Can I discern what is pleasant and what is not?" (2 Samuel 19:35). And it is the weighing of words in a dispute: "Let us choose what is right; let us know among ourselves what is good" (Job 34:4).
- **Refusing.** The Hebrew *māʾas*, "to refuse, reject, despise", is refusing the evil (Isaiah 7:15) and refusing "the waters of Shiloah that flow gently" (8:6). Elihu uses it of refusing God's terms (Job 34:33). Job turns it on himself: "therefore I despise myself, and repent" (42:6).
- **Choosing.** The Hebrew *bāḥar*, "to choose", is the choice of a master (Joshua 24:15), of a place to live (Deuteronomy 23:16), of a way (Psalm 119:30; Isaiah 66:3), of wisdom over silver (Proverbs 16:16), and of a verdict (Job 34:4).
- **Delight.** The Hebrew *ḥāpēṣ*, "to delight in", is the soul's own delight in what it chose: "their soul delights in their abominations" (Isaiah 66:3). It is also the Lord's delight as the measure of a choice. That delight is not met when people "chose what I did not delight in" (65:12), and met in those "who choose the things that please me" (56:4). The noun *ḥēpheṣ* names his settled purpose: "he shall fulfill all my purpose" (Isaiah 44:28). It names what a man cares about, and that stops at his death: "what do they care for their houses after them" (Job 21:21).
- **Good, said of the eye.** "Whoever has a bountiful eye will be blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor" (Proverbs 22:9). "Bountiful" is literally "good" (10.6).
- **God's delight in a person.** It is the thanks of the rescued: "he rescued me, because he delighted in me" (Psalm 18:19). It is the mockers' taunt over a sufferer: "let him rescue him, for he delights in him!" (Psalm 22:8). The claim is the same. The sufferer does not answer the mockers; he answers God: "Yet you are he who took me from the womb" (22:9) (13.1).
- **An offering.** "For you will not delight in sacrifice, or I would give it" (Psalm 51:16). Three verses on: "then will you delight in right sacrifices, in burnt offerings and whole burnt offerings" (51:19). It is the same offering. Between the two stands "a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise" (51:17) (13.1).
- **Being well pleased.** The Greek *eudokeō* is the Father's word over the Son: "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased" (Matthew 3:17). It is also Paul's word for weaknesses he had pleaded three times to lose: "I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities" (2 Corinthians 12:10). Between his pleading and his contentment stands the answer, "My grace is sufficient for you" (12:9) (10.1).
- **Choosing a person.** God chooses "before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him" (Ephesians 1:4). He chooses people who are "blind, yet have eyes" (Isaiah 43:8, 10), and "those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith" (James 2:5). People choose by what they can already see: "men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom" (Acts 6:3). Section 10.7 sets this out.
- **Holiness.** It is the purpose of being chosen: "that we should be holy and blameless before him" (Ephesians 1:4). It is also a name the chosen already carry, while the inner qualities are still to be put on: "Put on then, as God's chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts" (Colossians 3:12). The verses do not say how the two fit.
- **Desire beside a choice.** The soul's desire for meat is given room away from the place God chose: "you may eat within your towns whenever you desire" (Deuteronomy 12:21). The same words for the soul's desire draw a Levite to that place: "he may come when he desires" (18:6). And the soul's delight goes with a wrong choice: "These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations" (Isaiah 66:3). Section 10.7 sets this out.
- **Despising.** Michal "despised him in her heart" when she saw the chosen king dancing before the Lord (2 Samuel 6:16). The same verb describes the servant, "one deeply despised", before whom kings will bow (Isaiah 49:7). People despise the chosen people, judging that God has rejected them (Jeremiah 33:24). And the chosen people themselves "despised the pleasant land" (Psalm 106:24). Each verse gives its own ground: honour before people, a verdict drawn from ruin, no faith in the promise.
- **Knowing that a choice was made.** Peter's hearers know it, and a quarrel ends in silence: "you know that in the early days God made a choice among you" (Acts 15:7, 12). Paul knows it of others from what he saw: "we know … that he has chosen you, because our gospel came to you not only in word, but also in power" (1 Thessalonians 1:4–5). Cyrus is called for the sake of the chosen "though you do not know me" (Isaiah 45:4). The world hates the chosen "because they do not know him who sent me" (John 15:21).
- **Precious.** The Hebrew *yāqār* is wisdom weighed above *"nothing you desire"* (Proverbs 3:15), the word *"rare in those days"* (1 Samuel 3:1), a visit kept *seldom* (Proverbs 25:17), *"the moon moving in splendor"* that entices a heart (Job 31:26–27), a name *"highly esteemed"* (1 Samuel 18:30), *"the lordly price"* set on a shepherd (Zechariah 11:13), and a son *"dear"* while spoken against (Jeremiah 31:20). The Greek *timios* is faith tested by fire (1 Peter 1:7), the blood of Christ (1:19), and the jewels of Babylon (Revelation 17:4). What differs is who values, what the thing is weighed against, and whether its worth is known: man does not know wisdom's worth (Job 28:13), and Saul would not give the esteem the others gave (1 Samuel 18:29–30). (10.6 *Precious*.)
- **Imperishable.** The Greek *aphthartos* and its noun name what the dead are raised: "the dead will be raised imperishable" (1 Corinthians 15:52). The same words name love, "love incorruptible" (Ephesians 6:24), the seed of new birth (1 Peter 1:23), an inheritance (1:4), "the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit" (3:4), the wreath that self-control runs for (1 Corinthians 9:25), and God himself, "immortal, invisible" (1 Timothy 1:17). (Chapter 2, *Changed*; 13.1, *Immortal*.)
- **Writhing.** The Hebrew *ḥûl*, "to twist, writhe", is a woman in labour ("Writhe and groan, O daughter of Zion, like a woman in labor", Micah 4:10), the earth before God ("tremble before him, all the earth!", Psalm 96:9), and the heart in anguish (Psalm 55:4). It is also the daughters of Shiloh who come out "to dance in the dances" (Judges 21:21), "a whirling tempest" (Jeremiah 23:19), and patient waiting: "Be still before the Lord and wait patiently for him" (Psalm 37:7). Struck people can be without it: "You have struck them down, but they felt no anguish" (Jeremiah 5:3). One twisting is pain, trembling, birth, the dance and waiting (10.12, *Fear in the body*).

blocks.section: 4. One word, opposite values > What changes the character
blocks.text:
### What changes the character

A word, or an activity, does not carry its value inside itself. The same act changes character with its circumstances. When I set the cases side by side, the verses themselves point to what makes the difference. I give these as what I have found so far, not as a fixed list.

- **Which way it faces.** For someone or against them. "Discretion will watch over you" (Proverbs 2:11). "All their thoughts are against me for evil" (Psalm 56:5). But "against" alone does not decide it. God's plan against a nation is open to its turning: "if that nation … turns from its evil, I will relent" (Jeremiah 18:8). What decides is what the act is *for*.
- **The company it keeps.** Discretion keeps company with knowledge and prudence (Proverbs 1:4; 8:12), the evil device with arrogance and pride (Psalm 10:2, 4) and a quick temper (Proverbs 14:17). Plans are established by counsel (Proverbs 20:18) and by being committed to the Lord (16:3). Whispering together makes a plot (Psalm 41:7).
- **The state of the heart it rises from.** The same tender heart is cowardice in one place and repentance in another (Deuteronomy 20:8; 2 Kings 22:19, above). Paul names the order of cause: people are "darkened in their understanding … due to their hardness of heart" (Ephesians 4:18).
- **Ease or distress.** "In the thought of one who is at ease there is contempt for misfortune" (Job 12:5). Under suffering, God's reckoning is felt as enmity: "Why do you hide your face and count me as your enemy?" (Job 13:24). This is still a small set of verses, and I hold it loosely.
- **Distress turns people both ways.** In distress Manasseh "humbled himself greatly" (2 Chronicles 33:12), and Ahaz "became yet more faithless" (28:22). The texts set the cases side by side without saying why. Under siege, "The hands of compassionate women have boiled their own children" (Lamentations 4:10; 10.10). Ease cuts both ways too: "I am exceedingly angry with the nations that are at ease" (Zechariah 1:15).
- **What it is joined with.** Anger joined with grief heals (Mark 3:5). Joined with jealousy, it "will accept no compensation" (Proverbs 6:34–35).
- **How long it lasts.** For anger, time is part of what it is. It is to end before sunset (Ephesians 4:26). It turns away as a brother forgets (Genesis 27:45). God's is "but for a moment" (Psalm 30:5). Edom "kept his wrath forever" (Amos 1:11).
- **Whether it is seen truly.** Anger kindled by a lie still acts (Genesis 39:19). The heavy hand of God, felt from fear, is misread (Matthew 25:24–25).
- **The answer it meets.** "A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger" (Proverbs 15:1). A question, or a new way of seeing, does more than a rebuke (Genesis 4:6; 45:8; Luke 15:32).
- **What the one who brings it brings first.** The same offering is refused and then delighted in, and what comes between is a broken heart (Psalm 51:16–19, §4 above). The same weakness is pleaded against and then pleases, and what comes between is God's answer (2 Corinthians 12:8–10).
- **Haste or a pause.** "Everyone who is hasty comes only to poverty" (Proverbs 21:5). "Be not quick in your spirit to become angry" (Ecclesiastes 7:9). "The heart of the righteous ponders how to answer" (Proverbs 15:28).
- **Where it happens.** The bed holds plotting and prayer (Psalm 36:4; 63:6). But one place does change what thinking can see: "until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end" (Psalm 73:17).
- **What it is turned toward.** At the sea "they feared greatly" as Egypt marched (Exodus 14:10). After the crossing, "the people feared the Lord, and they believed in the Lord" (14:31). The sailors "were afraid" in the storm, and when the sea was calm "the men feared the Lord exceedingly" (Jonah 1:5, 16). Fear of man is set against him: "who are you that you are afraid of man who dies … and have forgotten the Lord, your Maker" (Isaiah 51:12–13). The same holds for refusing and choosing. Refusing the evil is right and refusing the gentle waters is wrong (Isaiah 7:15; 8:6). The act is the same, and what it is aimed at decides. The one knowing is turned to right and wrong, to taste and to judgement (Isaiah 7:15; 2 Samuel 19:35; Job 34:4). The one verb for choosing is turned to whatever is set before a person (10.7). The soul's desire is allowed for meat in the towns and for the Levite's coming to the chosen place (Deuteronomy 12:21; 18:6), and the soul's delight in abominations goes with a wrong choice (Isaiah 66:3).
- **Whether the heart is in it.** Fear of God can be "a commandment taught by men" while "their hearts are far from me" (Isaiah 29:13). God promises the other: "I will put the fear of me in their hearts, that they may not turn from me" (Jeremiah 32:40).
- **Who chooses.** When God chooses a person, the inner life is what the choosing is for: "that you may know and believe me and understand" (Isaiah 43:10). When people choose a person, the inner life is what they choose by (Acts 6:3, 5). The same verb is used of both (10.7).
- **Whose eyes, and whose delight.** "Evil in your eyes" is where turning from the Lord could begin (Joshua 24:15), and "good to you" is a choice the king honours (2 Samuel 19:38). In Joshua the choice is between the Lord and other gods. With Barzillai it is where an old man who served will live. Delight is the soul's own in Isaiah 66:3 and the Lord's in 65:12 and 56:4. The word is the same; whose it is decides (10.7). When God chooses, the people around often hold another measure: "everyone doing whatever is right in his own eyes" (Deuteronomy 12:8), "before the eyes of his servants' female servants" (2 Samuel 6:20), "in their sight" (Jeremiah 33:24), "rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen" (1 Peter 2:4). The words "what seems good to you" carry different acts: loyalty in Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 19:27), fear in the rulers before Jehu (2 Kings 10:5), a cover in the men of Jabesh (1 Samuel 11:10), a people handed over in a king's word (Esther 3:11), and yielding to God in Eli and David (1 Samuel 3:18; 2 Samuel 15:26). The words are the same; the setting decides (10.7, 10.10, 10.11).
- **Who speaks it, and to what end.** The same words of comfort, "do not fear", come from God, from a friend, and from one who means harm (§4 above; 10.5; 10.10).
- **Whose mouth it is in.** That God delights in a man is thanks from the one rescued and a taunt from those who watch him suffer (Psalm 18:19; 22:8, §4 above).
- **Who hears it.** The same scroll was read to the officials and to the king. The officials "turned one to another in fear" (Jeremiah 36:16). The king and his servants "who heard all these words" were not afraid (36:24).
- **Whether it pulls the person to many things or to one.** Martha was "anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary" (Luke 10:41–42). Paul wants "undivided devotion to the Lord" (1 Corinthians 7:35). The double-minded man is "unstable in all his ways" (James 1:8).
- **Who acts on whom.** God hiding a person is safety, and God hiding his face is dismay (Psalm 27:5, 9). Losing heart is always done by another (10.1).
- **Whether it is brought before God.** "When I am afraid, I put my trust in you" (Psalm 56:3). Many cares, met by his consolations (Psalm 94:19). Anxiety made known to God, and his peace guarding the heart (Philippians 4:6–7). Thoughts offered to be searched (Psalm 139:23). Thoughts taken "captive to obey Christ" (2 Corinthians 10:5).
- **What comes back.** What is devised returns on the deviser (Esther 9:25; Micah 2:1–3), and the diligent plan returns as abundance (Proverbs 21:5).
- **What it is set against.** "To live" is said of a span of years, of escaping hunger or the sword, of recovering from illness, of the dead given life again, and of the heart and spirit revived (Chapter 2). The verses pair it with what it escapes: "that we may live and not die" (Genesis 42:2); "so turn, and live" (Ezekiel 18:32); "why will you die, O house of Israel?" (33:11). The breath God gives can come back out of a person as lies: "a false witness breathes out lies" (Proverbs 14:5).
- **What brings it about, and who acts.** "Die" is said of the body's end, of a sentence passed by people, of a judgment from God, of the end of a way taken, and of something that happens inside a living person: "sin came alive and I died" (Romans 7:9); "Whoever does not love abides in death" (1 John 3:14). It is said of a death undergone on purpose: "How can we who died to sin still live in it?" (Romans 6:2). It is said of a death that belongs to the Lord: "if we die, we die to the Lord" (Romans 14:8). The verses name what brings death: sin (Romans 5:12), "vexation" and "jealousy" (Job 5:2), "the desire of the sluggard" (Proverbs 21:25), and God, who says "I kill and I make alive" (Deuteronomy 32:39). "Put to death" is said both of executing a person and of "what is earthly in you" (Colossians 3:5). "Dead dog" is said of oneself in lowliness (2 Samuel 9:8) and of another in contempt (2 Samuel 16:9). Chapter 2 gives the account.
- **Who swears it, and what for.** "As the Lord lives" is said in loyalty (2 Kings 2:2), in anger (2 Samuel 12:5), in a rash vow the people overturn (1 Samuel 14:39, 45), and on the way to greed (2 Kings 5:20). The words stay the same. The verses give the measure: "in truth, in justice, and in righteousness" (Jeremiah 4:2).
- **What it is joined to.** "Long" is days promised with honouring parents (Exodus 20:12), the wicked who "prolongs his life in his evildoing" (Ecclesiastes 7:15), and, with anger, patience: "Good sense makes one slow to anger" (Proverbs 19:11). "Life" is something loathed (Job 10:1), and in Elihu's words it is itself what loathes: "his life loathes bread" (Job 33:20).
- **Who rouses, and toward what.** The same word for rousing is used when God rouses himself (Zechariah 2:13) and when he is begged to (Psalm 44:23). It is used when God stirs a spirit to build (Ezra 1:5) or to destroy (Jeremiah 51:1, 11), and when hatred stirs up strife (Proverbs 10:12). Love is not to be stirred "until it pleases" (Song of Songs 2:7). Its power shows when it is withheld: God "did not stir up all his wrath" (Psalm 78:38). And some things cannot be roused at all: the dead man "till the heavens are no more" (Job 14:12), and the idol with "no breath at all in it" (Habakkuk 2:19). Haggai gives the order on the building side: obedience, the fear of the Lord, "I am with you", then the stirring, then the work (Haggai 1:12–14; 13.1, *Stirring*).
- **Before whom it is said, and what it rests on.** "Eat, drink, be merry" is folly in the rich man who says it to his own soul over goods laid up (Luke 12:19–20), and it is commended by the Preacher as "his lot" in "the few days of his life that God has given him" (Ecclesiastes 5:18; 8:15). The words are nearly the same (10.6).
- **Whose jealousy, and for whom.** Jealousy is God's for his people against those who scorned them (Ezekiel 36:5), and over his people's own spirit, met with grace (James 4:5–6). It is Elijah's for God (1 Kings 19:10), Joshua's for Moses, refused by Moses (Numbers 11:29), a husband's that will take no compensation (Proverbs 6:34–35), and envy of the wicked that embitters the soul (Psalm 73:3, 21). The word stays the same. What differs is whose it is, whom it is for, and whether it wants God's gift kept narrow (10.6; 13.1). Zeal can be sincere, aimed at God and still wrong for lack of knowledge (Romans 10:2; Philippians 3:6). It consumes the one who has it (Psalm 69:9). It can be put on show (2 Kings 10:16), or set an oath aside (2 Samuel 21:2). Against a person it spoils what it cannot take (Genesis 26:14–15) and claims equality (Numbers 16:3; Psalm 106:16). A husband's jealousy, which may be wrong, is put before God (Numbers 5:14, 30).
- **What it is aimed at.** Job rouses himself against the godless and is upright in it (Job 17:8). He disowns rousing himself at an enemy's ruin (31:29). It is the same act of rousing oneself (10.10).
- **When the cost appears.** The nearer redeemer was willing for the land and unwilling when Ruth came with it (Ruth 4:4–6). The will turned when his own inheritance was touched (10.7).
- **Whose will, and whether it can carry itself out.** The same verb, "want", is a will that wants the good and cannot do it (Romans 7:19), a will asked out by Jesus, "What do you want me to do for you?" (Mark 10:51), a will made absolute (Daniel 11:3), a will that gives way to a crowd (Luke 23:25), and a will taken up and turned, "If anyone would be first" (Mark 9:35). Willing God's will comes before knowing it (John 7:17) (10.7).
- **Whom the need is spoken to.** The same thirst accuses Moses at Rephidim (Exodus 17:3) and asks God at Lehi (Judges 15:18) (10.6).

- **Whose desire, and whether rule stands beside it.** *tĕšûqāh*: "Your desire shall be for your husband, and he shall rule over you" (Genesis 3:16); sin's "desire is for you, and you must rule over it" (4:7); "I am my beloved's, and his desire is for me" (Song of Songs 7:10) (10.6).
- **What the panting reaches for.** The verb for panting or longing is used of a worn slave who "longs for the shadow" (Job 7:2), of the thirsty who "pant after his wealth" (Job 5:5), of the sun that "hastens" (Ecclesiastes 1:5), of the wild donkey "sniffing the wind" (Jeremiah 2:24), of the psalmist who pants for the commandments (Psalm 119:131), and of God, who will "gasp and pant" like a woman in labour (Isaiah 42:14). What it reaches for decides its character (10.6; 13.1; 13.4).

- **Who lowers whom, and before whom.** A king humbling himself before God is answered (2 Chronicles 12:7). A people humbled by God may turn or harden (2 Chronicles 33:12; 28:22). A nation humbled by an enemy is only "subdued" (Judges 3:30). The noun for humility toward one another also names a self-made severity that puffs a person up (Colossians 2:18, 23), and submission is right before God and wrong to those who would enslave the gospel (Galatians 2:5) (10.14).
- **The story around it.** A single verse rarely settles which face a word wears. Jeremiah 18:8–18 does, and so does Genesis 50:20.

I find this freeing. Scripture does not hand me a list of good feelings and bad feelings, or good thoughts and bad thoughts. Each new part of the inner life I read adds to this list, and I expect it to grow.

blocks.section: 8. God has a heart and a soul
blocks.text:
## 8. God has a heart and a soul

The inner words are not only for humans. Scripture gives God a heart and a soul, and lets them act.

- "It grieved him to his heart" (Genesis 6:6).
- "My heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender" (Hosea 11:8).
- "I will rejoice in doing them good … with all my heart and all my soul" (Jeremiah 32:41).
- "My soul delights" in his chosen servant (Isaiah 42:1). "My soul hates" empty feasts held with bloodied hands (Isaiah 1:14–15).
- He swears "by himself" (Amos 6:8), literally by his soul.
- He "does not afflict from his heart" (Lamentations 3:33).
- He holds back his anger for reasons of his own: "I will not execute my burning anger … for I am God and not a man" (Hosea 11:9).
- And the one place where his inner self turns away from a people is not hardness: "Though Moses and Samuel stood before me, yet my heart would not turn toward this people" (Jeremiah 15:1).

Leviticus 26 shows God's soul and the people's soul in a movement back and forth. God promises: "my soul shall not abhor you" (26:11). The people's "soul abhors my rules" (26:15). God answers in kind: "my soul will abhor you" (26:30). Then, at the end, God breaks the exchange: "Yet for all that … I will not spurn them, neither will I abhor them so as to destroy them utterly and break my covenant with them" (26:44). The same verb passes between two souls, and God refuses to return it a final time.

God also thinks and plans. "The counsel of the Lord stands forever, the plans of his heart to all generations" (Psalm 33:11). "My thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways" (Isaiah 55:8). Where human plans and his cross, his stand: "As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good" (Genesis 50:20). Even a cold calculation can be taken up into his purpose. Caiaphas reckoned "that it is better for you that one man should die for the people" (John 11:50). John adds: "He did not say this of his own accord, but being high priest that year he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation" (11:51).

And God speaks in his heart. After the flood, "the Lord said in his heart, 'I will never again curse the ground because of man, for the intention of man's heart is evil from his youth'" (Genesis 8:21). Before the flood he saw "that every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually" (6:5), and "the Lord regretted that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him to his heart" (6:6). Now he names it again, and it is the reason he gives for holding back.

God names his heart with a place. "I have consecrated this house that you have built, by putting my name there forever. My eyes and my heart will be there for all time" (1 Kings 9:3; 13.1, *Choosing*).

## The heart as the source

- "The Lord saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually" (Genesis 6:5).
- "The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?" (Jeremiah 17:9).
- "For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false witness, slander" (Matthew 15:19). What defiles comes "from within, out of the heart of man" (Mark 7:21).
- "The sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron; with a point of diamond it is engraved on the tablet of their heart" (Jeremiah 17:1).
- "Transgression speaks to the wicked deep in his heart" (Psalm 36:1).

The word translated "intention" in Genesis 6:5 is *yēṣer*: the inclination or shape of the heart (Chapter 10.4). It returns straight after the flood: "the intention of man's heart is evil from his youth" (Genesis 8:21). But there God says it in his heart as the reason he will not curse the ground again. Scripture sets the evil inclination beside God's forbearance, not only beside his judgement. I do not want to quote Genesis 6:5 without 8:21.

The heart is the place where wrongdoing starts, is stored and is written. It is also where God looks when he judges: "I the Lord search the heart and test the mind" (Jeremiah 17:10).

The psalm names the inner self with a word that elsewhere means desire: *"there is no truth in their mouth; their inmost self is destruction; their throat is an open grave; they flatter with their tongue"* (Psalm 5:9). In Proverbs the same word is the captor: *"the treacherous are taken captive by their lust"* (Proverbs 11:6; 10.6).

The Preacher says the heart's state lasts as long as the life: "the hearts of the children of man are full of evil, and madness is in their hearts while they live, and after that they go to the dead" (Ecclesiastes 9:3). The psalmist asks not to be judged, "for no one living is righteous before you" (Psalm 143:2). Paul traces a life cut off from God to the heart: "alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them, due to their hardness of heart" (Ephesians 4:18). Chapter 2 ("Life weighed", "Death in the living") gives the setting.

## The heart deceives its owner

The heart does not only do wrong. It hides the wrong from the person whose heart it is.

- "The pride of your heart has deceived you" (Obadiah 3).
- "A deluded heart has led him astray" (Isaiah 44:20), said of the man who bows to a block of wood.
- The heart says to itself what is not true: "There is no God" (Psalm 14:1). "My power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth" (Deuteronomy 8:17).
- It tells itself it is unseen: "God has forgotten, he has hidden his face, he will never see it" (Psalm 10:11). "You felt secure in your wickedness; you said, 'No one sees me'" (Isaiah 47:10).
- What it fails to say is also telling: "They do not say in their hearts, 'Let us fear the Lord our God'" (Jeremiah 5:24).
- It hides a purpose to catch another: "They hold fast to their evil purpose; they talk of laying snares secretly, thinking, 'Who can see them?'" The next verse says where it was hidden first: "For the inward mind and heart of a man are deep" (Psalm 64:5–6). The trap set in the path was first planned in the heart: "who plan evil things in their heart" (Psalm 140:2, 5). Section 10.11 follows the hidden trap and the wrong that is concealed.
- Its evil hides behind the mouth: "His speech was smooth as butter, yet war was in his heart" (Psalm 55:21). "Like the glaze covering an earthen vessel are fervent lips with an evil heart" (Proverbs 26:23).

blocks.section: Pride and the lifted-up heart and spirit
blocks.text:
## Pride and the lifted-up heart and spirit

Pride is placed in the heart and in the spirit. The whole account of pride, with the boast and the mock, is in 10.15. Here I keep what shows the inner being going wrong.

- The heart is "lifted up" (Deuteronomy 8:14). "Everyone who is arrogant in heart is an abomination to the Lord" (Proverbs 16:5).
- "Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall" (Proverbs 16:18). The next verse: "It is better to be of a lowly spirit with the poor than to divide the spoil with the proud" (16:19).
- Of Nebuchadnezzar: "when his heart was lifted up and his spirit was hardened so that he dealt proudly, he was brought down from his kingly throne" (Daniel 5:20).

Pride is also a false likeness. "You said in your heart, 'I will ascend to heaven … I will make myself like the Most High'" (Isaiah 14:13–14). The prince of Tyre: "you have said, 'I am a god'" (Ezekiel 28:2). The opposite mistake shrinks God to my size: "you thought that I was one like yourself" (Psalm 50:21). Either way, thinking has gone wrong at the point of comparing. Mary sings of what God does with it: "he has scattered the proud in the thoughts of their hearts" (Luke 1:51).

Pride can grow from a beauty that was given. Of the great tree: *"I made it beautiful in the mass of its branches, and all the trees of Eden envied it"* (Ezekiel 31:9); *"Because it towered high and set its top among the clouds, and its heart was proud of its height"* (31:10). The others envied the gift, and the tree was proud of it (10.6). Section 10.15 shows the same order with strength, healing, wealth and majesty: given, then held as one's own.

The king of Tyre is lamented in the same way. *"You were in Eden, the garden of God; every precious stone was your covering"* (Ezekiel 28:13). *"You were blameless in your ways from the day you were created, till unrighteousness was found in you"* (28:15). *"In the abundance of your trade you were filled with violence in your midst, and you sinned"* (28:16). *"Your heart was proud because of your beauty; you corrupted your wisdom for the sake of your splendor"* (28:17). The covering was prepared for him on the day he was made. The heart took the beauty as its ground, and wisdom was spent for splendour. I read the order the verses give: given, blameless, then trade, violence and a proud heart.

The human spirit is judged here beside the heart. Pride and humility are where the spirit is weighed: haughty or lowly, proud or poor in spirit.

The counterpart is humbling oneself (10.14). Hezekiah "humbled himself for the pride of his heart" (2 Chronicles 32:26), the verse after "his heart was proud" (32:25). Belshazzar knew what had come of his father's lifted-up heart, and was told, "you … have not humbled your heart, though you knew all this" (Daniel 5:22). The day against pride is named for its end: "The haughty looks of man shall be brought low, and the lofty pride of men shall be humbled, and the Lord alone will be exalted in that day" (Isaiah 2:11).

Death brings pride down. In Isaiah's taunt over the king of Babylon (Isaiah 14:4), the dead greet him: "You too have become as weak as we! You have become like us! Your pomp is brought down to Sheol, the sound of your harps; maggots are laid as a bed beneath you, and worms are your covers" (14:10–11).
